conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Graves' disease (most common) · toxic multinodular goitre · toxic adenoma · thyroiditis · excess T4 · TSH-secreting adenoma
TSH receptor antibody (TRAb/TSHR-Ab) — stimulates TSH receptor → autonomous T4/T3 production
Proptosis/exophthalmos · lid retraction · lid lag · ophthalmoplegia · chemosis · corneal exposure
Non-pitting brawny oedema of shins — glycosaminoglycan deposition
TSH (suppressed) + free T4/T3 (raised) + TRAb
Pregnancy · breastfeeding · active moderate-severe thyroid eye disease
Blocks thyroid peroxidase → inhibits synthesis of T4/T3 (takes 4–8 weeks to deplete stores)
Agranulocytosis (urgent FBC if sore throat) · acute pancreatitis · teratogenic
Fever >38.5°C · HR >140 · AF · confusion/agitation · vomiting · ↑↑ T4/T3. Treat: PTU + beta-blocker + iodine (Lugol's) + dexamethasone + IVF.
PTU in 1st trimester (carbimazole → aplasia cutis). Carbimazole 2nd/3rd (PTU → hepatotoxicity).
Propranolol — symptom control (tremor, palpitations, anxiety) while awaiting definitive treatment
Low T3 (normal/low T4, normal TSH) in acute illness — do NOT treat
Both hyperthyroid (excess iodine) and hypothyroid (Wolff-Chaikoff effect). Check TFTs every 6 months.
Suppressed TSH with normal free T4/T3. Treat if TSH <0.1 + cardiac risk/osteoporosis.
De Quervain's (painful, post-viral) · silent/postpartum (painless, autoimmune) · Hashimoto's thyrotoxic phase
Excess thyroid hormone production causing increased metabolic rate — commonest cause: Graves' disease (autoimmune, TSH receptor antibody-stimulating).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Graves' disease (~75%) — autoimmune, TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies (TSI/TRAb). Mainly women aged 20–40.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What are the clinical features of hyperthyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Weight loss despite good appetite; heat intolerance/sweating; palpitations/tachycardia/AF; tremor; anxiety/irritability; diarrhoea; oligomenorrhoea; proximal myopathy; onycholysis; pretibial myxoedema (Graves' specific).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What signs are specific to Graves' disease (not other causes)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Graves-specific: exophthalmos (proptosis), pretibial myxoedema (orange-peel skin on shins), thyroid acropachy (clubbing). Diffuse goitre.
Autoimmune orbital inflammation in Graves' — TSH receptor antibodies cross-react with orbital fibroblasts → glycosaminoglycan deposition → proptosis, lid lag, diplopia, corneal exposure.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What is the biochemical profile of hyperthyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Low/suppressed TSH + raised T4 and/or T3. Subclinical hyperthyroidism: low TSH + normal T4/T3.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What is the first-line treatment for hyperthyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Antithyroid drugs (ATDs) — carbimazole (or propylthiouracil in pregnancy) — block thyroid peroxidase → reduce hormone synthesis. Beta-blocker (propranolol) for symptom control.
Inhibits thyroid peroxidase → blocks organification of iodine → reduces thyroid hormone synthesis. Does NOT affect pre-formed hormone (takes 4–6 weeks to see effect).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What is the serious side effect of carbimazole?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Agranulocytosis (rare, ~0.5%) — bone marrow suppression causing dangerously low neutrophils → life-threatening infections. Patient must stop carbimazole and seek emergency review if fever/sore throat.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What are the two antithyroid drug regimens?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Titration regimen: dose adjusted by thyroid function tests to maintain euthyroidism. Block-and-replace: fixed high-dose carbimazole + levothyroxine added to prevent hypothyroidism.
Oral ¹³¹I — concentrated in thyroid, destroys thyroid tissue by local β radiation. Definitive treatment — often causes hypothyroidism (requiring lifelong levothyroxine).
Pregnancy; breastfeeding; active Graves' ophthalmopathy (may worsen TED); young children. Women must avoid pregnancy for 6 months after RAI.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What is thyroidectomy used for in hyperthyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Large goitre with compressive symptoms; patient choice; failure of medical/RAI; Graves' with severe TED. Complications: hypoparathyroidism, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy.

Life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism — fever, tachycardia/AF, confusion/agitation, vomiting, precipitated by illness, surgery, or stopping ATDs. Treat: propylthiouracil + Lugol's iodine + propranolol + hydrocortisone + supportive.
Low TSH with normal T4/T3 and no/minimal symptoms — risk of AF and osteoporosis. Treat if AF develops, >65 years, post-menopausal women, or TSH persistently <0.1.
Multiple autonomous nodules secreting excess thyroid hormone — usually in older patients with long-standing nodular goitre. Gradual onset. Treated with RAI or thyroidectomy.
Single autonomously functioning thyroid nodule secreting excess T3/T4. Suppresses TSH + rest of thyroid. On scan: 'hot nodule' with suppressed surrounding tissue. Treated with RAI or surgery.
Another name for toxic multinodular goitre — common in elderly, iodine-deficient areas. Multiple hot nodules. NOT autoimmune (no TRAb).
Antithyroid drug — preferred in first trimester of pregnancy (carbimazole teratogenic in T1), thyroid storm (also inhibits T4→T3 conversion), liver toxicity risk (not first-line).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: EXAM PEARL: What ECG finding should prompt thyroid function tests?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Atrial fibrillation (AF) in a young person or AF with no obvious cause — always check TFTs. Thyrotoxicosis is an important reversible cause of AF.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: EXAM PEARL: What are TRAb and what do they do?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Thyroid-stimulating receptor antibodies — bind and activate TSH receptors → continuous thyroid stimulation → Graves' hyperthyroidism. Also cause thyroid eye disease (orbital cross-reactivity).
Amiodarone contains 37% iodine — can cause AIT Type 1 (iodine excess in pre-existing goitre) or Type 2 (destructive thyroiditis). Treat Type 1 with carbimazole; Type 2 with prednisolone.
Transient hyperthyroidism in Hashimoto's thyroiditis — destruction of follicles releases pre-formed hormone. Self-limiting. Does not require antithyroid drugs (TSI-negative).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What is the TFT result in thyroid storm?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Very low/undetectable TSH + very high free T4 and T3. But diagnosis is clinical (Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale ≥45 = thyroid storm likely).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: EXAM PEARL: What is pretibial myxoedema?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Non-pitting, brawny, orange-peel skin on anterior shins — specific to Graves' disease. Despite the name, it occurs in hyperthyroidism (not hypothyroidism), caused by TSH-receptor antibody-stimulated fibroblast deposition.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What is the single decisive fork in hyperthyroidism (radioiodine uptake)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: High uptake on radioiodine scan = gland is making it (true hyperthyroidism — antithyroid drugs work). Low uptake = hormone is leaking from damage (thyrotoxicosis without hyperthyroidism — antithyroid drugs are useless here).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: What is subclinical hyperthyroidism, and when is it treated?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: TSH suppressed + normal T3/T4. Often asymptomatic. Treat if TSH <0.1 with AF risk, osteoporosis, age >65, or cardiac disease.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Aetiology (low uptake): what are the exogenous/ectopic low-uptake causes of thyrotoxicosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Excess levothyroxine — exogenous; TSH suppressed; gland not active. Struma ovarii — ectopic thyroid in ovarian teratoma. Metastatic follicular cancer — functioning ectopic tissue.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Why do antithyroid drugs only work in the high-uptake group?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, PTU) block thyroid synthesis — they only work in the high-uptake group. In thyroiditis/exogenous T4, there is nothing to block.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Radioiodine scan patterns: what does diffuse high uptake vs focal/patchy high uptake indicate?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Diffuse high uptake → Graves' disease. Focal/patchy high uptake → toxic adenoma / toxic multinodular goitre.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Radioiodine scan patterns: what do low/absent uptake and a cold nodule indicate?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Low/absent uptake → thyroiditis, exogenous levothyroxine, struma ovarii. Cold nodule (non-uptake focus) → cancer until proven otherwise; USS + FNA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Thyroid storm — what is the four-arm bundle (hit every step of the pathway)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: 1) Block synthesis — high-dose carbimazole 20–40mg 8-hourly (or PTU 200mg 4-hourly if preferred). 2) Block release — potassium iodide (KI/Lugol's iodine) given ≥1h after carbimazole (must block synthesis first or iodine will fuel more hormone). 3) Block conversion — hydrocortisone 100mg IV 6-hourly (inhibits peripheral T4→T3; also covers relative adrenal insufficiency). 4) Block effect — propranolol IV/oral (blocks adrenergic symptoms; reduces tachycardia/AF).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Thyroid storm — why must KI be given after carbimazole, and what else supports treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: KI must be given ≥1h after carbimazole — block synthesis first or iodine will fuel more hormone. Plus: IV fluids, treat precipitant (antibiotics if sepsis), cooling, intensive care monitoring. Cholestyramine can bind thyroid hormone in gut (reduces enterohepatic recycling).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Thyroid malignancy: what is papillary cancer — frequency and key features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: 70% — most common. Young females; excellent prognosis; lymph node spread; Psammoma bodies on histology.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Thyroid malignancy: what is follicular cancer — frequency and key features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: 20%. Solitary nodule; haematogenous spread (lung/bone); cannot distinguish benign from malignant on FNA alone — needs histology.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Thyroid malignancy: what is medullary cancer — frequency and key features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: 5%. C-cells → calcitonin raised; part of MEN-2A/2B; RET oncogene; screen family.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: Thyroid malignancy: what is anaplastic cancer — frequency and key features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: 1%. Elderly; rapidly enlarging; very poor prognosis; pressure symptoms → stridor.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: How are papillary and follicular thyroid cancers managed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Total thyroidectomy + I-131 ablation of residual tissue + lifelong levothyroxine (TSH-suppressive dosing).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the thyroid storm bundle and why order matters.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.back: Carbimazole (synthesis) → KI after 1h (release) → hydrocortisone (conversion) → propranolol (effect). Order matters — KI before carbimazole can worsen storm.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What do the hypothalamus and pituitary form, and what is their relationship?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: They form the central control hub of the endocrine system — the hypothalamus integrates signals from the brain and body and directs the pituitary, which in turn controls the peripheral endocrine glands.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the organising principle of the endocrine axes.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Most hormones are controlled by an axis — hypothalamus → pituitary → target gland → hormone — regulated by negative feedback (the final hormone switches off the levels above it). Almost every endocrine disease and test is understood by asking 'where in the axis is the problem, and which way is the feedback going?'

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why does the hypothalamic-pituitary framework matter clinically?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: This single framework explains primary vs secondary endocrine disease, why we measure paired hormones (e.g. TSH + T4), dynamic testing (suppression/stimulation), and steroid HPA suppression.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Contrast the origin and connection of the anterior versus posterior pituitary.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Anterior (adenohypophysis): glandular tissue, connected by hypophyseal portal blood vessels (hormones travel down). Posterior (neurohypophysis): neural (extension of hypothalamus), connected by direct neurons (axons from hypothalamus).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How is each pituitary lobe controlled, and which hormones does each release?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Anterior: controlled by hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones; releases ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, GH, prolactin. Posterior: hormones made in the hypothalamus, stored + released here; releases ADH and oxytocin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the key structural distinction between the two pituitary lobes.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The anterior pituitary is controlled by hypothalamic hormones via the portal blood supply; the posterior pituitary is just a storage/release site for hypothalamic neurons (ADH + oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus, not the pituitary).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Which hypothalamic hormone drives ACTH, and what is the resulting axis and target?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: CRH → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol (the HPA axis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Which hypothalamic hormone drives TSH, and what is the resulting axis and target?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: TRH → TSH → thyroid → T3/T4 (the thyroid axis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Which hypothalamic hormone drives LH + FSH, and what is the resulting axis and target?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: GnRH → LH + FSH → gonads → sex steroids + gametes (the gonadal axis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Which hypothalamic hormone drives GH, and what inhibits it and its effect?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: GHRH → GH → liver/tissues → IGF-1, growth (somatostatin inhibits GH).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How is prolactin controlled, and what is its target?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Dopamine inhibits prolactin (which acts on the breast → milk production).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why is prolactin the high-yield exception among pituitary hormones (the 'stalk effect')?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Prolactin is under tonic inhibition by dopamine (the hypothalamus suppresses it by default). So anything that interrupts the pituitary stalk (tumour, compression) → loss of dopamine inhibition → ↑prolactin ('stalk effect'); and dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) → ↑prolactin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why can primary hypothyroidism cause mild hyperprolactinaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: TRH also stimulates prolactin → so primary hypothyroidism (high TRH) can cause mild hyperprolactinaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the negative feedback loop of endocrine axes with an example.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The final hormone (e.g. cortisol, T4) feeds back to suppress the hypothalamus + pituitary → keeps levels stable. E.g. ↑cortisol → ↓CRH + ↓ACTH (cortisol controls its own production).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How is the pattern 'low target + HIGH pituitary hormone' interpreted?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Primary gland failure (gland can't respond; pituitary shouting louder) — e.g. ↓T4 + ↑TSH = primary hypothyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How is the pattern 'low target + LOW/normal pituitary hormone' interpreted?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Secondary (pituitary) failure (pituitary not driving it) — e.g. ↓T4 + ↓TSH = secondary hypothyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How is the pattern 'high target + LOW pituitary hormone' interpreted?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Primary gland overactivity (feedback suppressing pituitary) — e.g. ↑T4 + ↓TSH = primary hyperthyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How is the pattern 'high target + HIGH pituitary hormone' interpreted?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Pituitary-driven (secondary) overactivity — e.g. ↑cortisol + ↑ACTH = Cushing's disease (pituitary).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why do endocrine tests measure hormones in pairs?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Because the combination (e.g. TSH + T4, ACTH + cortisol, LH/FSH + sex steroids) localises the lesion to gland vs pituitary.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is a suppression test, and give examples?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: For suspected overproduction: give something that should switch the axis off; failure to suppress = autonomous overproduction. E.g. dexamethasone suppression test (Cushing's), oral glucose tolerance test (acromegaly).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is a stimulation test, and give an example?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: For suspected underproduction: give the stimulating hormone; failure to respond = gland can't produce. E.g. short Synacthen test (ACTH → cortisol, for Addison's).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is ADH, where is it made/stored, what does it act on, and what results from too little or too much?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ADH (vasopressin): made in the hypothalamus, stored/released posteriorly → acts on the renal collecting duct (water reabsorption). Too little = diabetes insipidus, too much = SIADH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the actions of oxytocin?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Uterine contraction (labour) + milk ejection (let-down reflex).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What causes hyperprolactinaemia from a pituitary tumour, and what causes panhypopituitarism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Hyperprolactinaemia from a pituitary tumour = 'stalk effect' (loss of dopamine inhibition). Panhypopituitarism = loss of multiple pituitary hormones (tumour, Sheehan's, apoplexy).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Explain steroid HPA suppression and its clinical consequence.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Exogenous steroids suppress CRH/ACTH → adrenal atrophy → why you cannot stop steroids abruptly (sick-day rules).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the mass effect of pituitary tumours?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Visual fields — bitemporal hemianopia — plus hormone excess/deficiency.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What does the thyroid produce, and what does it set?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Hormones that set the body's basal metabolic rate — influencing nearly every tissue's metabolism, growth, and (in children) development.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the organising principle of the thyroid axis.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The TRH → TSH → T3/T4 axis (a specific instance of the hypothalamic-pituitary framework), governed by negative feedback — and the TSH + T4 pairing is the single most useful endocrine test, decoding hypo/hyperthyroidism into primary vs secondary.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Map the three levels of the thyroid axis to their hormone and action.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Hypothalamus: TRH (thyrotropin-releasing hormone) → stimulates the pituitary. Anterior pituitary: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) → stimulates the thyroid. Thyroid: T4 (thyroxine) + T3 (triiodothyronine) → act on all tissues → metabolic effects.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does negative feedback operate in the thyroid axis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: T3/T4 suppress both TRH and TSH → keeps levels stable (the loop that makes TSH such a sensitive test).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the steps of thyroid hormone synthesis (the iodine story).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Iodide trapping (iodide pumped into the follicular cell, Na⁺/I⁻ symporter) → oxidation + organification (thyroid peroxidase, TPO, oxidises iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin → forms MIT + DIT) → coupling (MIT + DIT combine → T3 (3 iodines) and T4 (4 iodines), stored bound to thyroglobulin in the colloid) → release (TSH stimulates release of T3/T4 into the blood).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why is iodine essential, and what does iodine deficiency cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Iodine is essential (it is literally in the hormone) → iodine deficiency → goitre/hypothyroidism (the commonest cause worldwide).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the drug link for antithyroid drugs and thyroid synthesis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Carbimazole/propylthiouracil block TPO (→ ↓synthesis); PTU also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Compare T4 and T3 by amount made, activity, conversion and half-life.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: T4 (thyroxine): ~90% (main secreted form), less active (a prohormone), converted to T3 peripherally (by deiodinase), long half-life (~7 days). T3 (triiodothyronine): ~10%, the active hormone (~4× more potent), the active product, short half-life.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the key concept of T4 as a prohormone.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The thyroid mostly secretes T4, converted to the active T3 in peripheral tissues → T4 is essentially a circulating prohormone/reservoir (its long half-life is why levothyroxine [T4] is the treatment — stable, once-daily).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why do we measure free T4/T3 rather than total?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Most thyroid hormone is protein-bound (to thyroxine-binding globulin) → only the free fraction is active.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the effects of thyroid hormone on metabolic rate and the cardiovascular system?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Metabolic rate: ↑basal metabolic rate, ↑O₂ consumption, ↑heat production. Cardiovascular: ↑heart rate + contractility (↑β-adrenergic sensitivity).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the effects of thyroid hormone on CNS/development and growth?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: CNS/development: essential for brain development (deficiency in infancy → cretinism); ↑alertness. Growth: needed for normal growth (with GH).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the unifying idea of thyroid hormone actions.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Thyroid hormone sets the 'metabolic thermostat' → hyperthyroidism = everything sped up (weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, anxiety, diarrhoea) and hypothyroidism = everything slowed (weight gain, bradycardia, cold intolerance, lethargy, constipation) — the symptoms are derivable from the physiology, not memorised.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does a HIGH TSH + LOW free T4 pattern decode, with an example?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Primary hypothyroidism (thyroid fails → ↓T4 → feedback drives TSH up) — e.g. Hashimoto's.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does a LOW TSH + LOW free T4 pattern decode?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Secondary (central) hypothyroidism (pituitary not driving — rare).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does a LOW TSH + HIGH free T4 pattern decode, with an example?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Primary hyperthyroidism (thyroid overactive → ↑T4 → suppresses TSH) — e.g. Graves'.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How do HIGH TSH + HIGH free T4, and HIGH TSH + normal free T4, decode?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: HIGH TSH + HIGH T4 = secondary hyperthyroidism (TSH-secreting tumour — rare). HIGH TSH + normal T4 = subclinical hypothyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why is TSH the screening test for thyroid status?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The feedback loop is so sensitive that TSH changes early + dramatically before T4 moves much → TSH is the most sensitive marker of thyroid status.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the pattern logic distinguishing primary from secondary thyroid disease.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: In primary disease, TSH moves opposite to T4 (high TSH + low T4, or low TSH + high T4); in secondary disease, they move together.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why is levothyroxine (T4) used as thyroid replacement, and how is it dosed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: It replaces the prohormone; its long half-life means once-daily dosing, titrated to TSH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why is congenital hypothyroidism screened for at birth?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Thyroid hormone is needed for brain development → newborn screening (heel-prick).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why are β-blockers used in hyperthyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The thyroid ↑β-adrenergic sensitivity → propranolol controls tremor/tachycardia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the two functionally separate parts of the adrenal gland, and what does each make?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The cortex (steroid hormones) and the medulla (catecholamines) — with different embryological origins, control, and products.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the organising principle of adrenal physiology.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The cortex is organised into three zones, each making a different steroid class, and the cortisol arm is controlled by the HPA axis (CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with negative feedback). Understanding the zones + the axis explains Addison's, Cushing's, Conn's, and steroid therapy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Compare the origin, products and control of the adrenal cortex versus medulla.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Cortex (outer): origin mesoderm, products steroid hormones (from cholesterol), controlled mostly by ACTH (+ RAAS for aldosterone). Medulla (inner): origin neural crest (modified sympathetic ganglion), products catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline), controlled by the sympathetic nervous system.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Name the three cortical zones and their products (mnemonic 'GFR → salt, sugar, sex').
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Zona glomerulosa → aldosterone (mineralocorticoid, 'salt'). Zona fasciculata → cortisol (glucocorticoid, 'sugar'). Zona reticularis → androgens/DHEA (sex steroids, 'sex').

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What controls each cortical zone?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Zona glomerulosa (aldosterone) is controlled by RAAS (angiotensin II, K⁺) — not mainly ACTH. Zona fasciculata (cortisol) is controlled by ACTH (the HPA axis). Zona reticularis (androgens) is controlled by ACTH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the key control distinction between the adrenal steroids, and its consequence for adrenal insufficiency.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Cortisol + androgens are ACTH-driven, but aldosterone is primarily RAAS-driven (angiotensin II + potassium), not ACTH. This is why in secondary adrenal insufficiency (↓ACTH) aldosterone is preserved (RAAS still works), whereas in primary (Addison's) both are lost.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the HPA axis for cortisol.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: CRH (hypothalamus) → ACTH (pituitary) → cortisol (zona fasciculata), with cortisol negative feedback on CRH + ACTH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the diurnal rhythm of cortisol and its relevance.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Cortisol peaks in the early morning, troughs at night (why cortisol is measured at 9am, and why timing matters in testing).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the cortisol stress response and the basis of sick-day rules.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Physical/psychological stress → ↑CRH/ACTH → ↑cortisol (the body's stress hormone) — the basis of sick-day rules: a stressed body needs more cortisol.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are cortisol's metabolic and cardiovascular actions?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Metabolic: ↑blood glucose (gluconeogenesis, insulin antagonism — 'gluco-corticoid'), ↑protein breakdown, ↑lipolysis. Cardiovascular: maintains BP (permissive for catecholamines, mild mineralocorticoid effect).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are cortisol's immune/inflammatory and other actions?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Immune/inflammatory: anti-inflammatory + immunosuppressive (the basis of therapeutic steroids). Other: ↑gastric acid, bone resorption, mood effects.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the clinical logic linking excess and deficient cortisol to disease (derivable).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Excess cortisol (Cushing's) = ↑glucose (diabetes), ↑BP, central obesity, immunosuppression, osteoporosis, thin skin, mood change. Deficiency (Addison's) = ↓glucose, ↓BP, fatigue, weight loss.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Explain the therapeutic-steroid link and HPA suppression.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The anti-inflammatory action is why steroids are used as drugs — chronic use → HPA suppression (exogenous cortisol suppresses CRH/ACTH → adrenal atrophy) → cannot mount a stress response → sick-day rules + cannot stop abruptly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Where is aldosterone made, what controls it, and what is its action?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Made in the zona glomerulosa, controlled by RAAS (angiotensin II) + potassium. Action: acts on the renal collecting duct → ↑Na⁺ reabsorption + ↑K⁺ and H⁺ excretion → ↑blood volume/BP.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the clinical logic of aldosterone excess and deficiency.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Excess (Conn's / primary hyperaldosteronism) = hypertension + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis. Deficiency (part of Addison's) = hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypotension — derivable from the Na⁺-retaining/K⁺-excreting action.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What does the adrenal medulla secrete, in what proportion, and in response to what?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: A modified sympathetic ganglion → secretes adrenaline (~80%) + noradrenaline directly into the blood in response to sympathetic stimulation (the 'fight or flight' hormonal arm).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the systemic actions of adrenal catecholamines?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↑heart rate + contractility, vasoconstriction, bronchodilation, ↑glucose, pupil dilation — the systemic sympathetic response.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is a phaeochromocytoma and its clinical features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: A catecholamine-secreting medullary tumour → episodic hypertension, palpitations, sweating, headache — derivable from excess catecholamines.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Summarise the adrenal picture of Addison's (primary adrenal failure).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↓cortisol + ↓aldosterone (both zones fail) → fatigue, ↓BP, ↓glucose, hyperkalaemia + hyponatraemia; ↑ACTH (feedback) → pigmentation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Summarise the adrenal picture of secondary adrenal insufficiency, and how it differs from Addison's.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↓ACTH (pituitary/steroid suppression) → ↓cortisol but aldosterone preserved (RAAS intact) → no hyperkalaemia, no pigmentation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the Synacthen test used for in adrenal disease?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Give ACTH → measure cortisol response (tests the adrenal — Addison's) — the stimulation test from the framework.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the normal blood glucose range, and why is it kept there?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ~4–7 mmol/L, because the brain depends on a constant glucose supply while sustained high glucose damages tissues — regulated chiefly by the opposing hormones insulin and glucagon from the pancreas.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the organising principle of glucose homeostasis.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Glucose homeostasis is a balance between insulin (the only hormone that lowers glucose) and its counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline, GH, which raise it) — and the fed vs fasted state determines which dominates.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What do the islets of Langerhans contain, and what is their proportion of pancreatic mass?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The endocrine pancreas, ~1–2% of pancreatic mass, containing β cells (insulin), α cells (glucagon), and δ cells (somatostatin).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Which islet cell makes which hormone and what is its effect on glucose?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: β (beta) cells → insulin → LOWERS glucose (the only hormone that does). α (alpha) cells → glucagon → RAISES glucose. δ (delta) cells → somatostatin → inhibits both (+ other hormones).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the key hormonal asymmetry of glucose control and why it matters.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Many hormones raise glucose (glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline, GH — 'counter-regulatory') but only insulin lowers it → this is why insulin deficiency (diabetes) is so impactful, and why hypoglycaemia is dangerous (redundant defences against high glucose, single defence against low).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What triggers insulin release, and what is its overarching role?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Released by β cells in response to ↑blood glucose (also amino acids, incretins like GLP-1). Its role is the 'fed state' / anabolic / storage hormone — 'fuel is plentiful, store it'.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is insulin's action on the liver, muscle and adipose tissue?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Liver: ↑glycogen synthesis, ↓gluconeogenesis (stops making glucose). Muscle: ↑glucose uptake (via GLUT4), ↑glycogen + protein synthesis. Adipose: ↑glucose uptake (GLUT4), ↑fat storage (lipogenesis), ↓lipolysis. Overall: ↓blood glucose; promotes storage of glucose, fat, protein.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the GLUT4 point, and why is the brain vulnerable to hypoglycaemia rather than lack of insulin?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Insulin causes GLUT4 glucose transporters to move to the cell surface in muscle + fat → glucose uptake. The brain and liver use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT1/2/3) → so the brain can still take up glucose without insulin (and is vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, not lack of insulin).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: By what receptor mechanism does insulin act?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Insulin binds a tyrosine kinase receptor → signalling cascade → GLUT4 translocation + enzyme effects.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What triggers glucagon release, and what is its overarching role?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Released by α cells in response to ↓blood glucose (fasting). Its role is the 'fasted state' / catabolic / mobilising hormone — 'fuel is low, release stores'.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is glucagon's action on the liver and adipose tissue?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Liver: ↑glycogenolysis (break down glycogen) + ↑gluconeogenesis (make new glucose) → release glucose. Adipose: ↑lipolysis → free fatty acids + glycerol. Overall: ↑blood glucose + mobilises fat (→ ketones in prolonged fasting). Glucagon acts mainly on the liver.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does the fed state differ from the fasted state (dominant hormone, liver, fuel, net effect)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Fed (high insulin:glucagon): dominant hormone insulin; liver stores glucose as glycogen; fuel = glucose; net = store. Fasted (low insulin:glucagon): dominant hormone glucagon (+ counter-regulatory); liver does glycogenolysis → gluconeogenesis; fuel = fat (→ ketones if prolonged); net = mobilise.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the progression of fasting.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Glycogen stores (hours) → gluconeogenesis (from amino acids/glycerol) → ketogenesis (fat-derived ketones fuel the brain in prolonged starvation, sparing protein).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: List the counter-regulatory hormones and their effects on glucose.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Glucagon (the primary acute responder — glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis); adrenaline (↑glycogenolysis + ↑lipolysis, acute stress); cortisol (↑gluconeogenesis + insulin resistance); growth hormone (↑glucose, insulin antagonist).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the clinical link explaining why stress, steroids and adrenaline raise glucose?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: These counter-regulatory hormones raise glucose (and worsen diabetes control), driving the hyperglycaemia of acute illness.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Explain the glucose-homeostasis mechanism of type 1 diabetes.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Autoimmune β-cell destruction → no insulin → cannot store glucose, unopposed glucagon → hyperglycaemia + ketogenesis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Explain the mechanism of type 2 diabetes.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Insulin resistance (+ relative deficiency) → hyperglycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Explain the mechanism of DKA in glucose-homeostasis terms.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Absolute insulin deficiency → unrestrained lipolysis → ketogenesis → ketoacidosis (the fasted state gone unchecked).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why is hypoglycaemia rapidly dangerous?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Only one hormone (insulin) lowers glucose, but the brain depends on glucose → hypoglycaemia is rapidly dangerous; counter-regulation (glucagon/adrenaline) defends it.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Map the main diabetes drugs to their mechanisms.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Metformin (↓hepatic gluconeogenesis), sulfonylureas (↑insulin release), GLP-1 agonists (↑insulin/incretin), SGLT2i (renal glucose loss), insulin (replacement).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why do steroids cause hyperglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Cortisol is counter-regulatory (↑gluconeogenesis + insulin resistance).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does insulin affect potassium, and what is the clinical application?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Insulin drives K⁺ into cells (the basis of insulin-dextrose for hyperkalaemia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the normal blood calcium range, and why is calcium tightly controlled?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ~2.2–2.6 mmol/L, because calcium is critical for neuromuscular function, cardiac action potentials, clotting, and bone — controlled by PTH and vitamin D (raising calcium) opposed by calcitonin (minor).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the organising principle of calcium homeostasis.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Calcium is regulated across three organs — bone, kidney, gut — and PTH is the master minute-to-minute controller, with vitamin D as its essential partner (especially for gut absorption). Phosphate moves in the opposite direction to calcium in much of this system.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is calcium essential for physiologically?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Neuromuscular excitability (low Ca²⁺ → tetany; high Ca²⁺ → weakness), cardiac action potentials (the plateau), clotting (factor IV), bone, enzyme function.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How is calcium carried in blood, and what is the albumin correction point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ~Half is free (ionised) — the active fraction; the rest is bound (mainly to albumin). So total calcium must be 'corrected' for albumin (low albumin → low total Ca²⁺ but normal ionised Ca²⁺).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does pH (alkalosis) affect ionised calcium, and what is the clinical result?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Alkalosis → ↑binding → ↓ionised Ca²⁺ → tetany (why hyperventilation causes peri-oral tingling/carpopedal spasm).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: For each calcium-controlling hormone, give its source, effect on calcium and trigger.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: PTH (parathyroid glands, 4, behind thyroid): ↑calcium (the master regulator), triggered by ↓calcium. Vitamin D/calcitriol (skin/diet → liver → kidney): ↑calcium (esp. gut absorption), triggered by PTH, ↓calcium/phosphate. Calcitonin (thyroid C cells): ↓calcium (minor role in humans), triggered by ↑calcium.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does PTH raise calcium via bone, kidney and gut?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Triggered by low calcium (via calcium-sensing receptors). Bone: ↑osteoclast activity → bone resorption → releases calcium + phosphate. Kidney: ↑calcium reabsorption (distal tubule) + ↑phosphate excretion + ↑activation of vitamin D (stimulates 1-α-hydroxylase). Gut (indirect): ↑calcium absorption via activating vitamin D.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the phosphate point regarding PTH, and the diagnostic pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: PTH raises calcium but LOWERS phosphate (↑renal phosphate excretion) → so primary hyperparathyroidism = ↑Ca²⁺ + ↓phosphate (a key diagnostic pattern).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why is PTH's effect on gut calcium described as indirect?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: PTH works by stimulating the kidney to activate vitamin D, which then does the gut absorption.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the three-step vitamin D activation pathway (site and product).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Source: skin (UV on 7-dehydrocholesterol) + diet → vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol). 1st hydroxylation: liver (25-hydroxylase) → 25-OH vitamin D (storage form — what we measure). 2nd hydroxylation: kidney (1-α-hydroxylase, stimulated by PTH) → 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D (calcitriol — active form).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the actions of active vitamin D?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↑gut calcium AND phosphate absorption (the main one), ↑bone mineralisation, ↑renal calcium reabsorption.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does CKD cause bone disease via vitamin D?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The failing kidney can't do the 1-α-hydroxylation → ↓active vitamin D → ↓calcium → ↑PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) + phosphate retention → renal osteodystrophy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What does vitamin D deficiency cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↓gut calcium/phosphate absorption → osteomalacia (adults) / rickets (children) + secondary hyperparathyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the integrated response when calcium falls.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↓Calcium → parathyroids release PTH → (1) bone resorption releases Ca²⁺, (2) kidney reabsorbs Ca²⁺ + excretes phosphate + activates vitamin D, (3) active vitamin D ↑gut Ca²⁺ absorption → calcium restored → PTH switches off (negative feedback). ↑Calcium → ↓PTH (+ minor calcitonin) → less bone resorption, more renal excretion → calcium falls.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Give the Ca²⁺/PTH/phosphate pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism and its mechanism.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↑calcium, ↑PTH (inappropriately), ↓phosphate. Mechanism: autonomous PTH (adenoma).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Give the Ca²⁺/PTH pattern of secondary hyperparathyroidism and its mechanism.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↓/normal calcium, ↑PTH (↑phosphate in CKD). Mechanism: PTH responding to low Ca²⁺ (CKD, vitamin D deficiency).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Give the pattern of tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↑calcium, ↑↑PTH, ↑phosphate. Mechanism: autonomous after prolonged secondary (CKD).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Give the Ca²⁺/PTH/phosphate pattern of hypoparathyroidism and its cause.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↓calcium, ↓PTH, ↑phosphate. Mechanism: ↓PTH (post-thyroidectomy).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Give the pattern of vitamin D deficiency and of malignancy-related hypercalcaemia.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Vitamin D deficiency: ↓/normal calcium, ↑PTH, ↓phosphate (osteomalacia/rickets). Malignancy (PTHrP/mets): ↑calcium, ↓PTH (suppressed), variable phosphate — non-PTH hypercalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the two commonest causes of hypercalcaemia, and what discriminates them?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Primary hyperparathyroidism (↑Ca²⁺ + ↑PTH) vs malignancy (↑Ca²⁺ + ↓PTH suppressed) — PTH is the discriminator.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the clinical features and mnemonic for hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: 'Stones, bones, groans, moans'; distinguish PTH-driven (1° hyperPTH) vs malignancy (PTH suppressed).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the clinical features and causes of hypocalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Tetany, Trousseau/Chvostek, long QT; causes = hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, CKD.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Why does post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia occur?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Accidental parathyroid damage → ↓PTH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What controls the reproductive system, and what does it produce?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis — producing sex steroids that drive gamete production, secondary sexual characteristics, and (in females) the menstrual cycle.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: State the organising principle of the reproductive axes, including the key exception.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: The same axis — GnRH → LH/FSH → gonadal sex steroids — operates in both sexes, governed by negative feedback, with one crucial exception: the mid-cycle positive feedback that triggers ovulation. It is the hypothalamic-pituitary framework applied to the gonads.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Map the three levels of the HPG axis to their hormone and action.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Hypothalamus: GnRH (pulsatile) → stimulates the pituitary. Anterior pituitary: LH + FSH (gonadotrophins) → act on the gonads. Gonads: testosterone (testes) / oestrogen + progesterone (ovaries) → sex steroids → feedback + peripheral effects.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the pulsatility point of GnRH, and its clinical basis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: GnRH must be released in pulses — continuous GnRH paradoxically suppresses the axis (downregulates receptors). This is the basis of GnRH analogues used to suppress sex hormones (prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What provides negative feedback in the HPG axis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Sex steroids + inhibin suppress GnRH/LH/FSH (the standard loop).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the jobs of LH versus FSH in males?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: LH stimulates Leydig cells → testosterone. FSH stimulates Sertoli cells → spermatogenesis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the jobs of LH versus FSH in females?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: LH triggers ovulation + corpus luteum (→ progesterone). FSH stimulates follicle development (+ oestrogen).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the memory hook for LH and FSH, and what does inhibin do?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: LH → Leydig (+ ovuLation); FSH → Follicle (+ Sertoli/sperm). Inhibin (Sertoli/granulosa cells) selectively feeds back to suppress FSH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are testosterone's roles in males, and what supports spermatogenesis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Testosterone (from Leydig cells, LH-driven) drives male secondary sexual characteristics, libido, muscle/bone mass, spermatogenesis (with FSH/Sertoli support). Spermatogenesis needs both FSH (Sertoli cells) + local testosterone.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the conversions of testosterone and their clinical relevance?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Testosterone → dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5-α-reductase (active in prostate/skin — the basis of finasteride in BPH/hair loss) and → oestrogen by aromatase. The male axis is relatively steady (no cycle), under simple negative feedback.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle (days, ovary, hormones, endometrium).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Follicular (~days 1–14): follicle develops (FSH); ↑oestrogen; endometrium proliferative (oestrogen thickens it).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe ovulation and the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Ovulation (~day 14): egg released; LH surge (from the oestrogen peak). Luteal (~days 14–28): corpus luteum; ↑progesterone (+ oestrogen); endometrium secretory (progesterone prepares for implantation).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Describe menstruation in the cycle.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Menstruation (~days 1–5): corpus luteum regresses; ↓progesterone + oestrogen; endometrium sheds.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Explain the ovulation trigger — the positive-feedback exception.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: For most of the cycle oestrogen gives negative feedback, BUT at the mid-cycle oestrogen peak, feedback switches to positive → triggers the LH surge → ovulation. This is the one place in endocrinology where feedback is positive.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What happens to the corpus luteum with and without pregnancy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: After ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum → secretes progesterone (maintains the endometrium). No pregnancy → it regresses → progesterone falls → menstruation. Pregnancy → hCG (from the embryo) rescues the corpus luteum → progesterone maintained (the link to pregnancy + pregnancy tests).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What are the peripheral effects of oestrogen and progesterone?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Oestrogen: female secondary sexual characteristics, endometrial proliferation, bone protection (↓ at menopause → osteoporosis), breast development. Progesterone: prepares/maintains endometrium, pregnancy maintenance, ↑basal body temperature (the ovulation marker).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What happens at puberty in HPG-axis terms?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Reactivation of pulsatile GnRH → HPG axis switches on → sex steroid surge → secondary sexual characteristics; precocious/delayed puberty = early/late axis activation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What happens at menopause, including the diagnostic pattern and consequences?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Ovarian follicles depleted → ↓oestrogen → loss of negative feedback → ↑↑FSH/LH (the diagnostic pattern: high FSH = menopause); consequences = vasomotor symptoms, osteoporosis, urogenital atrophy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does the combined oral contraceptive work via the HPG axis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Oestrogen + progesterone → negative feedback → ↓FSH/LH → no follicle/ovulation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: What is the HPG picture of PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: ↑LH:FSH ratio, ↑androgens, anovulation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: Distinguish primary from secondary male hypogonadism using the framework.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Primary (testes) → ↑LH/FSH; secondary (pituitary/hypothalamus) → ↓LH/FSH — the framework's primary/secondary logic.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does finasteride work, and what is hCG used for clinically?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: Finasteride (5-α-reductase inhibitor) blocks testosterone→DHT (BPH, hair loss). hCG rescues the corpus luteum → the basis of pregnancy tests.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.front: How does an infertility workup localise the problem?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.back: LH/FSH/oestrogen/testosterone localise the problem (gonad vs pituitary).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Most common cause UK?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Autoimmune (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) — anti-TPO antibodies

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Clinical features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Fatigue · weight gain · cold intolerance · constipation · bradycardia · dry skin/hair · hoarse voice · periorbital puffiness · slow relaxing reflexes

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: TSH in primary hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: TSH raised (pituitary increases TRH/TSH to try to drive failing thyroid)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) — start low 25–50mcg daily, ↑every 6–8 weeks by 25mcg

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Aim of treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: TSH 0.4–2.5 mU/L for most patients. Symptom relief over target TSH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Myxoedema coma: features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Hypothermia · confusion/coma · bradycardia · hyponatraemia · hypoglycaemia. Emergency: IV T3 + hydrocortisone + warmed IV fluids.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Why hydrocortisone in myxoedema coma?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Give before T4/T3 — hypothyroidism masks Addison's. Thyroxine → ↑cortisol demand → Addisonian crisis if undetected.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Subclinical hypothyroidism: when treat?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: TSH >10 OR TSH 4.5–10 with symptoms/anti-TPO positive/high CV risk/pregnancy/trying to conceive

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Levothyroxine in pregnancy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Increase dose by ~30–50% from start of pregnancy. Monitor TFTs monthly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Amiodarone → hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Excess iodine → Wolff-Chaikoff effect (↓organification). Treat: levothyroxine if symptomatic.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Drug interactions with levothyroxine?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Calcium · iron · antacids · cholestyramine · PPIs (all ↓absorption). Take 30–60 min before food.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Congenital hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Neonatal thyroid screen (heel prick TSH). Cretinism if untreated: intellectual disability + growth failure.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Anti-TPO antibodies positive: risk?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: ~3–5% per year risk of developing overt hypothyroidism → monitor TFTs annually

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Thyroxine overdose?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Thyrotoxicosis → propranolol for symptoms. Cholestyramine reduces absorption.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Down syndrome + hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Increased risk (15–20%) — screen annually

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Deficiency of thyroid hormone — commonest cause: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune) in developed countries; iodine deficiency worldwide.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in the UK?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune) — anti-TPO antibodies destroy thyroid. Associated with other autoimmune conditions.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What are the clinical features of hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, slow reflexes (hung-up), menorrhagia, myalgia, depression, periorbital oedema, hoarse voice, goitre.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the biochemical profile of hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Primary: raised TSH + low T4. Subclinical: raised TSH + normal T4. Secondary (pituitary failure): low TSH + low T4 (inappropriately normal TSH).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the treatment for hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) — once daily, same time each day, on empty stomach. Aim for TSH in range 0.4–2.0 mU/L. Titrate dose every 6–8 weeks.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the starting levothyroxine dose and how is it adjusted?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Start 50 μg/day (25 μg in elderly or IHD). Increase by 25 μg every 6–8 weeks targeting TSH 0.4–2.0 mU/L. Most patients settle on 100–150 μg/day.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Why start low-dose levothyroxine in elderly patients with IHD?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Too-rapid correction of hypothyroidism increases cardiac demand → risk of precipitating angina or MI in IHD. Start 25 μg and increase slowly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is myxoedema coma?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Life-threatening severe hypothyroidism — hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia, altered consciousness. Triggered by cold, infection, sedatives. Treat with IV T3/T4 + hydrocortisone + warming.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Autoimmune thyroiditis — anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies destroy the thyroid. Leads to progressive hypothyroidism. Initially may have transient hyperthyroidism (Hashitoxicosis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the most sensitive marker of thyroid function?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: TSH — small changes in T4 cause large log-linear changes in TSH. TSH is the first-line test and most sensitive for hypothyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What drugs interfere with levothyroxine absorption?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Calcium carbonate, ferrous sulphate, proton pump inhibitors, aluminium antacids — all reduce LT4 absorption. Take LT4 at least 4 hours apart from these medications.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is secondary hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Pituitary failure → reduced TSH → reduced thyroid stimulation → low T4. Caused by pituitary tumour, apoplexy, Sheehan's syndrome, surgery. TFTs: low T4 + low/normal TSH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is congenital hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Present at birth — due to thyroid agenesis or dyshormonogenesis. Screened at birth (heel-prick Guthrie test — TSH). If untreated → cretinism (irreversible intellectual disability + growth failure).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is subclinical hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Raised TSH with normal T4/T3 and minimal/no symptoms. Treat if: TSH >10 mU/L; positive TPO antibodies; symptomatic; planning pregnancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What are the characteristic neurological signs of hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Slow-relaxing (hung-up) reflexes — especially ankle jerk. Also: carpal tunnel syndrome, cerebellar ataxia (severe), peripheral neuropathy, psychosis ('myxoedema madness').

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the thyroid function test pattern in sick euthyroid syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Low T3 (rT3 elevated), T4 may be low/normal, TSH may be low/normal/mildly raised — all due to non-thyroidal illness suppressing conversion. NOT true hypothyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the association between Hashimoto's and malignancy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Hashimoto's increases risk of thyroid lymphoma (primary thyroid lymphoma — B-cell). Also small increased risk of papillary thyroid carcinoma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What cardiovascular findings occur in hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Bradycardia; raised diastolic BP; pericardial effusion (myxoedematous fluid); raised LDL/cholesterol (reduced LDL receptor expression); low-voltage ECG.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the goitre in Hashimoto's thyroiditis like on examination?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Firm, rubbery, non-tender goitre with characteristic lobulated texture — 'bumpy' feel. Unlike Graves' (smooth, diffuse, bruit) or malignancy (hard, fixed, irregular).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the 'classic' signs of severe hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Periorbital/facial oedema (non-pitting myxoedema), bradycardia, hung-up reflexes, hoarse voice, dry coarse skin, hair loss — plus raised cholesterol.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: EXAM PEARL: What TFT pattern diagnoses primary vs secondary hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Primary (thyroid failure): high TSH + low T4. Secondary (pituitary failure): low/normal TSH + low T4 — the pituitary is not responding appropriately.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the risk of levothyroxine over-treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH) → AF, osteoporosis, atrial arrhythmias. Monitor TSH every 6–12 months once stable to avoid overtreatment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is Sheehan's syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Post-partum pituitary necrosis from severe haemorrhage at delivery → panhypopituitarism including secondary hypothyroidism + secondary adrenal insufficiency.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the role of anti-TPO antibodies in subclinical hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Positive anti-TPO in subclinical hypothyroidism predicts progression to overt hypothyroidism — one of the indications to treat subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the indications to treat subclinical hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: TSH >10 mU/L; positive anti-TPO antibodies; symptoms consistent with hypothyroidism; pregnancy or planning pregnancy; children — these indicate high risk of progression or significant impact.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What are the screening triggers for checking TFTs (hypothyroidism as a reversible cause)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Always check TFTs in new menorrhagia, infertility, hyperprolactinaemia, dyslipidaemia, depression, or carpal tunnel syndrome — hypothyroidism is the reversible cause behind all of these.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is Riedel's thyroiditis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: A rare fibrous infiltration; hard fixed painless goitre; mimics malignancy. A primary (gland pathology) cause of hypothyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the Hashimoto's autoimmune cluster?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Coeliac disease, T1DM, vitiligo, pernicious anaemia, Addison's disease.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Why is LDL/cholesterol raised in hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Reduced LDL-receptor expression. Reverses with levothyroxine treatment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Why is prolactin raised in hypothyroidism, and what can it cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: TRH stimulates prolactin — can cause galactorrhoea.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What does the FBC show in hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Macrocytic or normocytic anaemia (can coexist with pernicious anaemia in Hashimoto's).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the role of liothyronine (T3) in hypothyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Rarely used; shorter half-life; some patients on T4 alone remain symptomatic despite normal TSH — consider T4/T3 combination in specialist care.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Why is only passive rewarming used in myxoedema coma?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Active rewarming causes vasodilation and cardiovascular collapse.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the mirror pearl linking myxoedema coma and thyroid storm?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: They are the two thyroid emergencies. Steroids feature in both — in storm to block T4→T3 conversion; in coma to cover adrenal insufficiency. Steroids always before thyroid hormone in coma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the classic hypothyroid discriminators (vs hyperthyroid)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Slow-relaxing reflexes + loss of outer eyebrow + raised CK + low Na + raised lipids. Brisk reflexes = hyperthyroid (same axis, opposite direction).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the amiodarone, lithium, and Sheehan's points.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Amiodarone causes both hypo- and hyperthyroidism (contains 37% iodine). Lithium causes hypothyroidism. Sheehan's = post-partum pituitary necrosis → secondary hypothyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: EXAM PEARL: Congenital hypothyroidism — detection and consequence if untreated.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Detected on Guthrie heel-prick test (day 5–8). Untreated → cretinism (irreversible intellectual disability). Early T4 treatment is curative.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the single most important clinical sign that distinguishes a thyroid lump from all other neck lumps?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back: Movement on swallowing. The thyroid gland is enveloped in pretracheal fascia and moves superiorly with the larynx during swallowing. Ask the patient to swallow a sip of water while you observe/palpate. A thyroglossal cyst also moves on swallowing AND on tongue protrusion (pathognomonic of thyroglossal cyst).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What is the Thy (Bethesda) classification for thyroid FNA cytology, and which categories require surgery?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back:
Thy1 = Non-diagnostic / inadequate (repeat FNA)
Thy2 = Benign (observe; USS surveillance)
Thy3a = Atypia of undetermined significance
Thy3f = Follicular lesion / neoplasm (diagnostic lobectomy -- cannot exclude follicular carcinoma on cytology alone)
Thy4 = Suspicious for malignancy (surgery)
Thy5 = Malignant (surgery)
Thy3-5 require surgical intervention.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What does a 'cold' nodule on isotope scan mean, and how does it compare to a 'hot' nodule?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back:
Cold nodule = does not take up isotope -> non-functioning -> ~5-15% malignancy risk -> requires FNA.
Hot nodule = autonomous functioning nodule -> takes up isotope, suppresses rest of gland -> almost always benign (rarely malignant) -> may cause hyperthyroidism (toxic adenoma).
Warm nodule = intermediate uptake -> indeterminate -> further assessment needed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What are the four main types of thyroid carcinoma and their key distinguishing features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back:
1. Papillary (70-80%): most common; excellent prognosis; psammoma bodies; RET/PTC rearrangement; spreads to lymph nodes
2. Follicular (10-15%): haematogenous spread (bone, lung); cannot diagnose on FNA (need capsular invasion on histology)
3. Medullary (5%): calcitonin-secreting C-cells; associated with MEN2 (RET mutation); check calcitonin + CEA
4. Anaplastic (<2%): worst prognosis; rapidly growing; elderly patients; often inoperable at presentation

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: What are the five main indications for thyroidectomy in a patient with goitre?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back:
1. Compressive symptoms: dysphagia, dyspnoea, stridor, SVC obstruction, tracheal deviation
2. Suspicious/malignant FNA: Thy3f (diagnostic lobectomy), Thy4 or Thy5 (total thyroidectomy)
3. Retrosternal goitre causing symptoms
4. Hyperthyroidism uncontrolled medically (toxic MNG, refractory Graves')
5. Cosmetic / rapid growth / clinical concern for malignancy

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.front: Describe the clinical features that suggest thyroid malignancy in a patient presenting with a neck lump.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypothyroidis.back:
Red flags for thyroid malignancy:
- Hard, irregular, fixed (not mobile) nodule
- Rapid growth
- Hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion)
- Cervical lymphadenopathy
- Dysphagia or stridor (tracheal/oesophageal invasion)
- Age <20 or >70 years (higher malignancy risk)
- Male sex (goitres less common, higher malignancy rate)
- History of neck irradiation
- Family history of thyroid cancer or MEN2

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Definition?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Prolonged exposure to excess glucocorticoids — exogenous (most common) or endogenous

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: ACTH-dependent causes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease, 70%) · Ectopic ACTH (SCLC, carcinoid, 15%)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: ACTH-independent causes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Adrenal adenoma · adrenal carcinoma · exogenous steroids

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Clinical features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Central obesity · moon face · buffalo hump · striae (violaceous) · proximal myopathy · hypertension · diabetes · osteoporosis · easy bruising · thin skin · hirsutism

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: First-line screening test?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: 24h urinary free cortisol (×3) OR late-night salivary cortisol × 2 OR 1mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Overnight DST: interpretation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Cortisol suppressed to <50 nmol/L = normal. Failure to suppress = Cushing's likely.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Confirming ACTH-dependent: test?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: High-dose DST (8mg) + CRH stimulation test. Pituitary: suppresses with 8mg DST + responds to CRH. Ectopic: neither.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Imaging for Cushing's disease?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: MRI pituitary (may miss microadenoma <3mm). IPSS (inferior petrosal sinus sampling) if MRI negative.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Treatment of Cushing's disease?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Transsphenoidal adenomectomy. If fails: radiotherapy or bilateral adrenalectomy (Nelson's syndrome risk).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Nelson's syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Rapid expansion of pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy (loss of cortisol feedback) → hyperpigmentation + mass effect

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Pseudo-Cushing's?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Alcohol excess or depression → elevated cortisol + failed DST. Normalises with abstinence/treatment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Metyrapone?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Inhibits 11-β-hydroxylase → blocks cortisol synthesis. Medical treatment to reduce cortisol pre-op.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Ectopic ACTH vs Cushing's disease: clinical?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Ectopic: rapid onset · severe hypokalaemia · very high ACTH · often no typical Cushingoid features (too rapid)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Adrenal adenoma finding?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Adrenal CT/MRI: unilateral mass. ACTH undetectable (ACTH-independent). Low DHEA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: Pregnancy + Cushing's?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Adrenal adenoma most common cause (not pituitary) in pregnancy. Very high maternal/fetal morbidity.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: What is Cushing's syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Syndrome of chronic glucocorticoid excess — causes: exogenous steroids (most common), pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (Cushing's disease), ectopic ACTH, adrenal adenoma/carcinoma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: What is the most common cause of Cushing's syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Exogenous steroids (iatrogenic) — the most common cause overall. Cushing's disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma) is the most common endogenous cause (~70%).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: What is the difference between Cushing's syndrome and Cushing's disease?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Cushing's syndrome = any cause of glucocorticoid excess. Cushing's disease = specifically a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma causing Cushing's syndrome (bilateral adrenal hyperplasia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: What are the clinical features of Cushing's syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Central obesity + moon face + buffalo hump; thin skin + easy bruising + purple striae; proximal myopathy; hypertension; diabetes/hyperglycaemia; osteoporosis; depression/psychosis; hirsutism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: What is the most discriminatory clinical feature of Cushing's syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: Purple/violaceous striae + proximal myopathy — these are the most specific features. General obesity alone is not sufficient.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: What is the first-line screening test for Cushing's syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) — or late-night salivary cortisol — or overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test. All three are used as screening.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: What does the overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) involve?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.back: 1 mg dexamethasone at 11pm — check cortisol at 9am. Normal: cortisol suppresses to <50 nmol/L. Cushing's: cortisol fails to suppress (>50 nmol/L).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Cushing's Syn.front: What is the low-dose DST vs high-dose DST?
