conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Posterior pituitary over-secretion OR ectopic (classically SCLC). SCLC also causes ectopic ACTH → Cushing's; SCLC is the paraneoplastic workhorse.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: How does Diabetes Insipidus mirror SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Diabetes Insipidus = too little ADH → dilute urine + hypernatraemia. SIADH and DI are the water-balance pair, examined as opposites.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: Within the hyponatraemia algorithm, which volume box does SIADH occupy and why does this matter?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: The first step in any hyponatraemia is volume status — SIADH occupies the euvolaemic box. This is why the diagnosis is exclusion-based: you must rule out the hypovolaemic and hypervolaemic columns AND the euvolaemic mimics (hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: In the hyponatraemia volume table, what are the causes and key feature of the HYPOVOLAEMIC state?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Causes: D&V, diuretics, Addison's, burns. Key feature: dry / low BP — SIADH is NOT dry.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: In the hyponatraemia volume table, what are the causes and key feature of the EUVOLAEMIC state (where SIADH lives)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Causes: SIADH, hypothyroidism, primary polydipsia. Key feature: no oedema, no dehydration.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: In the hyponatraemia volume table, what are the causes and key feature of the HYPERVOLAEMIC state?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Causes: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Key feature: oedematous — SIADH is NOT overloaded.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What are the top 3 causes of SIADH to know?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Post-op, SSRIs, SCLC.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: List the CNS causes of SIADH.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Head injury, stroke / ICH, meningitis, SAH, encephalitis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: List the pulmonary & malignancy causes of SIADH.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Atypical pneumonia (Legionella, mycoplasma), lung abscess, SCLC (ectopic ADH — commonest malignant cause), other carcinomas, HIV.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: Which drugs cause SIADH, and which is the commonest drug cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: SSRIs (commonest drug cause), carbamazepine, NSAIDs, PPIs, opiates, cyclophosphamide, antipsychotics.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: List the 'other' causes of SIADH, noting which are mimics rather than true causes.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Post-operative (especially after major surgery); hypothyroidism — mimic, not cause; adrenal insufficiency — mimic, not cause.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: Where do the clinical features of SIADH come from?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Features come entirely from the hyponatraemia — ADH excess itself causes no symptoms. Symptoms track Na level and rate of fall.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What are the symptoms of mild/chronic hyponatraemia (Na 125–135) in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Often asymptomatic; fatigue, nausea, headache, muscle cramps.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What are the symptoms of moderate hyponatraemia (Na 120–125) in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Confusion, disorientation, unsteady gait.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What are the symptoms of severe/acute hyponatraemia (Na <120) in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Seizures, reduced consciousness, coma (cerebral oedema) — EMERGENCY.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What are the core diagnostic criteria for SIADH (serum)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Serum Na + serum osmolality: hyponatraemia + LOW serum osmolality (<275 mOsm/kg).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the key urine osmolality finding in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Inappropriately HIGH (>100 mOsm/kg, typically >500) despite low serum osmolality — the key paradox.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the urine Na finding in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Elevated (>40 mmol/L) — kidney retaining Na along with water.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What does clinical assessment of volume status show in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Euvolaemia on clinical assessment — no signs of dehydration or oedema.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What must be excluded to diagnose SIADH (diagnosis of exclusion checklist)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: No diuretics (cause false-positive urine Na); no hypovolaemia (D&V, burns); no hypervolaemia (HF, cirrhosis); no CKD/AKI; no excess water intake; TFTs (hypothyroidism mimic); Short Synacthen Test (adrenal insufficiency mimic — Addison's causes euvolaemic/hypovolaemic hyponatraemia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What cause-finding investigations are used in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: CXR (pneumonia, abscess, lung mass — SCLC); CT CAP / MRI head (if malignancy or CNS cause suspected); drug / surgical history (SSRIs, carbamazepine, post-op context).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is step 1 of SIADH management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Treat the underlying cause: stop offending drug (SSRI, carbamazepine); treat pneumonia; manage malignancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the first-line management for mild/chronic SIADH, and the key exception?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Fluid restriction 750–1000 mL/day = first-line for mild SIADH. EXCEPTION: avoid fluid restriction in SIADH from SAH — risks hypovolaemia → cerebral vasospasm/infarction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is tolvaptan and when is it used in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Tolvaptan (resistant SIADH): vasopressin/ADH-receptor antagonist (vaptan); promotes free water excretion; requires 6-hourly Na monitoring (risk of over-rapid correction).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: How is severe SIADH (seizures/coma) managed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Hypertonic saline: 1.8% or 3% NaCl ± furosemide; HDU/ITU setting; strict Na monitoring. Correct slowly: ≤8–10 mmol/L per 24h — risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the critical rule for correcting Na in SIADH and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Correct Na no faster than 8–10 mmol/L per 24 hours. Too-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia → osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis). The danger is treating too fast, not the hyponatraemia itself.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Over-rapid correction of chronic severe hyponatraemia (Na <120).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the mechanism of osmotic demyelination syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Brain cells extrude solutes to adapt to chronic low Na → rapid Na rise pulls water out of cells → demyelination of pons.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: Describe the two-phase course of osmotic demyelination syndrome.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Phase 1 (early): confusion, seizures, encephalopathy. Phase 2 (days later): spastic quadriparesis, pseudobulbar palsy, locked-in syndrome, cognitive/behavioural change.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: How is osmotic demyelination syndrome prevented?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Always correct slowly ≤8–10 mmol/L/24h.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What are the two indications for hypertonic (1.8% or 3%) saline in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: (1) Severe SIADH with seizures or coma — life-threatening. (2) Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia (<48h duration) — rapid correction is safer because brain has not yet adapted. Give 150 mL 3% NaCl IV over 20 min, may repeat ×2. Target: Na rise of 5 mmol/L to abort the seizure.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: How does urea work in SIADH, and what are its advantages?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Oral urea increases urinary solute excretion → obligatory water loss → rises serum Na. Advantages: cheap, effective in chronic SIADH, can be used long-term, does not require hospitalisation. Unpleasant taste is the main limitation. Used as 2nd/3rd line.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the SALT-1/SALT-2 trial relevance to tolvaptan in SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: SALT trials showed tolvaptan (V2 receptor antagonist) significantly raises serum sodium vs placebo in euvolaemic and hypervolaemic hyponatraemia. Licenced for SIADH. Risk: over-rapid correction; patients must have unrestricted access to water. Hepatotoxicity led to restrictions in cirrhosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the SIADH reset osmostat variant, and how does it behave differently?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: In reset osmostat: ADH is regulated normally but at a lower set-point. Serum Na stabilises at a lower-than-normal level (e.g. 128–132) without rising further. Fluid restriction does not correct it; the patient can concentrate urine normally. Common in pregnancy and malnutrition.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the role of demeclocycline in SIADH, and why has it been superseded?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Demeclocycline (tetracycline) → nephrogenic DI → dilute urine despite ADH → raises serum Na. Largely superseded by tolvaptan (more predictable). Demeclocycline causes nephrotoxicity and photosensitivity; unreliable in liver disease.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: Which malignancy-specific SIADH context is the highest-yield SBA trap?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) — the classic ectopic ADH source. SCLC is a neuroendocrine tumour; its neurosecretory granules produce ADH directly. Any patient with SIADH who smokes should have CT chest first.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the TURP syndrome and how does it relate to SIADH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: TURP syndrome: post-transurethral resection hyponatraemia from absorption of large volumes of glycine/sorbitol irrigant. Causes dilutional (factitious) hyponatraemia without true SIADH — ADH is not raised. Treated with hypertonic saline. Resembles SIADH clinically but mechanism differs.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.front: What is the beer potomania variant of hyponatraemia, and why is it an SIADH mimic?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Syndrome of I.back: Beer potomania: very low solute intake (beer is low in protein/salt) + high water intake → insufficient urinary solute to excrete free water. Serum Na falls without SIADH. Urine osmolality is low (dilute) — distinguishes it from SIADH (where urine is inappropriately concentrated). Treat with salt and protein intake.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the single decisive fork in diabetes insipidus, and what resolves it?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Cranial (no ADH made) vs nephrogenic (kidney can't respond to ADH). The diagnostic resolver: does giving desmopressin fix it? Cranial = hypothalamus/pituitary fails to produce ADH → kidney is fine and responds to desmopressin (urine concentrates). Nephrogenic = ADH present but kidney can't respond → desmopressin does nothing (urine stays dilute).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Where is ADH made and secreted, and what does it do?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: ADH is made in the hypothalamus, secreted by the posterior pituitary, and acts on collecting ducts to reabsorb water.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Define DI in terms of urine-concentrating ability and its consequences.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: DI = inability to concentrate urine → polyuria + polydipsia + dilute urine despite high/normal serum osmolality.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: How does DI mirror SIADH on the water-balance axis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: SIADH = too much ADH → concentrated urine + hyponatraemia. DI = too little/no response → dilute urine + hypernatraemia. They are the water-balance pair.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Why does the 'diabetes' in diabetes insipidus have nothing to do with glucose?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: 'Diabetes' here = Greek 'to pass through' (polyuria) — nothing to do with glucose; DI has normal blood sugar.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: List the cranial causes of DI (↓ADH production).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Idiopathic (commonest); tumour (craniopharyngioma, pituitary adenoma, metastases); trauma/surgery (pituitary/hypothalamic); infection (meningitis, encephalitis); infiltrative (sarcoidosis, histiocytosis X, haemochromatosis); genetic — Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) = DI + Diabetes Mellitus + Optic Atrophy + Deafness.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: List the nephrogenic causes of DI.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Idiopathic; lithium (most testable — classic cause); demeclocycline; hypercalcaemia (high Ca damages concentrating ability); hypokalaemia; polycystic kidney disease, CKD; genetic — ADH-receptor (AVPR2) mutation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Which is the most testable nephrogenic cause of DI, and what is the cross-reference theme?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Lithium = the most testable nephrogenic cause. Cross-ref: lithium also causes hypothyroidism — a recurring 'lithium does bad things to endocrine organs' theme.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the danger scenario in DI, and why does DI matter acutely?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: A DI patient who cannot access water (unconscious, post-op, child) → rapid dangerous hypernatraemia → confusion, seizures. This is why DI matters acutely.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What are the clinical features of DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Polyuria (large volumes often >3L/day; dilute, low osmolality); polydipsia (compensatory — patient drinks large volumes); nocturia (disrupted sleep from polyuria); dehydration/postural hypotension (if water intake can't keep up); hypernatraemia if water restricted (confusion, seizures, coma — the acute emergency).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What are the urine and serum osmolality findings on baseline tests in DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Urine osmolality: low (dilute) despite high/normal serum osmolality — the core paradox. Serum osmolality + serum Na: high/normal serum osmolality; hypernatraemia if dehydrated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What does the 24h urine volume confirm, and why check glucose in suspected DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: 24h urine volume: >3L/day confirms polyuria. Glucose: exclude diabetes mellitus (DM causes osmotic polyuria).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Why are Ca²⁺ and K⁺ checked in the baseline DI workup?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Check for nephrogenic causes (hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the logic of the water deprivation + desmopressin test in DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Water deprivation separates true DI (urine stays dilute) from primary polydipsia (concentrates normally). Desmopressin then separates cranial (responds → urine concentrates) from nephrogenic (no response → stays dilute).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: In primary polydipsia, what happens after water deprivation and is desmopressin needed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: After water deprivation: urine concentrates (high osmolality). Desmopressin: not needed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: In cranial DI, what happens after water deprivation and after desmopressin?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: After water deprivation: urine stays dilute (low). After desmopressin: urine concentrates (high) — responds.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: In nephrogenic DI, what happens after water deprivation and after desmopressin?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: After water deprivation: urine stays dilute (low). After desmopressin: urine stays dilute (low) — no response.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: When is MRI pituitary indicated in DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: If cranial DI confirmed; find the structural lesion.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is step 1 of DI management (treat the underlying cause)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Stop lithium; correct hypercalcaemia/hypokalaemia; manage underlying tumour/infiltrative disease.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: How is cranial DI managed, and what must be monitored?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Cranial DI → desmopressin: replace the missing ADH (intranasal or oral). Monitor Na closely — risk of hyponatraemia if over-treated (you've essentially induced SIADH — the mirror risk).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: How is nephrogenic DI managed (working around the kidney)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Cannot replace what the kidney ignores. Ensure water access. Thiazide diuretics (paradoxically reduce urine volume by causing mild volume depletion → proximal tubule reabsorption). NSAIDs (reduce prostaglandins that antagonise ADH). Low-salt + low-protein diet. ± high-dose desmopressin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: How do thiazide diuretics paradoxically help in nephrogenic DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: They paradoxically reduce urine volume by causing mild volume depletion → proximal tubule reabsorption.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the desmopressin caution in DI management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Over-treatment of cranial DI → hyponatraemia (induced SIADH effect). Monitor Na regularly. This is the mirror risk of the same drug.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Exam pearl: how does the water deprivation test distinguish primary polydipsia, cranial DI and nephrogenic DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Primary polydipsia concentrates with deprivation. Cranial concentrates only AFTER desmopressin. Nephrogenic concentrates neither.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Exam pearl: what does DIDMOAD stand for?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: DIDMOAD = Wolfram syndrome: DI + Diabetes Mellitus + Optic Atrophy + Deafness. Cross-ref: infiltrative causes (sarcoid, haemochromatosis) link to hypopituitarism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Exam pearl: how is DI distinguished from Diabetes Mellitus?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: DI ≠ Diabetes Mellitus. Normal glucose. 'Diabetes' = Greek for polyuria. Distinguish by glucose + osmolality.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is central DI — how does it differ from cranial DI in terminology?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Central DI and cranial DI are synonyms: both refer to insufficient ADH production from the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary. 'Central' is the preferred US/international term; 'cranial' is the UK term.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the role of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) in ADH action, and why does it matter in nephrogenic DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: ADH binds V2 receptors in collecting duct → inserts aquaporin-2 water channels → water reabsorption. In nephrogenic DI, V2 receptors or AQP2 are non-functional → no channel insertion → dilute urine despite normal/high ADH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What are the V2-receptor drugs used in DI management, and how do they differ?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Desmopressin (synthetic ADH analogue) acts at V2 receptors in the kidney. It is the treatment for cranial DI. It has minimal V1 activity (unlike native ADH), so less vasoconstriction. Given intranasally, sublingually, or oral tablet.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What does hypernatraemia in DI tell you about thirst mechanism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: If thirst is intact, patients drink enough to maintain near-normal sodium (hypernatraemia is mild). Severe hypernatraemia implies impaired thirst (adipsia) — seen after hypothalamic surgery or trauma. These patients are at extreme risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is adipsic DI and why is it dangerous?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Adipsic DI = loss of thirst (adipsia) + DI together, usually after hypothalamic damage. Patients do not feel thirsty despite rising sodium → cannot self-regulate → severe, life-threatening hypernatraemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Why must hypernatraemia in DI be corrected slowly, and what is the risk of rapid correction?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Chronic hypernatraemia → brain accumulates osmoles to compensate. Rapid correction → cerebral oedema (reverse of SIADH correction). Correct Na at ≤10 mmol/L per 24h.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is nephrogenic DI from demeclocycline use, and in what context is it intentional?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Demeclocycline (a tetracycline) blocks ADH action in the collecting duct → intentional nephrogenic DI. Used therapeutically in SIADH to induce dilute urine when fluid restriction fails. The DI mechanism is the treatment goal.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the urine:plasma osmolality ratio in DI after water deprivation, and what does it indicate?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Normal: urine:plasma osmolality >2 (urine much more concentrated). In DI: urine:plasma ≈1 or <1 (urine fails to concentrate above plasma) — this is the core water deprivation test failure.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: How does DI present post-operatively after pituitary surgery, and what triphasic pattern can occur?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Triphasic: (1) immediate DI from surgical ADH disruption → (2) SIADH from dying cells releasing stored ADH → (3) permanent DI if >80% of magnocellular neurones destroyed. Monitor fluid balance and sodium closely.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the serum sodium expected in untreated cranial DI if thirst is intact?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Serum sodium is high-normal or mildly elevated (145–150 mmol/L). Thirst-driven polydipsia compensates for urinary loss, so frank hypernatraemia is often absent unless thirst is impaired.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: In the context of DI, what does a low urine specific gravity indicate?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Urine specific gravity <1.005 indicates dilute urine. In DI, the inability to concentrate urine produces SG <1.005. Normal urine SG is 1.010–1.030. Used as a bedside approximation of urine osmolality.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the Brattleboro rat model and what did it teach about DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: The Brattleboro rat has a congenital ADH gene mutation → natural cranial DI model. Showed that ADH is essential for urinary concentration and that desmopressin fully corrects the phenotype. Established the V2-receptor pathway.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Which congenital condition causes X-linked nephrogenic DI, and what is the molecular defect?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: X-linked nephrogenic DI = V2 receptor gene mutation (AVPR2 on chromosome Xq28). Boys affected; mothers are carriers. Resistant to desmopressin. Managed with thiazides + amiloride + low-sodium/protein diet.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Exam pearl: what is the treatment distinction between cranial and nephrogenic DI?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Cranial DI → desmopressin works (ADH deficiency treated). Nephrogenic DI → desmopressin does NOT work (end-organ resistance); use thiazides, amiloride, NSAIDs, low-solute diet.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the most common cause of hypernatraemia in hospitalised patients?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Inadequate free water intake (especially in elderly, intubated, or cognitively impaired patients). Water loss exceeding intake is more common than sodium gain. Always review fluid prescription and access to oral fluids.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Give the formula for Free Water Deficit (FWD) and what it represents.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back:
FWD (L) = TBW x (Na_measured / 140 - 1)
TBW = 0.6 x weight (men), 0.5 x weight (women/elderly).
FWD estimates the volume of free water needed to restore normonatraemia. Must also account for ongoing losses.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What urine osmolality findings help distinguish diabetes insipidus from extrarenal water loss in hypernatraemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back:
U_osm >700 mOsm/kg: appropriate renal response -> extrarenal loss (fever, diarrhoea) or inadequate intake
U_osm <300 mOsm/kg: diabetes insipidus (cranial or nephrogenic)
U_osm 300-700: partial DI or osmotic diuresis
Follow with water deprivation test +/- desmopressin to differentiate cranial vs nephrogenic DI.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Why must chronic hypernatraemia be corrected slowly, and what is the safe maximum rate?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back:
Brain cells adapt to hyperosmolality by generating idiogenic osmoles (taurine, myoinositol). Rapid correction causes water to rush into brain cells -> cerebral oedema -> seizures, herniation.
Max rate: 10-12 mmol/L/day (0.5 mmol/L/hr) for chronic (>48h) hypernatraemia.
Acute (<48h): can correct at ~1-2 mmol/L/hr.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What are the causes of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back:
Acquired (common): Lithium toxicity (most common drug cause), hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, tubulointerstitial nephritis, sickle cell disease
Congenital (rare): AVPR2 (V2 receptor) mutation (X-linked), AQP2 (aquaporin-2) mutation (autosomal)
Key: does NOT respond to desmopressin -- treat with low-sodium diet + thiazide diuretics.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: List four causes of hypernatraemia due to sodium gain (hypervolaemic hypernatraemia).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back:
1. Iatrogenic: hypertonic saline (3% NaCl), sodium bicarbonate infusions, TPN with insufficient free water
2. Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) -- sodium retention + hypokalaemia
3. Cushing's syndrome -- mineralocorticoid activity of cortisol
4. Salt poisoning -- accidental ingestion, child abuse, sea-water drowning (rare)
Clue: urine sodium is HIGH in sodium-gain causes.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the definition of hypernatraemia, and what deficit does it always reflect?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Serum sodium >145 mmol/L. Always reflects a deficit of water relative to sodium. Hypernatraemia is a hyperosmolar state — water moves out of cells, causing cellular dehydration. The most common cause is inadequate water intake rather than excess sodium.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Hypernatraemia from water loss — insensible and GI losses: examples and key features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Insensible losses: fever, burns, sweating, tachypnoea — urine concentrated (U_osm >700); kidney conserving water appropriately. GI losses: diarrhoea, vomiting, fistulae without adequate water replacement — often hypotonic fluid loss; urine concentrated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Hypernatraemia from water loss — cranial vs nephrogenic DI: examples and urine response?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Cranial DI: ADH deficiency (trauma, pituitary surgery, tumour, sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis) — polyuria, dilute urine (U_osm <300); responds to desmopressin. Nephrogenic DI: lithium toxicity, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, inherited (AVPR2/AQP2 mutations), tubulointerstitial disease — dilute urine; does not respond to desmopressin; aquaporin-2 defect.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Hypernatraemia from water loss — osmotic diuresis and loop diuretics: examples and key features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Osmotic diuresis: hyperglycaemia (DKA/HHS), mannitol, urea, contrast agents — polyuria with isosthenuric/mildly concentrated urine; glucosuria in DKA. Loop diuretics: furosemide, bumetanide — hypotonic urine loss; commonly combined with poor oral intake in elderly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Hypernatraemia from sodium gain — iatrogenic causes and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Iatrogenic: hypertonic saline (3% NaCl), sodium bicarbonate infusion, TPN with insufficient free water. Most common sodium-gain cause in hospital; review fluid prescriptions.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Hypernatraemia from sodium gain — hyperaldosteronism and Cushing's syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Hyperaldosteronism: Conn's syndrome, secondary hyperaldosteronism — sodium retention + hypokalaemia; hypertension; hypernatraemia often mild. Cushing's syndrome: excess cortisol (mineralocorticoid activity) — sodium and water retention; hypokalaemic alkalosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Hypernatraemia from sodium gain — salt poisoning?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Salt poisoning: child abuse, accidental ingestion, sea-water drowning. Rare; urine sodium high; hypervolaemic hypernatraemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Why is impaired thirst a key category of hypernatraemia, and what is it called?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Even with intact ADH, thirst is the primary defence against hypernatraemia. Impaired thirst leads to essential hypernatraemia (adipsia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What groups are at risk of hypernatraemia from impaired thirst / access to water?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Hypothalamic damage: tumours (craniopharyngioma), surgery, sarcoidosis, trauma — destroys osmoreceptors. Elderly patients: blunted thirst perception; reduced renal concentrating ability; common in care homes. Intubated / obtunded patients: cannot self-regulate fluid intake; entirely dependent on prescribed fluids. Infants: dependent on carers; at risk with formula errors or diarrhoeal illness.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the diagnostic approach to hypernatraemia (first two steps)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: 1. Assess volume status (hypovolaemic / euvolaemic / hypervolaemic hypernatraemia). 2. Urine osmolality + urine sodium.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: How does urine osmolality direct the diagnosis in hypernatraemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: U_osm >700 → appropriate renal response (extrarenal loss or inadequate intake). U_osm <300 → diabetes insipidus. U_osm 300–700 → partial DI or osmotic diuresis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What test distinguishes cranial from nephrogenic DI in the hypernatraemia workup?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Water deprivation test ± desmopressin to distinguish cranial vs nephrogenic DI.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What is the Critical Rule for correcting hypernatraemia, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Correct hypernatraemia SLOWLY. Brain cells adapt to hyperosmolality by accumulating idiogenic osmoles. Rapid correction → rapid cerebral swelling → cerebral oedema, seizures, herniation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What are the maximum correction rates for chronic vs acute hypernatraemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Chronic hypernatraemia (>48h or unknown duration): max 10–12 mmol/L/day (0.5 mmol/L/hr). Acute hypernatraemia (<48h, known onset): can correct faster (1–2 mmol/L/hr).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: How is the free water deficit (FWD) calculated in hypernatraemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: FWD (L) = TBW × (Na_measured / 140 − 1). TBW = 0.6 × weight (men), 0.5 × weight (women/elderly). e.g. 70 kg man, Na 160: TBW = 42 L; FWD = 42 × (160/140 − 1) = 6 L.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Over what period is the deficit replaced in hypernatraemia, and what is added?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Replace deficit over 48–72h. Add ongoing losses + insensible losses (~500–1000 mL/day) to the total replacement volume.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: What are the fluid choices for correcting hypernatraemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Oral water (preferred if patient can swallow); IV 5% dextrose (free water; monitor glucose); IV 0.45% NaCl (hypotonic saline — if also volume-depleted); 0.9% NaCl if severely hypovolaemic (haemodynamic priority first).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: How often is serum sodium monitored during hypernatraemia correction?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Check serum Na every 4–6 hours; adjust infusion rate accordingly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Treatment summary by cause — how are cranial DI and nephrogenic DI managed in hypernatraemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Cranial DI: intranasal/oral desmopressin (DDAVP) + free water. Nephrogenic DI: low-sodium diet, thiazide diuretics (paradoxically reduce urine output), NSAIDs (indomethacin), amiloride (for lithium-induced).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.front: Treatment summary by cause — how are osmotic diuresis and iatrogenic hypernatraemia managed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Insi.back: Osmotic diuresis: treat hyperglycaemia; stop mannitol; ensure free water replacement. Iatrogenic: stop hypertonic fluids; replace free water deficit.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the decisive fork that divides all hypocalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: The PTH level divides ALL hypocalcaemia. Low PTH = hypoparathyroidism (gland failure). High PTH = secondary response (Vit D deficiency, CKD, malabsorption). PTH appropriately high but calcium still low = secondary hyperparathyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What are the three physiological actions of PTH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: PTH raises Ca: bone resorption; renal Ca reabsorption; activates vit D to absorb Ca from the gut.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What does the 'mirror' show for the causes of hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Hypercalcaemia = too much PTH [primary hyperparathyroidism] OR vit D excess / malignancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What does the 'mirror' show for the causes of hypocalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Hypocalcaemia = too little PTH [hypoparathyroidism] OR PTH present but unable to work [Vit D deficiency, CKD].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: On the diagnostic table, what relationship do PTH and phosphate have?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: PTH and phosphate move in opposite directions. Use the table to crack any hypocalcaemia question.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: In hypoparathyroidism, what are the PTH, phosphate, vit D (25-OH) and ALP levels?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: PTH low, phosphate high, vit D (25-OH) normal, alkaline phosphatase normal.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: In vit D deficiency / osteomalacia, what are the PTH, phosphate, vit D (25-OH) and ALP levels?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: PTH high, phosphate low, vit D (25-OH) low, alkaline phosphatase high.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: In CKD (renal osteodystrophy), what are the PTH, phosphate, vit D (25-OH) and ALP levels?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: PTH high, phosphate high, vit D low (1,25-OH), alkaline phosphatase high.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: In pseudohypoparathyroidism, what are the PTH, phosphate, vit D (25-OH) and ALP levels?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: PTH high, phosphate high, vit D (25-OH) normal, alkaline phosphatase normal.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What does 'pseudo' mean in the context of the PTH/phosphate table?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Pseudo = PTH resistance; the body makes PTH but target organs don't respond.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the commonest cause of hypoparathyroidism (low PTH)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Surgical: post-thyroidectomy / parathyroidectomy — inadvertent removal or devascularisation of parathyroid glands. Commonest cause overall.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Describe the autoimmune causes of hypoparathyroidism.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Isolated autoimmune hypoparathyroidism OR as part of APS-1 [autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1: hypoparathyroidism + Addison's + candidiasis — HAC triad].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: List the 'other causes' of hypoparathyroidism.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: DiGeorge syndrome [22q11 deletion — absent parathyroids + cardiac defects + T-cell immunodeficiency]; hypomagnesaemia [Mg required for PTH secretion and action — check Mg in refractory hypocalcaemia]; infiltration [haemochromatosis, sarcoidosis]; radiation damage.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is DiGeorge syndrome and its features relevant to hypoparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: 22q11 deletion — absent parathyroids + cardiac defects + T-cell immunodeficiency.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Why does hypomagnesaemia cause hypoparathyroidism, and when should Mg be checked?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Mg is required for PTH secretion and action — check Mg in refractory hypocalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the biochemical picture and classic exam trap of pseudohypoparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Pseudohypo: PTH is HIGH (body makes PTH correctly) but target organs (kidney, bone) don't respond → hypocalcaemia + hyperphosphataemia. Classic exam trap: HIGH PTH with LOW calcium — don't assume primary hyperparathyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What are the features of pseudohypoparathyroidism (Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Short stature, round face, shortened 4th/5th metacarpals, intellectual disability, subcutaneous calcification. Genetic: Gsα protein mutation [GNAS1 gene].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the hallmark of hypocalcaemia's clinical features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Hypocalcaemia affects excitable membranes — neuromuscular irritability is the hallmark.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: List the neuromuscular features of hypocalcaemia.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Paraesthesiae (perioral, fingertips); muscle cramps; tetany [carpopedal spasm]; seizures; laryngospasm [life-threatening].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is Chvostek's sign and its specificity in hypocalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Chvostek's sign: tap facial nerve → facial twitch [NOT specific — positive in 10% of normals].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is Trousseau's sign and how does it compare to Chvostek's?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Trousseau's sign: inflate BP cuff above systolic for 3 min → carpopedal spasm [MORE specific/sensitive than Chvostek's].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What are the cardiac features of hypocalcaemia, and what investigation is mandatory?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Prolonged QT interval → risk of torsades de pointes / VF. ALWAYS do an ECG in hypocalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Which investigations are used to work up hypocalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Serum Ca (corrected for albumin) + Mg + phosphate + ALP; PTH level (distinguishes low PTH from high PTH causes); 25-OH vit D (low in deficiency/malabsorption); ECG (prolonged QT — torsades risk).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the corrected calcium formula and why is it used?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Corrected calcium = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin). Always correct for albumin before treating.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Why does hypomagnesaemia cause refractory hypocalcaemia, and what is the action?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: PTH secretion requires adequate Mg. Check and replace Mg if Ca fails to respond to treatment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: How is acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia (seizures, tetany, laryngospasm, prolonged QT) managed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: IV calcium gluconate 10% slowly over 10 min + cardiac monitoring. DO NOT give IV calcium rapidly — arrhythmia risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the regimen for acute IV calcium gluconate 10% in hypocalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: 10–20 mL slowly over 10+ min; cardiac monitoring; repeat if needed; followed by IV infusion if severe.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What oral supplementation is used in hypocalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Calcium carbonate supplements (give with food). Vitamin D supplementation: cholecalciferol (D3) for deficiency / malabsorption.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Why does hypoparathyroidism specifically require alfacalcidol or calcitriol rather than plain vitamin D?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: 1-alpha-hydroxylated vit D — these bypass the renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation step that requires PTH. Plain cholecalciferol DOES NOT WORK without PTH-driven activation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the key exam point on vitamin D treatment in hypoparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Hypoparathyroidism requires alfacalcidol/calcitriol — NOT plain vitamin D. PTH is needed to activate plain vit D; without PTH, the final activation step in the kidney cannot occur.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Exam pearl: summarise the PTH fork.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Low PTH = hypoparathyroidism (gland gone). High PTH + low Ca = secondary (Vit D def, CKD) or pseudohypo (PTH resistance).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Exam pearl: which history question should always be asked in hypocalcaemia, given the commonest cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Surgical cause is commonest: post-thyroidectomy/parathyroidectomy. Ask about neck surgery in any hypocalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Exam pearl: why is IV calcium gluconate preferred over calcium chloride peripherally, and why give it slowly?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Acute = IV calcium gluconate (NOT calcium chloride peripherally — causes tissue necrosis). Give slowly — rapid IV Ca = arrhythmia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Exam pearl: what biochemical combination and physical features indicate pseudohypoparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: High PTH + low Ca + high phosphate = pseudohypoparathyroidism (PTH resistance). Short stature + shortened 4th metacarpal = Albright's osteodystrophy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the clinical significance of hypocalcaemia's effect on cardiac action potential?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: ↓Ca²⁺ → delayed ventricular repolarisation → prolonged QT interval on ECG → risk of ventricular arrhythmia (torsades de pointes → VF). This is a cardiac emergency. Always check ECG when serum Ca²⁺ is low. Correct Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ simultaneously.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the corrected calcium formula, and when is it used?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Corrected Ca²⁺ = measured Ca²⁺ + 0.02 × (40 – albumin). Used because calcium circulates bound to albumin; low albumin → falsely low measured Ca²⁺. Must always correct for albumin before diagnosing hypocalcaemia. In hypoalbuminaemia, corrected Ca may be normal despite low measured Ca.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is laryngospasm and how does hypocalcaemia cause it?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Laryngospasm = involuntary spasm of the laryngeal muscles → stridor → risk of airway obstruction. Hypocalcaemia → increased neuromuscular excitability → laryngeal muscle hypertonicity → laryngospasm. A life-threatening complication of severe hypocalcaemia alongside seizures and cardiac arrhythmia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What investigation distinguishes hypoparathyroidism from pseudohypoparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: PTH level: hypoparathyroidism = low PTH. Pseudohypoparathyroidism = HIGH PTH (end-organ resistance). Both have low Ca, high phosphate. Physical features of Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy (brachydactyly, short stature, round face) are seen in PHP but not in hypoparathyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: What is the management of post-surgical hypoparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Acute: IV calcium gluconate. Chronic: oral calcium supplements + alfacalcidol (active vitamin D — needed because PTH is absent to activate 25-OH vit D in the kidney). Monitor Ca²⁺ and urine calcium (risk of hypercalciuria → renal stones). Target Ca low-normal (avoiding hypercalciuria).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.front: Exam pearl: what is the difference between plain vitamin D and alfacalcidol in hypoparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hypoparathyro.back: Plain vitamin D (cholecalciferol) requires PTH to activate (hydroxylation at kidney, 1α-hydroxylase). In hypoparathyroidism, PTH is absent → plain vit D cannot be activated → ineffective. Must use alfacalcidol (1α-hydroxycholecalciferol) or calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) — already activated, bypasses PTH requirement.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the single mechanism spine of PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Insulin resistance → ↑insulin → ↑LH → ↑androgen production by ovarian theca cells → anovulation + hyperandrogenism. This one chain explains PCOS, its metabolic complications, and its treatments.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the LH:FSH ratio in PCOS and what does it drive?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: ↑LH:FSH ratio [typically >2:1] — LH dominates → drives androgen production.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: How does insulin affect SHBG in PCOS, and what is the consequence?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: ↑Insulin suppresses SHBG [sex hormone binding globulin] → more free androgen circulates.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: On the hormonal axis, what does excess androgen lead to in PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: ↑Androgen → anovulation → oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea + polycystic ovaries.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What are the metabolic axis consequences of insulin resistance in PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Insulin resistance → hyperinsulinaemia → type 2 DM risk; obesity worsens insulin resistance [present in ~50–80%]; dyslipidaemia [↑triglycerides, ↓HDL]; ↑cardiovascular risk long-term; endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed oestrogen [anovulation means no progesterone phase].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the Rotterdam criteria requirement for diagnosing PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Rotterdam criteria: diagnosis requires 2 of 3 features. Other causes of hyperandrogenism (CAH, Cushing's, androgen-secreting tumour, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease) must be excluded first.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What are the three Rotterdam criteria for PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: 1. Oligo/anovulation; 2. clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism; 3. polycystic ovaries on ultrasound.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What defines the 'oligo/anovulation' Rotterdam criterion?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Irregular periods [oligomenorrhoea <9/year or amenorrhoea]; anovulatory cycles → infertility.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What defines the 'clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism' Rotterdam criterion?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Clinical: hirsutism [Ferriman-Gallwey score], acne, male-pattern alopecia. Biochemical: raised total/free testosterone, raised DHEAS.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What defines the 'polycystic ovaries on ultrasound' Rotterdam criterion, and what is the key caveat?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: ≥20 follicles (2–9 mm) per ovary OR ovarian volume ≥10 mL (updated 2018/2023 international guideline threshold with modern high-resolution transducers; the old cut-off was ≥12). Caveat: polycystic morphology alone is NOT diagnostic (20–30% of normal women have it) and ultrasound should not be used within 8 years of menarche.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Which investigations are used in PCOS and what does each show?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: LH, FSH (↑LH:FSH ratio >2:1); free/total testosterone + DHEAS (hyperandrogenism); fasting glucose + HbA1c (insulin resistance / DM screen); fasting lipids (dyslipidaemia); TVUS pelvic ultrasound (polycystic morphology); TFTs + prolactin (exclude thyroid disease and hyperprolactinaemia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Which differential causes must be excluded before diagnosing PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: 17-OHP (CAH); 24h urinary cortisol or dexamethasone suppression (Cushing's); prolactin (hyperprolactinaemia); TFTs (thyroid). Androgen-secreting tumour — suspect if testosterone very high (>5 nmol/L) or virilisation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: When should an androgen-secreting tumour be suspected in suspected PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Suspect if testosterone is very high (>5 nmol/L) or there is virilisation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What are the reproductive clinical features of PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Oligomenorrhoea / amenorrhoea [irregular or absent periods]; anovulatory infertility [cannot conceive naturally without ovulation]; recurrent miscarriage; endometrial hyperplasia / carcinoma risk [unopposed oestrogen from anovulation].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What are the hyperandrogenic clinical features of PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Hirsutism [excess terminal hair in male distribution — face, chest, abdomen, thighs]; acne [androgen-driven sebum production]; male-pattern alopecia [frontal/vertex hair thinning]; clitoromegaly [if severe].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What are the metabolic clinical features of PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Obesity [central adiposity, BMI often elevated]; acanthosis nigricans [velvety hyperpigmented skin at neck/axillae — insulin resistance marker]; ↑risk type 2 DM, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, cardiovascular disease; obstructive sleep apnoea [from obesity + androgen effects].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is acanthosis nigricans and what does it indicate in PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Velvety hyperpigmented skin at neck/axillae — an insulin resistance marker.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the critical conflict in PCOS management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: COCP treats cycles and hirsutism. Clomifene (or letrozole) is needed for fertility. You CANNOT use COCP if trying to conceive — these are mutually exclusive treatments. This conflict is the exam question.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is step 1 of PCOS management (all patients)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Lifestyle — weight loss improves all features (insulin resistance, periods, androgens, fertility). Even 5–10% weight loss restores ovulation in many. First-line before drugs.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is step 2 of PCOS management (irregular cycles + hirsutism/acne, NOT trying to conceive)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: COCP [combined oral contraceptive pill]. Regulates cycles [withdrawal bleeds], reduces androgen [oestrogen ↑SHBG, reduces free androgen]. Best: Dianette [co-cyprindiol — contains anti-androgen cyproterone acetate] for hirsutism/acne. Standard COCP also effective for cycle regulation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Why is Dianette (co-cyprindiol) considered best for hirsutism/acne in PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: It contains the anti-androgen cyproterone acetate.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is step 3 of PCOS management (fertility, trying to conceive)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Clomifene [anti-oestrogen — stimulates FSH → ovulation induction]. Now 2nd line — letrozole [aromatase inhibitor] preferred in many centres (better live birth rates, fewer multiple pregnancies). Metformin: insulin sensitiser; improves cycle regularity + may restore ovulation; adjunct to clomifene in insulin-resistant PCOS.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: How does clomifene work in PCOS fertility treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Clomifene is an anti-oestrogen — stimulates FSH → ovulation induction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Why is letrozole now preferred over clomifene in many centres?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Letrozole [aromatase inhibitor] gives better live birth rates and fewer/lower multiple pregnancy risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is step 4 of PCOS management (refractory / adjuncts)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling [surgical — ovarian diathermy restores ovulation in clomifene-resistant cases]; eflornithine cream [topical — slows facial hair growth, not a systemic treatment]; spironolactone [anti-androgen — used off-label for hirsutism, contraindicated in pregnancy].

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is laparoscopic ovarian drilling and when is it used?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Surgical — ovarian diathermy restores ovulation in clomifene-resistant cases.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the role of eflornithine cream in PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Topical — slows facial hair growth, not a systemic treatment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the role and caution of spironolactone in PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Anti-androgen — used off-label for hirsutism, contraindicated in pregnancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the role of metformin in PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Metformin reduces insulin resistance → lowers androgen → may restore ovulation. Can be used long-term for metabolic risk reduction. Does not directly treat hirsutism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Exam pearl: what makes up the Rotterdam 2-of-3, and does missing one feature rule out PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Rotterdam 2-of-3: oligo/anovulation + hyperandrogenism + polycystic morphology. Missing 1 feature ≠ ruled out.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Exam pearl: is polycystic morphology on ultrasound alone diagnostic of PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Polycystic morphology on ultrasound alone is NOT diagnostic — 20–30% of normal women have it. Needs 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Exam pearl: what is the conflict question in PCOS management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: COCP for cycles/hirsutism vs clomifene/letrozole for fertility. COCP prevents pregnancy — never use both together.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Exam pearl: what does acanthosis nigricans in a young woman with irregular periods suggest?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Acanthosis nigricans = insulin resistance marker. If seen in a young woman with irregular periods, think PCOS.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Exam pearl: is the LH:FSH ratio >2:1 a diagnostic criterion for PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: LH:FSH ratio >2:1 supports PCOS but is NOT a diagnostic criterion — Rotterdam is the standard.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Exam pearl: why is there endometrial cancer risk in PCOS, and what is the action?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Endometrial cancer risk from unopposed oestrogen (anovulation → no progesterone luteal phase). Induce withdrawal bleeds if amenorrhoeic for >3 months.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) in PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: AMH is produced by ovarian granulosa cells and is elevated in PCOS (reflecting the large number of small antral follicles). Used as a marker of ovarian reserve. In PCOS: AMH 2–3× above normal. Not currently in Rotterdam criteria but increasingly used as a diagnostic and treatment-monitoring marker.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Why is the endometrial cancer risk elevated in PCOS, and what is the protective measure?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Chronic anovulation → no progesterone → unopposed oestrogen → endometrial hyperplasia → endometrial cancer (3× risk). Protective measure: induce a withdrawal bleed at least every 3 months (via COCP, progestogen, or by confirming ovulation). Endometrial thickness on USS should prompt further investigation if thickened.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the PCOS screening investigation for insulin resistance, and what does it detect?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Fasting glucose/insulin ratio or OGTT with insulin levels. Fasting insulin >25 mU/L indicates insulin resistance. OGTT distinguishes impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) from T2DM. Annual fasting glucose (or HbA1c) is recommended in overweight PCOS. Insulin resistance predicts metabolic syndrome risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: What is the pregnancy complication profile of PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: PCOS patients have higher rates of: gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension/pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, miscarriage. These risks persist even after ovulation induction. Requires increased antenatal monitoring including GTT, serial growth scans, and BP monitoring.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.front: Exam pearl: what is the differential diagnosis of hirsutism in a woman presenting with suspected PCOS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Polycystic Ov.back: Differential: (1) PCOS — most common, (2) CAH (congenital adrenal hyperplasia — 17-OHP elevated), (3) androgen-secreting tumour (testosterone >5 nmol/L, rapid onset virilisation), (4) Cushing's syndrome (cortisol excess), (5) idiopathic hirsutism (normal androgens, normal cycles). Exclude each before diagnosing PCOS.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the single decisive fork in acid-base analysis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH tells you the disturbance; CO₂ vs HCO₃⁻ tells you the system. pH → acidosis (<7.35) or alkalosis (>7.45). CO₂ is the respiratory/lung control (fast, minutes). HCO₃⁻ is the metabolic/kidney control (slow, hours–days). Match the abnormal one to the pH direction and you have the primary disturbance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship in words?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ∝ HCO₃⁻ / CO₂ — bicarbonate on top (base), CO₂ on the bottom (acid).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: How do changes in CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ affect pH (core relationship)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: ↑CO₂ → more acid → pH ↓; ↓HCO₃⁻ → less base → pH ↓; ↓CO₂ → less acid → pH ↑; ↑HCO₃⁻ → more base → pH ↑.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What are the normal values to anchor acid-base analysis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH 7.35–7.45; CO₂ (PaCO₂) 4.7–6.0 kPa; HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/L; base excess (BE) ±2; PaO₂ 11–13 kPa (on air).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the reading rule that decodes the four primary disturbances?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Respiratory disturbances → pH and CO₂ move in OPPOSITE directions. Metabolic disturbances → pH and HCO₃⁻ move in the SAME direction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: In respiratory acidosis, what is the pH, primary problem and compensation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↓; primary problem: CO₂ ↑ (hypoventilation); compensation: kidneys retain HCO₃⁻ (days).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: In respiratory alkalosis, what is the pH, primary problem and compensation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↑; primary problem: CO₂ ↓ (hyperventilation); compensation: kidneys excrete HCO₃⁻ (days).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: In metabolic acidosis, what is the pH, primary problem and compensation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↓; primary problem: HCO₃⁻ ↓ (acid added or base lost); compensation: lungs blow off CO₂ — Kussmaul (minutes).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: In metabolic alkalosis, what is the pH, primary problem and compensation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↑; primary problem: HCO₃⁻ ↑ (base gained or H⁺ lost); compensation: lungs hypoventilate, retain CO₂ (limited).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the key principle about compensation in the 5-step ABG algorithm?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Compensation never fully overshoots — if pH has crossed to the opposite side, suspect a mixed (second primary) disturbance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is step 1 of the 5-step ABG algorithm (oxygenation)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: PaO₂ / SpO₂. Is there hypoxia or type 1/type 2 respiratory failure? (Separate question from the acid-base analysis.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is step 2 of the 5-step ABG algorithm (pH)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Acidosis (<7.35) or alkalosis (>7.45)? If mid-range, consider a compensated or mixed picture.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is step 3 of the 5-step ABG algorithm (CO₂)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Does it explain the pH? ↑CO₂ with ↓pH = respiratory acidosis. ↓CO₂ with ↑pH = respiratory alkalosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is step 4 of the 5-step ABG algorithm (HCO₃⁻)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Does it explain the pH? ↓HCO₃⁻ with ↓pH = metabolic acidosis. ↑HCO₃⁻ with ↑pH = metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is step 5 of the 5-step ABG algorithm (compensation)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Is the other system correcting? Partial (pH still abnormal) vs full (pH back in range). If pH has crossed the opposite direction → mixed disturbance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the mechanism of respiratory acidosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Hypoventilation — cannot clear CO₂ (↑CO₂).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: List the causes of respiratory acidosis.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: COPD / type 2 respiratory failure (commonest; chronic high HCO₃⁻ is the renal compensation clue); opioids / sedation / anaesthesia; neuromuscular disease (GBS, MG, motor neurone disease); chest wall deformity, obesity hypoventilation; severe asthma — late/exhausted (CO₂ rising = danger sign).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the mechanism of respiratory alkalosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Hyperventilation — blowing off CO₂ (↓CO₂).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: List the causes of respiratory alkalosis.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Anxiety / panic attack (commonest; perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm); pain; PE — hypoxia drives hyperventilation; high altitude; sepsis (early) — direct respiratory centre stimulation; salicylates (early) — direct resp centre stimulation before metabolic acidosis develops.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the COPD cross-reference regarding chronic respiratory acidosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation — chronically elevated HCO₃⁻ (often 30+) is normal for them. During exacerbation, CO₂ rises further. A 'normal' pH in a COPD patient may mask a worsening acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the anion gap, its normal range, and what does it separate?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Anion gap [= Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)], normal 8–14 mmol/L, is the key sub-fork. It separates added acid (gap raised — unmeasured anions present) from lost bicarbonate (gap normal — Cl⁻ replaces HCO₃⁻, hyperchloraemic acidosis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What does the MUDPILES mnemonic stand for (raised anion gap — added acid)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Methanol poisoning; Uraemia (renal failure); DKA — ketoacids; Propylene glycol; Isoniazid / Iron overdose; Lactate — lactic acidosis (sepsis, shock, ischaemia, metformin); Ethylene glycol (antifreeze); Salicylates (late metabolic component).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What are the causes of a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (lost HCO₃⁻)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Chloride rises to replace lost bicarbonate (hyperchloraemic acidosis): GI bicarbonate loss — diarrhoea (commonest); renal tubular acidosis (RTA types 1, 2, 4); Addison's disease; acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor); saline excess (dilutional); ureteric diversion (ileal conduit).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the compensation in metabolic acidosis, and what does failure to compensate suggest?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Compensation = Kussmaul respiration — deep, rapid breathing blowing off CO₂ to correct pH. Classic in DKA. If CO₂ is NOT low in metabolic acidosis, the patient is failing to compensate — respiratory fatigue or mixed disturbance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Why is compensation for metabolic alkalosis limited?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Hypoventilation to retain CO₂ is constrained by the hypoxic drive. pH rarely fully corrects.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: List the causes of metabolic alkalosis (loss of H⁺ or gain of base).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Vomiting — loss of gastric H⁺ (HCl); the classic cause; NG suction; loop/thiazide diuretics — H⁺ and K⁺ loss in urine; Conn's syndrome / hyperaldosteronism — aldosterone drives H⁺ and K⁺ excretion in exchange for Na⁺ reabsorption; hypokalaemia (intracellular H⁺ shift); antacid or alkali excess; milk-alkali syndrome.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: What is the biochemical pattern of metabolic alkalosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↑, HCO₃⁻ ↑ (primary); CO₂ ↑ (compensation — hypoventilation); K⁺ often LOW (co-lost with H⁺); Cl⁻ often LOW (co-lost in vomiting); urine Cl⁻ <20 = saline-responsive (vomiting, diuretics); >20 = saline-resistant (Conn's, Bartter's).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: How does urine Cl⁻ distinguish saline-responsive from saline-resistant metabolic alkalosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Urine Cl⁻ <20 = saline-responsive (vomiting, diuretics); >20 = saline-resistant (Conn's, Bartter's).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: ABG vignette: COPD exacerbation, drowsy — pH, CO₂, HCO₃⁻ and diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↓, CO₂ ↑↑, HCO₃⁻ ↑ (chronic comp) → respiratory acidosis, partly compensated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: ABG vignette: panic attack, tingling hands — pH, CO₂, HCO₃⁻ and diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↑, CO₂ ↓, HCO₃⁻ normal → respiratory alkalosis (acute).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: ABG vignette: DKA, Kussmaul breathing — pH, CO₂, HCO₃⁻ and diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↓, CO₂ ↓ (comp), HCO₃⁻ ↓↓ → raised-gap metabolic acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: ABG vignette: profuse vomiting — pH, CO₂, HCO₃⁻ and diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↑, CO₂ ↑ (comp), HCO₃⁻ ↑↑ → metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: ABG vignette: severe diarrhoea — pH, CO₂, HCO₃⁻ and diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH ↓, CO₂ ↓ (comp), HCO₃⁻ ↓↓ → normal-gap metabolic acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: ABG vignette: aspirin overdose — pH, CO₂, HCO₃⁻ and diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH variable, CO₂ ↓, HCO₃⁻ ↓ → MIXED: resp alkalosis + raised-gap metabolic acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Why is salicylate (aspirin) overdose the favourite SBA trap?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Early = direct respiratory centre stimulation → respiratory alkalosis (↓CO₂, ↑pH). Late = salicylate metabolism → raised-gap metabolic acidosis (↓HCO₃⁻, ↓pH). ABG shows a MIXED picture — respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis simultaneously. The CO₂ is low and the HCO₃⁻ is low, but the pH depends on which is dominant.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Exam pearl: summarise the whole topic in one sentence.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: pH = direction; CO₂ vs HCO₃⁻ = which system.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Exam pearl: how do respiratory and metabolic disturbances differ in the direction pH and the marker move?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Respiratory: pH and CO₂ move OPPOSITE. Metabolic: pH and HCO₃⁻ move SAME direction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Exam pearl: how fast are respiratory vs metabolic compensation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: CO₂ = lungs (fast, minutes). HCO₃⁻ = kidneys (slow, days). Respiratory compensation is quick; metabolic (renal) takes 3–5 days.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Exam pearl: what does it mean if pH has crossed the other side from where compensation would put it?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Compensation never overshoots. If pH crossed the other side, it is a mixed disturbance — two primary problems.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Exam pearl: what must always be calculated in metabolic acidosis, and what does it distinguish?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Metabolic acidosis → always calculate the anion gap → MUDPILES (raised) vs GI/renal loss (normal).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Exam pearl: what does Kussmaul breathing represent and where is it classically seen?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: Kussmaul breathing = respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. Seen in DKA. If CO₂ is not falling in metabolic acidosis → respiratory fatigue.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.front: Exam pearl: why should you not be reassured by a normal pH in a COPD patient?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Acid-Base Bal.back: COPD chronic adaption: do not be reassured by a normal pH in a COPD patient if HCO₃⁻ is chronically high — the true acidosis may be masked.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is hyperaldosteronism, and what is the KEY TRAP regarding potassium?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Hyperaldosteronism = excess aldosterone → hypertension + hypokalaemia. KEY TRAP: K⁺ is normal in 60–90% of cases — do NOT exclude on normal potassium.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is Conn's syndrome, and is it the commonest cause of hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Conn's syndrome = adrenal adenoma (one cause among several — bilateral hyperplasia is commoner).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the decisive fork in hyperaldosteronism (primary vs secondary)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Primary (adrenal autonomous, low renin) vs secondary (RAAS-driven, high renin).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Why does hyperaldosteronism matter clinically?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Common under-diagnosed cause of secondary / resistant hypertension. Cross-ref adrenal cluster: Cushing's (cortisol excess), Addison's (adrenal deficiency — the mirror), phaeochromocytoma (catecholamines).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the classic biochemical picture of hyperaldosteronism, with the caveat?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: HTN + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis. BUT K⁺ is normal in the majority — don't rely on it.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What are aldosterone's 3 actions that explain everything in hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: ↑Na⁺ reabsorption → ↑BP; ↑K⁺ secretion → hypokalaemia; ↑H⁺ secretion → metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the RAAS physiology chain that lets the whole topic deduce out?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Low BP → renin (juxtaglomerular cells) → angiotensin I (liver) → ACE (lungs) → angiotensin II → aldosterone (adrenal cortex zona glomerulosa) → acts on distal nephron.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the result and clinical consequence of aldosterone's ↑Na⁺ reabsorption?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Result: ↑water retention. Clinical consequence: hypertension (volume expansion).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the result and clinical consequence of aldosterone's ↑K⁺ secretion?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Result: ↓K⁺. Clinical consequence: hypokalaemia, muscle weakness, polyuria.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the result and clinical consequence of aldosterone's ↑H⁺ secretion?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Result: ↓H⁺. Clinical consequence: metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Aldosterone is high in both primary and secondary hyperaldosteronism — what separates them?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Renin separates them: LOW renin = adrenal autonomy (primary); HIGH renin = kidney/RAAS driving it (secondary).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: List the primary causes of hyperaldosteronism with their renin and mechanism.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (commonest) — LOW renin, adrenal autonomy independent of renin; adrenal adenoma — Conn's syndrome — LOW renin, single autonomous secreting tumour; familial hyperaldosteronism — LOW renin, genetic aldosterone excess.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: List the secondary causes of hyperaldosteronism with their renin and mechanism.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Renal artery stenosis — HIGH renin, renal hypoperfusion → ↑renin; heart failure / cirrhosis — HIGH renin, low effective circulating volume → ↑renin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the commonest primary cause of hyperaldosteronism overall?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What are the hypertension-related clinical features of hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Volume expansion from Na⁺ retention. Usually asymptomatic. Often diagnosed incidentally or when investigating resistant HTN. Long-standing → CKD, stroke, HF, retinopathy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What are the hypokalaemia features (minority) of hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Muscle weakness, fatigue, cramps. Paraesthesia. Polyuria / nocturia (nephrogenic DI mechanism — high K⁺ flux impairs concentrating ability). Mood disturbance. REMEMBER: K⁺ normal in 60–90% — absence of hypokalaemia does NOT rule out.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Why does hyperaldosteronism cause polyuria/nocturia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Nephrogenic DI mechanism — high K⁺ flux impairs concentrating ability.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: When should you screen for hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Resistant HTN (≥3 antihypertensives at adequate dose); HTN + spontaneous hypokalaemia (K⁺ <3.5 without diuretics); HTN + diuretic-induced severe hypokalaemia; HTN in young patient (<40); adrenal incidentaloma + HTN.
