conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is Step 1 of investigation — the screening test?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Aldosterone-to-Renin Ratio (ARR) = aldosterone ÷ renin. ↑Aldosterone + ↓renin → raised ARR → PRIMARY. ↑Aldosterone + ↑renin → SECONDARY.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Which interfering drugs must be stopped before the ARR, and for how long?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Spironolactone (4 weeks); ACEi/ARBs, β-blockers (2 weeks) — all distort results.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is Step 2 of investigation — the confirmatory test?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Saline Suppression Test: IV saline infusion — aldosterone fails to suppress in primary hyperaldosteronism (autonomous secretion). Confirms diagnosis if ARR raised.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is Step 3 of investigation — localisation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: CT/MRI → adrenal vein sampling. CT/MRI adrenals: identify adenoma vs hyperplasia (imaging alone insufficient — small adenomas missed). Adrenal vein sampling (AVS): gold standard to distinguish unilateral adenoma (→ surgery) from bilateral hyperplasia (→ medical).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the CRITICAL warning about adrenal vein sampling and CT?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Do NOT skip adrenal vein sampling to go straight to surgery based on CT alone. CT misses ~30% of small adenomas and may incorrectly lateralise.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is the decision node in management of hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: UNILATERAL adenoma → surgery (curative). BILATERAL hyperplasia → medical (lifelong MR antagonist). This fork is the entire management question.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: How is unilateral adenoma (Conn's) managed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy — curative in most. Pre-op: correct hypokalaemia; spironolactone while awaiting surgery. Post-op: BP often improves significantly; may resolve entirely.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: How is bilateral hyperplasia managed, and what are spironolactone's side effects?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Spironolactone (first-line MR antagonist). Side effects: gynaecomastia, erectile dysfunction, menstrual irregularity. Eplerenone — more selective, fewer anti-androgen effects; preferred if side effects problematic.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Why might eplerenone be chosen over spironolactone?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Eplerenone is more selective with fewer anti-androgen effects; preferred if side effects problematic.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: How is secondary hyperaldosteronism managed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Treat the underlying cause: renal artery stenosis (angioplasty ± stent); heart failure / cirrhosis (treat primary condition). ACEi/ARB address the RAAS axis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Exam pearl: how does renin discriminate primary from secondary hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Aldosterone HIGH in both. Renin discriminates — LOW renin = primary (adrenal autonomy); HIGH renin = secondary (kidney driving it).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Exam pearl: what is the K⁺ trap in hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Normal potassium in 60–90% of primary hyperaldosteronism. Do NOT exclude on normal K⁺.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Exam pearl: is Conn's the commonest cause of primary hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Conn's = adrenal adenoma — but bilateral hyperplasia is the COMMONEST cause of primary hyperaldosteronism overall.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Exam pearl: what is the ARR's role and what must precede it?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: ARR = screening test. Stop interfering drugs before: spironolactone (4 weeks), ACEi/ARBs, β-blockers (2 weeks).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Exam pearl: why is adrenal vein sampling the gold standard for lateralisation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Adrenal vein sampling = gold standard to lateralise. CT alone misses ~30% of adenomas and can mis-lateralise — never skip AVS.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Exam pearl: summarise the management decision.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Unilateral adenoma → laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone / eplerenone.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Exam pearl: how is Addison's the mirror of hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Addison's mirror: aldosterone deficiency → low Na⁺, high K⁺, metabolic acidosis — exact opposite of hyperaldosteronism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Exam pearl: what ABG combination should make you think of hyperaldosteronism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Metabolic alkalosis + hypokalaemia on any ABG → think hyperaldosteronism. Cross-ref Acid-Base Balance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What is adrenal vein sampling (AVS) — procedure, indication, and interpretation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: AVS: bilateral adrenal vein catheterisation (usually under fluoroscopy) → blood sampled from each adrenal vein + peripheral vein → aldosterone:cortisol ratio compared. Lateralisation index >2–4 (laboratory-dependent) = unilateral source → surgery. Done after ARR and CT confirm primary hyperaldosteronism — CT alone is insufficient for lateralisation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: Why does hyperaldosteronism cause metabolic alkalosis, and what are the ABG findings?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Aldosterone → ↑H⁺ secretion in distal tubule (alongside K⁺). Loss of H⁺ in urine → blood becomes alkaline. ABG: pH ↑, HCO₃⁻ ↑, PaCO₂ ↑ (respiratory compensation). Combined with hypokalaemia and hypertension: the classic 'hypertensive metabolic alkalosis' triad.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: What are the long-term cardiovascular consequences of hyperaldosteronism beyond hypertension?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Aldosterone excess causes direct cardiac and vascular damage beyond BP: (1) left ventricular hypertrophy (more than equivalent hypertension), (2) atrial fibrillation, (3) increased risk of stroke, MI, and renal damage independent of BP. Supports early diagnosis and treatment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.front: How is primary hyperaldosteronism managed in pregnancy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Conn's Syndro.back: Spironolactone and eplerenone are teratogenic (anti-androgenic) — avoid in pregnancy. Use amiloride (potassium-sparing diuretic) as a safer alternative during pregnancy. Surgical adrenalectomy can be performed in the second trimester if needed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the single decisive fork in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Is PTH high or suppressed? A normal parathyroid gland responds to high calcium by switching PTH off. If it hasn't switched off, the gland is the problem. If it has, hunt for the non-PTH cause — almost always malignancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: In hypercalcaemia with HIGH / inappropriately normal PTH, what are the causes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Primary HPT (adenoma), tertiary HPT, FHH (familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: In hypercalcaemia with SUPPRESSED (low) PTH, what are the causes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Malignancy (PTHrP, bone mets, myeloma), vit D excess, sarcoid, thiazides.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the 90% rule for hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Primary hyperparathyroidism + malignancy = 90% of all hypercalcaemia. Outpatient = usually adenoma; inpatient = usually malignancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the PTH physiology anchor, and what does it predict for primary HPT?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: PTH → ↑Ca and ↓phosphate — bone resorption, renal Ca reabsorption + phosphate excretion, activates vit D. Therefore primary HPT → ↑Ca + low phosphate.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the outpatient setting?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Primary hyperparathyroidism — parathyroid adenoma (commonest); commonest outpatient cause of hypercalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is tertiary hyperparathyroidism, and what is the classic context?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Autonomous hyperplasia after long-standing secondary HPT (post-renal transplant classic).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH), and the key management point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Ca-sensing receptor mutation; ↑Ca + ↑PTH but LOW urinary Ca; benign mimic — do NOT operate.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Why is malignancy the commonest inpatient cause of hypercalcaemia, and what are its mechanisms?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Malignancy (commonest inpatient cause): PTHrP (PTH-related peptide) — squamous cell carcinoma (lung, head & neck, oesophagus) and renal cell carcinoma; mimics PTH but PTH itself is suppressed. Bone metastases — direct osteolysis (breast, lung, prostate). Myeloma — local osteoclast-activating cytokines. (SCLC causes SIADH/ectopic ACTH, not PTHrP hypercalcaemia.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: How does PTHrP cause hypercalcaemia and what happens to PTH?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: PTHrP (PTH-related peptide) — from squamous cell carcinoma (lung, head & neck, oesophagus) and renal cell carcinoma; mimics PTH action but PTH itself is suppressed. (SCLC is the classic cause of SIADH/ectopic ACTH, not PTHrP.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: List the non-PTH causes of hypercalcaemia besides malignancy.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Vitamin D excess — supplementation overdose; sarcoidosis — granulomas contain 1α-hydroxylase → activate vit D autonomously; thiazide diuretics — reduce renal Ca excretion; milk-alkali syndrome, immobilisation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: How does sarcoidosis cause hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Granulomas contain 1α-hydroxylase → activate vit D autonomously.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: In the three types of hyperparathyroidism, what are the PTH and calcium in PRIMARY HPT, and the cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Cause: parathyroid adenoma/tumour (autonomous). PTH: ↑high. Calcium: ↑high.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: In the three types of hyperparathyroidism, what are the PTH and calcium in SECONDARY HPT, and the cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Cause: low vit D / CKD → reactive ↑PTH. PTH: ↑high. Calcium: low / normal.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: In the three types of hyperparathyroidism, what are the PTH and calcium in TERTIARY HPT, and the cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Cause: autonomous hyperplasia after chronic secondary HPT. PTH: ↑↑ very high. Calcium: ↑high.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the logic chain linking secondary to tertiary HPT?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Secondary HPT is an appropriate PTH response to low calcium (not a gland disease). After years of this stimulus, glands become autonomous — they keep secreting PTH even after the cause is fixed (e.g. post-renal transplant). This is tertiary HPT.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What mnemonic summarises the clinical features of hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: "Stones, bones, groans, moans."

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What are the 'stones' features of hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Renal calculi (Ca²⁺ stones); polyuria / nocturia (nephrogenic DI effect); chronic kidney disease.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What are the 'bones' features of hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Bone pain, osteoporosis, fractures; osteitis fibrosa cystica (severe/chronic); X-ray: pepperpot skull, subperiosteal resorption.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What are the 'groans & moans' features of hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Constipation, nausea, vomiting; pancreatitis, peptic ulcers; fatigue, depression, confusion, psychosis ("psychic overtones").

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the mirror pearl linking hypercalcaemia and hypocalcaemia on ECG?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Hypercalcaemia = sluggish membranes → short QT; hypocalcaemia = excitable membranes → long QT. They are the cardiac ECG pair.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the core triad of investigations in hypercalcaemia, and what does it show in primary HPT?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Calcium + phosphate + PTH. Core triad — primary HPT: ↑Ca, ↓phosphate, ↑PTH. PTH suppressed → hunt malignancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the role of 24h urinary calcium in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Exclude FHH (↑Ca + ↑PTH but LOW urinary Ca) — must not operate on FHH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What investigations are used if PTH is suppressed (PTHrP + myeloma screen)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: If PTH suppressed: PTHrP (SCLC/squamous), protein electrophoresis (myeloma), imaging for bone mets.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What localisation investigations are used if surgery is planned for hyperparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: USS neck + Sestamibi scan (parathyroid scintigraphy) ± parathyroid venous sampling.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What ECG findings are seen in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Shortened QT interval; Osborn (J) waves if severe.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What X-ray findings are seen in severe/chronic hyperparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Pepperpot skull, osteitis fibrosa cystica, subperiosteal resorption on the radial aspect of the middle phalanges.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: In acute severe hypercalcaemia, why does sequence matter?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: IV saline FIRST — then bisphosphonate. Never bisphosphonate before rehydration; never give dextrose (worsens hypercalcaemia risk).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is Step 1 of acute severe hypercalcaemia management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: IV saline rehydration: 0.9% NaCl 4–6 L/24h. These patients are profoundly dehydrated from calcium-driven polyuria. Rehydration is the single most important step.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is Step 2 of acute severe hypercalcaemia management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: IV bisphosphonate (pamidronate): only after adequate rehydration. Inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Takes 2–3 days for full effect — plan ahead.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What are the Step 3 adjuncts in acute severe hypercalcaemia management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Calcitonin (faster but transient effect). Steroids if myeloma, sarcoidosis, or vit D excess (block gut absorption and vit D activation).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the definitive treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Parathyroidectomy — definitive treatment (remove the adenoma).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: When can primary hyperparathyroidism be managed conservatively?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Conservative if ALL three criteria met: Ca <0.25 mmol/L above upper limit AND age >50 yrs AND no end-organ damage (stones, osteoporosis, CKD, symptoms).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is cinacalcet and when is it used in primary HPT?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Cinacalcet (calcimimetic) — activates the Ca-sensing receptor → ↓PTH secretion; for patients unfit for surgery or who decline.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: How are secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism managed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Secondary HPT — treat the underlying cause (vit D replacement, CKD management). Tertiary HPT — subtotal parathyroidectomy (remove the autonomous hyperplastic tissue).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Exam pearl: summarise the PTH fork in hypercalcaemia.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: High Ca + HIGH PTH = parathyroid (primary/tertiary/FHH). High Ca + SUPPRESSED PTH = malignancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Exam pearl: what is the primary HPT biochemical pattern and setting?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: ↑Ca, ↓phosphate, ↑PTH. Commonest outpatient hypercalcaemia cause (adenoma).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Exam pearl: what is the FHH trap?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: ↑Ca + ↑PTH but LOW urinary Ca — benign Ca-sensing receptor mutation. Do NOT operate. Always check 24h urine Ca before listing for surgery.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Exam pearl: what is the acute Rx sequence for severe hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: IV saline FIRST → then bisphosphonate (pamidronate). Rehydrate before bisphosphonate — never reverse the order.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Exam pearl: how does secondary HPT become tertiary, and the classic scenario?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Secondary HPT is appropriate (Ca low/normal). Tertiary = autonomous after chronic secondary. Classic: post-renal transplant with persisting high Ca.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the FIRST and most important step in managing acute severe hypercalcaemia, and what is its dual mechanism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back:
IV 0.9% Normal Saline (2-4 L/day)

Mechanism:
1. Rehydration — hypercalcaemia causes nephrogenic DI -> polyuria -> dehydration -> worsened hypercalcaemia (vicious cycle)
2. Calciuresis — volume expansion raises GFR and promotes urinary calcium excretion (calcium follows sodium in the proximal tubule)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Why must furosemide ONLY be given AFTER IV fluid rehydration in hypercalcaemia? What happens if given to a dehydrated patient?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back:
Furosemide causes calciuresis by blocking the Na+/K+/2Cl- transporter in the thick ascending limb, reducing paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption.

If given to a dehydrated patient:
- More water lost than calcium -> haemoconcentration
- Serum calcium concentration rises further
- Renal hypoperfusion -> AKI

Rule: Fluids first. Furosemide second.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: In which clinical scenarios is prednisolone indicated for hypercalcaemia? What is the mechanism in granulomatous disease?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back:
Indications:
- Granulomatous disease: sarcoidosis, TB, berylliosis, fungal infections
- Haematological malignancy: lymphoma, myeloma
- Vitamin D toxicity

Mechanism (granulomata): Activated macrophages within granulomata express 1alpha-hydroxylase, converting 25-OH-D to calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2-D) -> raised intestinal Ca2+ absorption.
Prednisolone inhibits this enzyme -> lower calcitriol -> lower calcium.

Not effective for primary HPT or PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the onset and main limitation of calcitonin in treating hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back:
Onset: Rapid — hours (fastest pharmacological agent available)

Main limitation: Tachyphylaxis — receptor downregulation within 24-48 hours -> effect wanes despite continued dosing

Role: Bridge therapy while bisphosphonates take effect (bisphosphonates onset 2-4 days, peak 4-7 days)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the mechanism of IV bisphosphonates in hypercalcaemia, and after how many days does peak effect occur?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back:
Mechanism: Bisphosphonates (zoledronate, pamidronate) bind hydroxyapatite in bone -> internalised by osteoclasts -> inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (mevalonate pathway) -> disrupt osteoclast cytoskeleton -> osteoclast apoptosis -> reduced bone resorption -> reduced Ca2+ release

Onset: 2-4 days
Peak effect: 4-7 days

Mainstay for malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is cinacalcet, what is its mechanism, and for which causes of hypercalcaemia is it used?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back:
Class: Calcimimetic agent

Mechanism: Allosteric activator of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells -> increased CaSR sensitivity to Ca2+ -> reduced PTH secretion

Indications:
- Primary hyperparathyroidism (patients unfit for surgery)
- Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in CKD
- Parathyroid carcinoma

Not effective for PTHrP-, calcitriol-, or vitamin-D-mediated hypercalcaemia (CaSR-independent mechanisms).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: When is hypercalcaemia a medical emergency, and what are the warning features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Severe / symptomatic hypercalcaemia (corrected Ca²⁺ > 3.0 mmol/L or symptomatic) is a medical emergency. Symptoms: bones (pain), stones (renal colic), groans (nausea/vomiting/constipation), psychic moans (confusion, lethargy, coma). ECG: shortened QT interval.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Acute hypercalcaemia management — what is Step 1 (intervention, dose/route)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Step 1 — first and most important: IV 0.9% normal saline, 2–4 L/day IV (guided by clinical assessment).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the mechanism of IV saline in acute hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Rehydration (hypercalcaemia causes nephrogenic DI → dehydration → worsened hypercalcaemia). Volume expansion → ↑GFR → calciuresis (calcium follows sodium excretion).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the key caveat when giving IV saline in acute hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Monitor for fluid overload (cardiac/renal disease); replace electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Acute hypercalcaemia management — what is Step 2 (intervention, dose/route, mechanism)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Step 2: furosemide (loop diuretic), 20–40 mg IV. Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter in thick ascending limb of loop of Henle. Reduces paracellular Ca²⁺ reabsorption → calciuresis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the key caveat for furosemide in acute hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: MUST only be given after adequate rehydration. If given to a dehydrated patient → haemoconcentration → worsens hypercalcaemia and risks AKI. Thiazides are contraindicated (↑Ca²⁺ reabsorption).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the Critical Rule on furosemide timing in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Furosemide must NEVER be given before adequate IV fluid rehydration. A dehydrated hypercalcaemic patient given furosemide will lose more water than calcium → haemoconcentration → higher serum calcium → renal vasoconstriction → AKI. Fluids first. Furosemide second.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Acute hypercalcaemia management — what is Step 3 (intervention, dose/route)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Step 3: IV bisphosphonates (zoledronate or pamidronate). Zoledronate 4 mg IV over 15 min (single dose); pamidronate 60–90 mg IV over 2–4 h.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the mechanism of IV bisphosphonates in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Bind hydroxyapatite in bone → taken up by osteoclasts → inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (mevalonate pathway) → osteoclast apoptosis → ↓bone resorption → ↓Ca²⁺ release.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What are the key caveats and onset for IV bisphosphonates in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Onset 2–4 days; peak effect 4–7 days. Check renal function before use (dose-adjust if eGFR < 35). Mainstay for malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Acute hypercalcaemia management — what is Step 4 (intervention, dose/route)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Step 4: prednisolone (corticosteroid), 40–60 mg/day oral (or equivalent IV hydrocortisone).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the mechanism of prednisolone in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: (a) Inhibits 1α-hydroxylase in activated macrophages (granuloma-associated) → ↓conversion of 25-OH-D to 1,25-(OH)₂-D (calcitriol) → ↓intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption. (b) Anti-cytokine effect → ↓osteoclast activation in lymphoma / myeloma. (c) ↓Intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption directly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is prednisolone specifically indicated for in hypercalcaemia, and what is it NOT effective for?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Specifically indicated for: granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB, berylliosis, fungal infections); haematological malignancy (lymphoma, myeloma); vitamin D toxicity. Not effective for primary hyperparathyroidism or solid-tumour PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Prednisolone mechanism summary — when is it effective in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Effective when hypercalcaemia is driven by excess calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) production or cytokine-driven osteoclast activation. Sarcoidosis/TB/granulomata: macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → ↑calcitriol → ↑gut Ca²⁺ absorption; prednisolone blocks this enzyme. Lymphoma/myeloma: cytokines activate osteoclasts; prednisolone suppresses cytokine drive. It does NOT lower PTH and is ineffective for primary hyperparathyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Acute hypercalcaemia management — what is Step 5 (intervention, dose/route, mechanism)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Step 5: calcitonin, 4–8 IU/kg SC/IM every 6–12 h. Inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption (calcitonin receptor). Promotes renal Ca²⁺ excretion.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is the key caveat for calcitonin in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Fastest onset of pharmacological agents (hours). Effect is short-lived due to tachyphylaxis (receptor downregulation within 24–48 h). Used as a bridge while bisphosphonates take effect.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Acute hypercalcaemia management — what is Step 6 (intervention, dose/route, mechanism)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Step 6: cinacalcet (calcimimetic), 30–90 mg oral BD. Allosteric activator of calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells → ↓PTH secretion.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: What is cinacalcet indicated for, and what is it NOT effective for?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Indicated for: primary hyperparathyroidism (unfit for surgery), tertiary hyperparathyroidism in CKD, parathyroid carcinoma. Not effective for PTHrP-mediated or vitamin-D-mediated hypercalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Acute hypercalcaemia management — what is Step 7 (intervention, dose/route, mechanism)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Step 7: haemodialysis (or haemodiafiltration), using low-calcium dialysate. Direct removal of calcium from plasma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: When is haemodialysis reserved for in hypercalcaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Reserved for refractory severe hypercalcaemia with renal failure, cardiac arrhythmias, or when other treatments are contraindicated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Causes of hypercalcaemia — mechanism and preferred treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Mechanism: ↑PTH → ↑bone resorption + ↑renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption + ↑calcitriol. Specific treatment: parathyroidectomy (definitive); cinacalcet (medical).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Causes of hypercalcaemia — mechanism and preferred treatment for malignancy (PTHrP)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Mechanism: PTHrP mimics PTH at same receptors; bone metastases cause lytic resorption. Specific treatment: IV bisphosphonates; treat underlying malignancy; IV fluids.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Causes of hypercalcaemia — mechanism and preferred treatment for sarcoidosis / granulomata?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Mechanism: macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → ↑calcitriol → ↑gut absorption. Specific treatment: prednisolone; avoid sun/vitamin D supplementation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Causes of hypercalcaemia — mechanism and preferred treatment for lymphoma / myeloma?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Mechanism: cytokine-driven osteoclast activation ± ectopic calcitriol production. Specific treatment: prednisolone; bisphosphonates; treat malignancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Causes of hypercalcaemia — mechanism and preferred treatment for tertiary hyperparathyroidism (CKD)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Mechanism: autonomous PTH hypersecretion after prolonged secondary HPT. Specific treatment: cinacalcet; parathyroidectomy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Causes of hypercalcaemia — mechanism and preferred treatment for vitamin D toxicity?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Mechanism: exogenous calcitriol excess → ↑gut Ca²⁺ absorption. Specific treatment: prednisolone; stop supplement; IV fluids.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.front: Causes of hypercalcaemia — mechanism and preferred treatment for thiazide diuretics?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperparathyr.back: Mechanism: ↑renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption in distal convoluted tubule. Specific treatment: stop thiazide; switch to loop diuretic (furosemide) if diuresis required.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is MEN, and what is the decisive gene fork?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN = autosomal dominant syndromes of multiple endocrine tumours. The fork: MEN1 gene (3 Ps) vs RET oncogene (MEN2A / 2B). Management = surgical excision + family screening.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What are the three facts that crack every MEN SBA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: 1. Parathyroid is in MEN1 + 2A but NOT 2B. 2. MTC + phaeo = both MEN2 types. 3. 3 Ps = MEN1 exclusively.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Which gene underlies MEN1, MEN2A and MEN2B?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN1: MEN1 (tumour suppressor). MEN2A: RET oncogene. MEN2B: RET oncogene.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: How does parathyroid involvement differ across the three MEN types?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN1: ✓ ~95% — commonest feature. MEN2A: ✓ ~20–30%. MEN2B: ✗ none.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Which MEN type features pituitary and pancreatic tumours, and at what frequency?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN1: pituitary ~70% (prolactinoma, acromegaly, Cushing's); pancreas ~50% (insulinoma, gastrinoma). MEN2A and MEN2B: neither pituitary nor pancreas (—).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Which MEN types feature medullary thyroid cancer and phaeochromocytoma?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Medullary thyroid cancer: MEN2A ✓ 70%, MEN2B ✓ (not in MEN1). Phaeochromocytoma: MEN2A ✓, MEN2B ✓ (not in MEN1).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What are the extra features unique to MEN2B?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Marfanoid habitus, mucosal neuromas.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: How is the family screened for each MEN type?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN1: serum calcium. MEN2A: RET genetic testing. MEN2B: RET genetic testing.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What are the three Ps of MEN1?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Parathyroid (95%), pituitary (70%), pancreas (50%).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the parathyroid involvement in MEN1, and its significance?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Parathyroid hyperplasia → hypercalcaemia. Commonest presenting feature. Young hypercalcaemia: check family history + 24h urinary Ca.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What pituitary tumours occur in MEN1?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Prolactinoma (commonest) → ↑prolactin, galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea; acromegaly (GH-secreting); Cushing's disease (ACTH-secreting).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What pancreatic tumours occur in MEN1?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Insulinoma → ↑insulin → hypoglycaemia (Whipple's triad); gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) → recurrent peptic ulcers; VIPoma, glucagonoma (rarer).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the gene in MEN1, and how is the family screened?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Gene: MEN1 tumour suppressor. Screen family: serum calcium (± prolactin, IGF-1, fasting glucose).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What are the features of medullary thyroid cancer in MEN2A?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Parafollicular C-cells → ↑calcitonin; presents as thyroid mass + diarrhoea; calcitonin = tumour marker. (70% in MEN2A.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What are the features of phaeochromocytoma in MEN2A?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Often bilateral and intra-adrenal (adrenal medulla); RET mutation is the genetic cause; α-blockade before β-blockade (cross-ref phaeo). (Extra-adrenal paragangliomas instead point to SDHx/VHL, not MEN2.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the parathyroid involvement in MEN2A, and what does its absence distinguish?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Parathyroid hyperplasia (~20–30%) → hypercalcaemia. Its presence distinguishes MEN2A from MEN2B.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Which tumours occur in MEN2B, and what is the key differentiator from MEN2A?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MTC + phaeochromocytoma (as in 2A). NO parathyroid disease — key differentiator. Most aggressive MTC variant.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the distinctive phenotype of MEN2B?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Marfanoid habitus — tall, slim, long limbs, arachnodactyly; mucosal neuromas — lips, tongue, eyelids; ganglioneuromatosis of gut.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: When is prophylactic thyroidectomy performed in MEN2B, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Prophylactic thyroidectomy in infancy for RET carriers — MEN2B is the most aggressive variant; earliest timing of all.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the gene in MEN2, and how is the family screened?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Gene: RET oncogene (both MEN2A and 2B). Screen family: RET genetic testing → if positive, prophylactic thyroidectomy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the 'phaeo first rule' in MEN2 management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Resect the phaeochromocytoma BEFORE thyroid or parathyroid surgery in any MEN2 patient. Operating on an unprepared phaeo → fatal hypertensive crisis. α-blockade before β-blockade (cross-ref phaeo note).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the definitive treatment across MEN syndromes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Surgical excision of all tumours; MEN2 RET-positive → prophylactic thyroidectomy; timing: risk level dependent; earliest in MEN2B (infancy).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: How is family screening performed in MEN1 vs MEN2 (autosomal dominant)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN1 → serum calcium (± prolactin, IGF-1, fasting glucose/insulin). MEN2A/2B → RET genetic testing; if positive → prophylactic thyroidectomy. All first-degree relatives.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Exam pearl: summarise MEN1 (genes, Ps, commonest presentation).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN1 = 3 Ps: parathyroid (95%), pituitary, pancreas. Gene = MEN1 tumour suppressor. Commonest presentation = hypercalcaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Exam pearl: what single difference separates MEN2A from MEN2B?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN2 = RET + MTC + phaeo. MEN2A has parathyroid (~60%); MEN2B does NOT. This single difference separates them.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Exam pearl: summarise the MEN2B phenotype.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Marfanoid habitus + mucosal neuromas + ganglioneuromatosis of gut — no parathyroid disease.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Exam pearl: what is the medullary thyroid cancer marker and its management implication?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Medullary thyroid cancer marker = calcitonin. RET-positive → prophylactic thyroidectomy (earliest in MEN2B — infancy).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Exam pearl: how does gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) present and which MEN does it suggest?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison): excess gastrin → acid hypersecretion → recurrent peptic ulcers refractory to PPI — think MEN1 pancreas.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Exam pearl: what is the phaeo-first principle and its danger?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Always resect phaeo before thyroid/parathyroid surgery in MEN2 — an unprepared phaeo → fatal hypertensive crisis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: Exam pearl: contrast screening in MEN1 vs MEN2 and who is screened.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Screening: serum Ca (MEN1) vs RET genetic testing (MEN2). Autosomal dominant → all first-degree relatives.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the clinical presentation of a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) in MEN1?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Recurrent peptic ulcers refractory to PPIs; high-volume diarrhoea; raised fasting gastrin. May perforate. Gastrinoma is the commonest pancreatic tumour in MEN1 and the commonest cause of peptic ulcer disease in MEN1.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the clinical presentation of an insulinoma in MEN1?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Whipple's triad: (1) symptoms of hypoglycaemia when fasting, (2) blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L at symptom onset, (3) relief of symptoms with glucose. Raised proinsulin:insulin ratio on biochemistry.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the Whipple's triad and which tumour does it diagnose?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: (1) Hypoglycaemic symptoms with fasting, (2) blood glucose <2.2 mmol/L at symptom time, (3) symptom relief with glucose. Diagnoses insulinoma. In MEN1, consider insulinoma in any patient with recurrent fasting hypoglycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is a VIPoma in MEN1 and what does it cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: VIPoma secretes vasoactive intestinal peptide → Verner-Morrison syndrome (WDHA): watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria (no stomach acid). Rare pancreatic NET in MEN1.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is a glucagonoma in MEN1 and what does it cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Glucagonoma secretes glucagon → 4 Ds: Dermatitis (necrolytic migratory erythema — rash), Diabetes, DVT, Depression. Also causes weight loss and glossitis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the biochemical screening schedule for MEN1 gene carriers?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Annual: calcium/PTH (hyperparathyroidism), fasting gut hormones (gastrin, insulin, glucagon, VIP), prolactin, IGF-1. MRI pancreas and pituitary every 3–5 years. Starts age 5–10 years in carriers.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the 'phaeo first' rule and what happens if it is violated?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: In MEN2, phaeochromocytoma must be excluded biochemically BEFORE any other surgery. If thyroid or parathyroid surgery is done first with an undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma, anaesthetic induction → catecholamine storm → hypertensive crisis → death.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the classic calcitonin level expected in medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) of MEN2?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Raised calcitonin — secreted by C cells (parafollicular cells). Calcitonin is used as both a diagnostic and surveillance tumour marker for MTC. A stimulated calcitonin (pentagastrin or calcium) may be done for early detection in RET-positive relatives.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What makes MEN2B medullary thyroid cancer the most aggressive of the MEN-related MTCs?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: MEN2B is associated with the most aggressive MTC, with earliest onset (may present in infancy/childhood). This is why prophylactic thyroidectomy in MEN2B RET carriers is recommended in the FIRST 6 MONTHS of life (earlier than MEN2A).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.front: What is the RET codon correlation in MEN2 — why does it matter clinically?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Multiple Endo.back: Different RET codon mutations correlate with disease aggressiveness. Codon 918 (M918T) in exon 16 = MEN2B = highest risk. Codon 634 = MEN2A = high risk. Lower-risk codons allow later prophylactic thyroidectomy. Guides timing of surgery.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is T1DM, and what is the decisive fork distinguishing it from T2?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: T1DM = autoimmune destruction of β-cells → absolute insulin deficiency → hyperglycaemia + ketosis. The fork: T1 = absolute deficiency (autoimmune, ketosis-prone, insulin-dependent) vs T2 = relative deficiency + resistance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the mechanism anchor chain in T1DM, and where does it end?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: No insulin → ↑glycogenolysis / gluconeogenesis, ↓glucose uptake, ↑lipolysis → ketones. This chain ends in DKA — raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: How do T1 and T2 diabetes compare on age and body habitus?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Age: T1 younger (<30), T2 older (>30). Body habitus: T1 lean, T2 often overweight.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: How do T1 and T2 diabetes compare on onset and pathogenesis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Onset: T1 days–weeks (rapid), T2 months–years (insidious). Pathogenesis: T1 autoimmune, T2 insulin resistance + relative deficiency.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: How do T1 and T2 diabetes compare on HLA link and twin concordance?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: HLA: T1 HLA-DR3/DR4 (~95%), T2 no HLA link. Twin concordance: T1 30–50%, T2 ~50–90% (stronger genetic).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: How do T1 and T2 diabetes compare on ketosis, C-peptide and insulin requirement?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Ketosis: T1 DKA-prone, T2 HHS (hyperosmolar). C-peptide: T1 low/absent, T2 persists. Insulin: T1 always required, T2 sometimes.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What are the SBA discriminators between T1 and T2, and the single cleanest one?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Lean + young + rapid + ketones + antibodies = T1. Overweight + older + insidious + C-peptide present = T2. C-peptide is the single cleanest discriminator.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the autoimmune mechanism of T1DM and its trigger?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Autoimmune β-cell destruction in genetically susceptible individuals; triggered by environmental insult: Coxsackie B, enterovirus; HLA-DR3/DR4 in ~95%.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Which antibodies are associated with T1DM, and which is commonest?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Anti-GAD (80%) — commonest; islet cell antibodies, insulin antibodies.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the autoimmune cluster associated with T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Hashimoto's/Graves', coeliac, Addison's, pernicious anaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the classic presentation of T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Polyuria + polydipsia — osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia; weight loss — lipolysis + proteolysis (no insulin = catabolism); lethargy, blurred vision, recurrent infections.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: How does T1DM present as DKA (common in T1)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Rapid deterioration: confusion, dehydration, shock; Kussmaul respiration — deep, rapid; respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis; abdominal pain, vomiting; acetone breath (pear-drops).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is Kussmaul respiration in the context of T1DM/DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Deep, rapid breathing — respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What are the fasting and random/OGTT glucose thresholds for diagnosing diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Fasting glucose: ≥7 mmol/L for diagnosis. Random / OGTT 2h: ≥11.1 mmol/L for diagnosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the HbA1c diagnostic threshold, and why is it less useful in acute T1?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol. Less useful at acute T1 diagnosis — doesn't capture the rapid recent rise.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What does C-peptide show in T1 vs T2, and why is it a key discriminator?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Low / absent in T1 (no endogenous insulin). Persists in T2. Key discriminator.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Which antibodies confirm autoimmune T1?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Anti-GAD (80%), islet cell antibodies, insulin antibodies — confirm autoimmune T1.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What does urine dipstick show in T1DM, and what distinguishes T1 from T2?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Glucose + ketones — ketosis distinguishes T1 from T2.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What are the diagnostic criteria for diabetes (symptomatic vs asymptomatic)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Symptomatic: 1 abnormal glucose value sufficient. Asymptomatic: 2 abnormal values on separate occasions. Fasting ≥7 / random ≥11.1 / HbA1c ≥48.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What atypical features suggest LADA / MODY?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Age >50, BMI >25, slow evolution, no ketones, partial insulin response. Check C-peptide + antibodies when the picture is unclear.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What should new DM + weight loss prompt, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: New DM + weight loss → CT/MRI pancreas (exclude pancreatic cancer).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the first-line insulin regimen in T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Basal-bolus: long-acting once daily (basal) + short-acting before meals (bolus).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What are the alternatives to basal-bolus and the role of the insulin pump?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Alternatives: 1–3 injections/day; insulin pump (CSII) for severe hypoglycaemia unawareness or poor control.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: When is metformin considered in T1DM, and what is the role of transplant?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Consider metformin if BMI ≥25 (reduces insulin requirements). Pancreas / islet cell transplant for severe recurrent hypoglycaemia or alongside renal transplant.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the HbA1c target in T1DM, and how often is it checked?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: ≤48 mmol/mol. Check every 3–6 months.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the self-monitoring guidance in T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: 4×/day minimum. Waking 5–7; pre-meal 4–7. More frequent if ill, exercising, or pregnant.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What annual screening is required in T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Retinopathy (eyes), nephropathy (eGFR + ACR), diabetic foot, CVD risk (BP/lipids/smoking), thyroid function.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: summarise the T1 fork.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: T1 = autoimmune, absolute deficiency, ketosis-prone, insulin-dependent. The fork vs T2.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: which combination of features points to T1, and how is it confirmed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Lean + young + rapid onset + weight loss + ketones = T1. Confirm: low C-peptide + anti-GAD.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: what is the HLA association of T1DM and its autoimmune cluster?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: HLA-DR3/DR4. Associated with thyroid, coeliac, Addison's, pernicious anaemia — the autoimmune cluster.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: how does T1 often present and what are the signs?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Often presents as DKA — raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul respiration, pear-drop breath.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: why is HbA1c less useful at T1 diagnosis, and what is used instead?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: HbA1c less useful at T1 diagnosis — doesn't capture the rapid recent rise. Use glucose + ketones + C-peptide + antibodies.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: summarise the insulin regimen, HbA1c target and self-monitoring.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Basal-bolus insulin = regimen of choice. HbA1c target ≤48. Self-monitor 4×/day.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: what should new DM + weight loss prompt?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: New DM + weight loss → exclude pancreatic cancer (CT/MRI pancreas).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: what is the role of C-peptide and what do atypical T1 features suggest?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: C-peptide low in T1, persists in T2 — the cleanest single discriminator. Atypical T1 → consider LADA/MODY.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What are the 'honeymoon period' features of T1DM, and why does it end?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Shortly after insulin therapy starts, residual β-cell function briefly recovers → reduced insulin requirement ('honeymoon'). Lasts weeks–months. Ends as autoimmune destruction completes → absolute insulin dependence resumes. Must not be mistaken for remission.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the Somogyi effect vs the Dawn phenomenon in T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: Dawn phenomenon: physiological rise in GH/cortisol in early morning → hepatic glucose output rises → fasting hyperglycaemia. Somogyi (rebounding): nocturnal hypoglycaemia → counter-regulatory hormone surge → morning hyperglycaemia. Distinguish by checking 3am blood glucose — low in Somogyi, normal/high in Dawn.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the sick day rule for insulin in T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: NEVER stop insulin when unwell — even if not eating. Illness is a physiological stress → counter-regulatory hormones rise → blood glucose and ketones rise even without food. Increase monitoring frequency; check ketones if glucose >13; dose-adjust. Stopping insulin in illness → DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA) and how does it differ from classical T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: LADA = slow-onset autoimmune diabetes in adults (>30 years), initially managed without insulin but progresses to insulin dependence. Distinguished from T2DM by: GAD antibody positive, lower C-peptide, no insulin resistance features. Often misdiagnosed as T2DM initially.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.front: What is the role of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in T1DM, and what metrics are used?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 1 Diabet.back: CGM measures interstitial glucose every 1–5 min → avoids fingerprick reliance. Key metric: time-in-range (TIR, target 3.9–10.0 mmol/L; aim >70%). Also measures time below range (<3.9) — aim <4%. Real-time and flash (FreeStyle Libre) variants. Approved for all T1DM on insulin in UK.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is T2DM, and what is the fork distinguishing it from T1?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: T2DM = peripheral insulin resistance + inadequate insulin secretion → chronic hyperglycaemia. The fork: T2 = relative deficiency + resistance (insidious, HHS-prone, stepwise treatment) vs T1 = absolute autoimmune deficiency.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the pathophysiology chain of T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Chronic glucose/insulin exposure → cells resist insulin → β-cells compensate, then fatigue → less insulin → chronic hyperglycaemia → micro/macrovascular complications.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the insulin physiology anchor in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Insulin stores nutrients (glycogenesis, ↓gluconeogenesis, ↓lipolysis, GLUT4 translocation). Opposed by counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, GH).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the non-modifiable risk factors for T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Older age; ethnicity — South Asian, Black, Chinese (higher prevalence at lower BMI); family history (stronger genetic link than T1 — twin concordance ~50–90%).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the modifiable risk factors for T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Obesity — central adiposity drives insulin resistance; sedentary lifestyle; metabolic syndrome cluster — cross-ref HTN, dyslipidaemia, PCOS (insulin resistance threads through all).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the osmotic/metabolic clinical features of T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Often risk-factor profile is the prompt; symptoms milder/slower than T1. Fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, glycosuria. Acanthosis nigricans — velvety hyperpigmentation of skin folds; hallmark of insulin resistance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What infection-related features occur in T2DM (glucose feeds pathogens)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Candida — oral thrush, balanitis, pruritus vulvae; slow-healing wounds, recurrent UTIs; younger patients can present acutely (even DKA); older patients insidiously.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is acanthosis nigricans, and what does it indicate in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Velvety hyperpigmentation of skin folds; hallmark of insulin resistance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the HbA1c values for pre-diabetes and diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Pre-diabetes: 42–47 mmol/mol. Diabetes: ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the fasting glucose values for pre-diabetes (IFG) and diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Pre-diabetes: 6.1–6.9 mmol/L (IFG). Diabetes: ≥7.0 mmol/L.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the OGTT 2h / random glucose values for pre-diabetes (IGT) and diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Pre-diabetes: 7.8–11.0 mmol/L (IGT). Diabetes: ≥11.1 mmol/L.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How many abnormal values are needed to diagnose diabetes (symptomatic vs asymptomatic)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Symptomatic: 1 abnormal value sufficient. Asymptomatic: 2 abnormal values on separate occasions.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What does HbA1c reflect, and when must plasma glucose be used instead?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: HbA1c reflects average glucose over RBC lifespan (~3 months). Anything altering RBC lifespan makes HbA1c unreliable — use plasma glucose instead.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Which conditions falsely LOWER HbA1c (RBC lifespan shortened)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Haemolytic anaemia — sickle cell disease, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis; acute blood loss.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Which conditions falsely RAISE HbA1c (RBC lifespan prolonged)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Iron deficiency anaemia; B12 / folate deficiency; post-splenectomy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the modern CVD fork in T2DM management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: All patients start with lifestyle + metformin. If established CVD, heart failure, or high CV risk → add an SGLT2 inhibitor (cardiorenal protection). This is the single most testable recent guideline shift.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the lifestyle and 1st-line management of T2DM (with and without high CVD risk)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Lifestyle (always): low-GI diet, exercise, weight loss, smoking cessation. 1st-line: no high CVD risk → metformin; established CVD/HF/high CV risk → metformin + SGLT2 inhibitor.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the 2nd-line management of T2DM (with and without high CVD risk)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: No high CVD risk → add DPP-4i / pioglitazone / sulfonylurea / SGLT2i. Established CVD/HF/high CV risk → add SGLT2i if not already started.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the 3rd-line management of T2DM (with and without high CVD risk)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: No high CVD risk → triple therapy or metformin + insulin. Established CVD/HF/high CV risk → escalate; GLP-1 agonist if BMI ≥35.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the key points about metformin in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Titrate slowly (GI side effects); modified-release if not tolerated. Contraindicated if eGFR <30 — lactic acidosis risk. Hold before contrast/surgery.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the key points about SGLT2 inhibitors in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Cardiorenal protection; risk of DKA (even euglycaemic), genital thrush, UTI.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the key points about GLP-1 agonists in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Weight loss + CV benefit; injectable; preferred if BMI ≥35.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the HbA1c targets in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: 48 mmol/mol — lifestyle alone or single agent. 53 mmol/mol — on ≥2 agents (hypoglycaemia risk).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the review frequency for HbA1c in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: HbA1c every 3–6 months until stable, then annually.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What annual surveillance is required in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Retinopathy, nephropathy (eGFR + ACR), neuropathy, diabetic foot, CVD risk (BP, statin, weight, smoking).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: summarise the T2 fork.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: T2 = insulin resistance + relative deficiency. Insidious, HHS-prone (insulin present suppresses ketones — not DKA). Cross-ref vs T1.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: what HbA1c diagnoses diabetes vs pre-diabetes, and how many values are needed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: HbA1c ≥48 (6.5%) = diagnosis. 42–47 = pre-diabetes. Symptomatic needs 1 value; asymptomatic needs 2.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: when is HbA1c falsely low vs falsely high, and what is used instead?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Falsely LOW in haemolysis (sickle cell, G6PD, spherocytosis). Falsely HIGH in iron/B12 deficiency and post-splenectomy. Use glucose instead.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: what is the key modern guideline fork in T2 management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Metformin first-line always. Add SGLT2i if established CVD / HF — the key modern guideline fork.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: what are the HbA1c targets and why do they differ?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: HbA1c targets: 48 (single agent), 53 (≥2 agents — hypoglycaemia risk rises with polypharmacy).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: what skin and infective signs are classic T2 presentation clues?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Acanthosis nigricans = hallmark of insulin resistance. Candida (thrush, balanitis) = classic T2 presentation clue.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: what is the acute decompensation of T2, and its T1 counterpart?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Acute decompensation = HHS (T2 emergency). Cross-ref DKA (T1 emergency) — the metabolic crisis pair.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Exam pearl: when is a GLP-1 agonist used, and what now drives 2nd-line choice?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: GLP-1 agonist if BMI ≥35. Cardiorenal benefits of SGLT2i and GLP-1 now drive 2nd-line choice over HbA1c alone.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the UKPDS trial and its key message for T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: UKPDS (UK Prospective Diabetes Study): showed intensive glucose control in T2DM reduces microvascular complications by ~25%. Also showed legacy effect (metabolic memory): benefits persist years after the trial. BP control also shown to reduce macrovascular events. Landmark trial establishing tight control benefit.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the SGLT2 inhibitor cardiovascular outcomes trials (CVOT) and their message?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: EMPA-REG (empagliflozin), CANVAS (canagliflozin), DECLARE (dapagliflozin): all showed SGLT2 inhibitors reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and hospitalisation for heart failure in T2DM with established CVD. Drove the 'CVD fork' in T2DM prescribing — SGLT2i or GLP-1 agonist second-line if CVD present.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the GLP-1 agonist CVOTs and their cardiovascular message?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: LEADER (liraglutide), SUSTAIN-6 (semaglutide), REWIND (dulaglutide): all showed reduction in MACE in T2DM with established CVD. GLP-1 agonists also reduce weight and are first-choice in obesity (BMI ≥35) alongside T2DM. Semaglutide also reduces cardiovascular events in non-diabetic obesity (SELECT trial).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is impaired fasting glucose (IFG) and impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) — the pre-diabetes states?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: IFG: fasting glucose 6.1–6.9 mmol/L (WHO/NICE); the ADA uses a lower 5.6–6.9 mmol/L. IGT: 2h glucose 7.8–11.0 mmol/L on OGTT. Both = 'pre-diabetes' (increased T2DM risk). Manage with lifestyle — 5–10% weight loss, exercise; metformin can be considered in high-risk IFG/IGT.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the ACCORD trial and its warning for T2DM management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: ACCORD (Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes): intensive glucose lowering (HbA1c target <6.0%) in high-risk T2DM patients increased all-cause mortality vs standard control. Excess hypoglycaemia implicated. Lesson: targets must be individualised; aggressive glucose lowering in frail/elderly patients is harmful.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the mechanism and benefit of GLP-1 agonists beyond glucose lowering in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: GLP-1 agonists: (1) weight loss (central appetite suppression + delayed gastric emptying), (2) CV benefit (reduce MACE), (3) renal protection (reduce albuminuria), (4) no hypoglycaemia (glucose-dependent insulin release). Subcutaneous injection (once daily or weekly) or oral (semaglutide). Key side effect: nausea.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the mechanism and benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors beyond glucose lowering in T2DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: SGLT2 inhibitors: (1) heart failure benefit (reduce hospitalisation for HF — proven in HFrEF and HFpEF), (2) renal protection (reduce progression of CKD), (3) weight loss (glucosuria), (4) BP lowering. Key risks: genitourinary infections, Fournier's gangrene, euglycaemic DKA (rare). Stop before surgery/fasting.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the mandatory criterion for diagnosing metabolic syndrome using IDF 2006 criteria?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Central obesity (elevated waist circumference) — it is mandatory; diagnosis then requires ≥2 of the remaining 4 features (↑TG, ↓HDL, ↑BP, ↑fasting glucose).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the IDF waist circumference thresholds for metabolic syndrome in Europid vs South Asian males?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Europid males: ≥94 cm | South Asian / Chinese / Japanese males: ≥90 cm | Females (both groups): ≥80 cm.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the central pathophysiological mechanism of metabolic syndrome and what does it lead to?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Insulin resistance (driven by visceral adiposity) → compensatory hyperinsulinaemia → dyslipidaemia (↑TG, ↓HDL), hypertension (Na⁺ retention), pro-inflammatory state → accelerated atherosclerosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Metabolic syndrome increases the risk of T2DM by ___ times and CV disease by ___ times.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: T2DM: 5× | Cardiovascular disease: 2×.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What percentage weight loss is needed to reverse metabolic syndrome, and which diet is most evidence-based?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: 5–10% weight loss reverses most components | Mediterranean or low-GI diet is most evidence-based.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Name two conditions that share a bidirectional relationship with metabolic syndrome via insulin resistance.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: NAFLD/NASH (hepatic steatosis from ↑VLDL synthesis) | PCOS (insulin resistance drives hyperandrogenaemia; 50% of PCOS meets MetS criteria).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Name the 5 pancreatic causes of secondary diabetes.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: 1. Chronic pancreatitis | 2. Acute pancreatitis (transient) | 3. Pancreatectomy (type 3c diabetes) | 4. Haemochromatosis ('bronze diabetes') | 5. Cystic fibrosis (CFRD) | Also: pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: A patient with Cushing's syndrome develops diabetes. What is the primary mechanism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Cortisol → ↑hepatic gluconeogenesis (from amino acids via proteolysis) + ↓GLUT4 expression → peripheral insulin resistance. C-peptide is normal/high (insulin resistance, not deficiency).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes, and what is its characteristic glycaemic pattern?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Glucocorticoids (most common). | Pattern: predominantly post-prandial / afternoon-evening hyperglycaemia; morning fasting glucose may be near-normal in early stages.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How does C-peptide help distinguish MODY from Type 1 DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: MODY: C-peptide is detectable (β-cell function preserved) + GAD/IA2 antibodies negative + autosomal dominant family history. | T1DM: C-peptide undetectable + GAD/IA2/ZnT8 antibodies positive. | Confirm MODY with genetic testing.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is DIDMOAD and which gene is mutated?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Wolfram syndrome: Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, Deafness. | Caused by WFS1 gene mutation (autosomal recessive). Progressive neurodegenerative course.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Which MODY subtype is most common, what gene is mutated, and what is its first-line treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: MODY3 (HNF-1α mutation) — most common (~70% of MODY). | Treatment: sulphonylureas (exquisitely sensitive — low-dose effective). | MODY2 (glucokinase) — mild, stable hyperglycaemia, usually no pharmacotherapy needed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is metabolic syndrome, and what risks does it amplify?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of cardiometabolic risk factors that occur together, significantly amplifying cardiovascular and type 2 diabetes risk. Two major frameworks are in common use (IDF and others).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the IDF Consensus Criteria (2006) for metabolic syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Requires central obesity PLUS ≥2 of: triglycerides ≥1.7 mmol/L (or on TG-lowering treatment); HDL-cholesterol <1.03 mmol/L (M) or <1.29 mmol/L (F) (or on HDL-raising treatment); blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg (or on antihypertensive treatment); fasting plasma glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L (or previously diagnosed T2DM).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the mandatory central-obesity criterion for metabolic syndrome, by ethnicity?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Central obesity (mandatory): waist circumference ≥94 cm (M) or ≥80 cm (F) — Europid; ≥90 cm (M) or ≥80 cm (F) — South Asian / Chinese / Japanese. WHO waist:hip ratio alternative: >0.90 (M), >0.85 (F).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the central driver of metabolic syndrome, and how does visceral fat contribute?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: The central driver is insulin resistance, closely linked to excess visceral adipose tissue. Visceral fat releases free fatty acids (FFAs) and adipokines (↓adiponectin, ↑TNF-α, ↑IL-6, ↑resistin) → hepatic and peripheral insulin resistance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How does compensatory hyperinsulinaemia contribute to metabolic syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Compensatory hyperinsulinaemia → promotes sodium retention (↑BP), stimulates hepatic VLDL synthesis (↑TG, ↓HDL), drives sympathetic overactivity.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the pro-inflammatory state in metabolic syndrome, and when does hyperglycaemia develop?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Pro-inflammatory state: ↑CRP, ↑fibrinogen, ↑PAI-1 → endothelial dysfunction → accelerated atherosclerosis. Hyperglycaemia develops when pancreatic β-cell compensation fails.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What are the key numbers for metabolic syndrome risk?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Metabolic syndrome confers a 5× increased risk of T2DM and a 2× increased cardiovascular risk compared with the general population.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How are NAFLD/NASH and PCOS related to metabolic syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: NAFLD / NASH: hepatic manifestation of insulin resistance; ↑VLDL synthesis → hepatic steatosis; present in ~70% of metabolic syndrome cases. PCOS: insulin resistance drives hyperandrogenaemia; 50% of PCOS patients meet metabolic syndrome criteria; metformin used in both.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How are hyperuricaemia/gout and obstructive sleep apnoea related to metabolic syndrome?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Hyperuricaemia / gout: hyperinsulinaemia reduces renal urate excretion. Obstructive sleep apnoea: bidirectional — obesity drives OSA; intermittent hypoxia worsens insulin resistance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the first-line management of metabolic syndrome, and what can it achieve?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Lifestyle modification is first-line and can reverse metabolic syndrome: weight loss 5–10% of body weight improves all components; Mediterranean or low-glycaemic-index diet; physical activity ≥150 min/week moderate intensity; smoking cessation (smoking worsens insulin resistance).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How is each component of metabolic syndrome targeted pharmacologically — lipids and BP?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Hypertriglyceridaemia: fibrates, omega-3 fatty acids; address secondary causes (alcohol, hypothyroidism). Low HDL: lifestyle is most effective; niacin (limited use due to side effects). Hypertension: ACE inhibitors / ARBs preferred (improve insulin sensitivity, renoprotective).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How is each component of metabolic syndrome targeted pharmacologically — glucose and overall CV risk?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Impaired fasting glucose / T2DM: metformin (also addresses insulin resistance); GLP-1 agonists, SGLT-2 inhibitors for weight benefit. Overall CV risk: statin therapy if 10-year CV risk ≥10%.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is secondary diabetes, and how common is it?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Secondary diabetes arises from an identifiable underlying cause other than primary autoimmune (T1DM) or polygenic insulin resistance (T2DM). It accounts for approximately 1–5% of all diabetes cases. Recognising the cause is essential as treatment of the underlying condition may improve or resolve hyperglycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How is C-peptide used as a diagnostic tool in secondary diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Low/absent C-peptide: absolute insulin deficiency — T1DM, total pancreatectomy, advanced chronic pancreatitis. Normal/high C-peptide: insulin resistance or excess insulin secretion — T2DM, Cushing's, acromegaly, drug-induced. Detectable C-peptide + young age + family history: consider MODY (helps distinguish from T1DM where C-peptide is undetectable).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Pancreatic causes of diabetes — chronic and acute pancreatitis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Chronic pancreatitis: progressive destruction of islet cells (both α and β) → both insulin AND glucagon deficiency → brittle, hypoglycaemia-prone diabetes; often alcohol-related. Acute pancreatitis: transient β-cell damage from inflammation; usually transient; ~40% develop persistent glucose intolerance post-acute pancreatitis; screen at 3 months.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Pancreatic causes of diabetes — pancreatectomy and haemochromatosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Pancreatectomy: surgical removal of islets; total pancreatectomy → type 3c diabetes; exocrine insufficiency + loss of glucagon → brittle; needs insulin + pancreatic enzyme replacement. Haemochromatosis: iron deposition destroys β-cells; 'bronze diabetes' — skin bronzing + diabetes + cirrhosis; HFE gene (C282Y mutation); treat with venesection (may reverse early diabetes).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Pancreatic causes of diabetes — cystic fibrosis and pancreatic cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Cystic fibrosis: fibrosis + fatty replacement of pancreas destroys islets; cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD) in ~50% of adults; insulin deficiency predominates; unique post-meal hyperglycaemia pattern; treat with insulin. Pancreatic cancer: tumour destroys islets; paraneoplastic insulin resistance; new-onset diabetes in a lean, older patient may be early sign of pancreatic adenocarcinoma; investigate if no other risk factors.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Endocrine cause of diabetes — Cushing's syndrome: hormone, mechanism, clues?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Hormone excess: cortisol. Mechanism: ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑proteolysis (→ gluconeogenic substrates), ↓GLUT4 expression → peripheral insulin resistance. Clues: central obesity, purple striae, proximal myopathy, buffalo hump, moon face; check 24h urinary cortisol / dexamethasone suppression test.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Endocrine cause of diabetes — acromegaly: hormone, mechanism, clues?
