conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Hormone excess: growth hormone (GH). Mechanism: GH antagonises insulin signalling (post-receptor); ↑lipolysis → ↑FFAs → further insulin resistance. Clues: coarse features, enlarged hands/feet, prognathism, bitemporal hemianopia; IGF-1 elevated; diagnose with OGTT (GH fails to suppress).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Endocrine cause of diabetes — phaeochromocytoma: hormone, mechanism, clues?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Hormone excess: adrenaline / noradrenaline. Mechanism: catecholamines inhibit insulin secretion (α₂-receptors on β-cells) and stimulate glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis. Clues: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, hypertension; 24h urine metanephrines; adrenal mass on imaging.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Endocrine cause of diabetes — glucagonoma: hormone, mechanism, clues?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Hormone excess: glucagon. Mechanism: direct stimulation of hepatic glucose output; inhibition of insulin release. Clues: necrolytic migratory erythema (pathognomonic), weight loss, diarrhoea; pancreatic tail tumour; ↑↑glucagon levels.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Endocrine cause of diabetes — hyperthyroidism: hormone, mechanism, clues?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Hormone excess: T3/T4. Mechanism: ↑glucose absorption, ↑glycogenolysis, ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑peripheral glucose utilisation also (net effect is hyperglycaemia in pre-existing insulin resistance). Clues: weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance; TSH suppressed; ↑free T4.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: What is the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes, and its characteristic glucose pattern?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Glucocorticoids are the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes. Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia characteristically peaks post-lunch/evening (post-prandial pattern) — morning fasting glucose may be near-normal initially. Treat with insulin if significant.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Drug-induced diabetes — glucocorticoids and thiazide diuretics: mechanism and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Glucocorticoids (prednisolone, dexamethasone): ↑hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↓peripheral insulin sensitivity, ↓β-cell insulin secretion; most common; dose-dependent; post-prandial predominant; may require insulin; usually reversible on cessation. Thiazide diuretics (bendroflumethiazide): hypokalaemia → inhibits insulin secretion (K⁺ required for β-cell depolarisation); low-dose thiazides have minimal effect; risk increases with hypokalaemia; SHEP/ALLHAT trials showed modest glycaemia effect.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Drug-induced diabetes — atypical antipsychotics: mechanism and monitoring?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine): weight gain (dopamine/serotonin blockade → ↑appetite); direct impairment of insulin signalling; clozapine may have direct β-cell toxicity. Monitor fasting glucose and lipids at baseline and 3-monthly; metabolic monitoring guidelines (NICE).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Drug-induced diabetes — tacrolimus/ciclosporin and protease inhibitors?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Tacrolimus / ciclosporin: calcineurin inhibitors → direct β-cell toxicity (inhibit insulin gene transcription); post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM); tacrolimus > ciclosporin for diabetes risk; may require insulin. Protease inhibitors (ritonavir, lopinavir): peripheral insulin resistance; lipodystrophy; HIV-related metabolic syndrome; peripheral fat wasting + central adiposity.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Genetic cause of diabetes — MODY: genetics, subtypes, and key features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: MODY (Maturity Onset Diabetes of the Young): autosomal dominant single-gene defects in β-cell function; HNF-1α (MODY3) most common (~70%); HNF-4α (MODY1); glucokinase (MODY2). Key features: young (<25 yrs), non-obese, strong family history (3 generations), C-peptide detectable (unlike T1DM); MODY3 responds to sulphonylureas; MODY2 (glucokinase) — mild stable hyperglycaemia, no treatment needed usually.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Genetic cause of diabetes — Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: WFS1 gene mutation; mitochondrial dysfunction in β-cells and neurons. Key features: Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, Deafness; progressive neurodegeneration; autosomal recessive.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Genetic causes of diabetes — Down and Turner syndromes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21): autoimmune predisposition (↑T1DM risk); also ↑T2DM due to obesity; both T1DM and T2DM more prevalent; check thyroid function (autoimmune thyroiditis also ↑). Turner syndrome (45,XO): insulin resistance; autoimmune T1DM predisposition; short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, webbed neck; diabetes prevalence 10×; also ↑HTN, aortic coarctation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: Genetic causes of diabetes — Klinefelter syndrome and myotonic dystrophy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY): insulin resistance; possibly reduced β-cell mass; tall stature, small testes, gynaecomastia; ↑T2DM and metabolic syndrome risk; ↑autoimmune disease. Myotonic dystrophy: DMPK gene (CTG repeat); post-receptor insulin resistance; defective GLUT4 translocation; muscle wasting, myotonia, frontal baldness, cataracts; diabetes in ~5–10%; autosomal dominant.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.front: How is MODY distinguished from T1DM?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.back: MODY: C-peptide detectable, GAD/islet-cell antibodies negative, strong family history (autosomal dominant — 50% of first-degree relatives affected), onset <25 years, non-obese. T1DM: C-peptide undetectable, GAD/IA2/ZnT8 antibodies positive. Confirm MODY with targeted genetic testing (next-generation sequencing panel).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the agent selection framework for diabetes treatments?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Pick agents by patient feature — not rote mechanism. The three axes that drive choice: hypoglycaemia risk · weight effect · special benefit/harm.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the incretin axis, and how do GLP-1 mimetics and DPP-4 inhibitors relate to it?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: GLP-1 (gut hormone) → ↑insulin, ↓glucagon, slows gastric emptying, ↓appetite. DPP-4 breaks down GLP-1. So GLP-1 mimetics replace it; DPP-4 inhibitors preserve it — same pathway, two ways in.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Which diabetes drugs cause hypoglycaemia, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Sulfonylureas + insulin only — they force insulin release regardless of glucose level.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Which diabetes drugs cause weight loss?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: GLP-1 mimetics + SGLT2 inhibitors — the obesity-friendly pair.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Metformin (biguanide): mechanism, hypo risk, weight effect, and key point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Mechanism: ↓hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↑insulin sensitivity. Hypo: no. Weight: neutral. Key point: 1st-line all T2DM; lactic acidosis → stop if eGFR <30; GI side effects.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Sulfonylurea (gliclazide): mechanism, hypo risk, weight effect, and key point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Mechanism: stimulate β-cell insulin release. Hypo: yes. Weight: gain. Key point: cheap, fast; hypo + weight gain; avoid elderly/renal (glibenclamide worst).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Pioglitazone (TZD): mechanism, hypo risk, weight effect, and key point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Mechanism: PPAR-γ → ↑peripheral insulin sensitivity. Hypo: no. Weight: gain. Key point: avoid in HF (fluid retention); fractures, bladder cancer.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: DPP-4 inhibitor (-gliptin): mechanism, hypo risk, weight effect, and key point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Mechanism: preserve endogenous GLP-1 (inhibit its breakdown). Hypo: no. Weight: neutral. Key point: oral, well-tolerated; pancreatitis risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: GLP-1 mimetic (-tide): mechanism, hypo risk, weight effect, and key point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Mechanism: mimic GLP-1 → ↑insulin, ↓glucagon, ↓appetite. Hypo: no. Weight: loss. Key point: injectable; BMI ≥35; CV benefit; GI side effects.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: SGLT2 inhibitor (-flozin): mechanism, hypo risk, weight effect, and key point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Mechanism: block renal glucose reabsorption → glucosuria. Hypo: no. Weight: loss. Key point: CVD/HF/renal benefit; DKA, genital thrush, Fournier's gangrene.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Insulin: mechanism, hypo risk, weight effect, and key point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Mechanism: direct replacement — all actions of endogenous insulin. Hypo: yes. Weight: gain. Key point: T1 always; T2 late-stage; hypo + weight gain + lipodystrophy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Best agent for established CVD / heart failure, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: SGLT2i (± GLP-1) — proven cardiorenal/HF benefit — the modern guideline fork.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Best agent for an obese patient (BMI ≥35), and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: GLP-1 mimetic — weight loss.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Which agents are avoided when hypos are dangerous (elderly, driver, lives alone), and what is used instead?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Avoid sulfonylureas/insulin. Use weight-neutral, hypo-safe agents (DPP-4i, metformin).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Which agent is avoided in heart failure, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Avoid pioglitazone — fluid retention worsens HF.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Which agent is stopped at eGFR <30 / renal impairment, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Stop metformin — lactic acidosis risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the best agent in pregnancy, and what is avoided?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Insulin (± metformin). Avoid sulfonylureas and most orals.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Metformin → lactic acidosis: when must it be stopped?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Stop if eGFR <30, renal/hepatic impairment, HF, contrast/sepsis/acute illness.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: SGLT2i → euglycaemic DKA: what is the trap, and what other harms occur?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Can occur at near-normal glucose — the trap. Also: genital thrush/UTI, Fournier's gangrene, amputation risk (peripheral ischaemia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Sulfonylurea → prolonged hypoglycaemia: what additional harms occur?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: + Weight gain; glibenclamide worst in elderly/renal; also SIADH/hyponatraemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: GLP-1 / DPP-4i → pancreatitis: which has more GI upset?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: GI upset (nausea, vomiting) common with GLP-1 mimetics; DPP-4i generally well-tolerated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Pioglitazone → fluid retention: what is avoided and what other harms occur?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Avoid in heart failure; also fractures, bladder cancer.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Insulin → hypoglycaemia + lipodystrophy: what precautions reduce harm?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Rotate injection sites to avoid lipohypertrophy/atrophy. Hypo risk ↑ with alcohol.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the spine of insulin regimens?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Basal (long-acting background) vs bolus (short-acting mealtime).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What are the examples and role of rapid-acting and short-acting insulins?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Rapid-acting (NovoRapid, Humalog): mealtime bolus. Short-acting (Actrapid, Humulin S): mealtime bolus (slower than rapid).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What are the examples and role of intermediate (NPH) and long-acting insulins?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Intermediate NPH (Humulin N, Insulatard): basal — T2 initial add-on. Long-acting (Lantus/glargine, Levemir): basal — flat 24h profile; preferred if hypos a problem.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is mixed (biphasic) insulin's example and role?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Humulin 70/30, NovoMix: twice-daily convenience; less flexible.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the T1DM insulin regimen?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Basal-bolus: long-acting once daily (basal) + rapid-acting before each meal (bolus). Regimen of choice.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the T2DM insulin add-on approach?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Usually NPH once/twice daily initially; switch to long-acting (glargine) if hypos a problem or carer-dependent; basal-bolus if needed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Exam pearl: which agents cause hypos and which are hypo-safe?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Only sulfonylureas + insulin cause hypos — they force insulin release regardless of glucose. All other agents are hypo-safe.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Exam pearl: which agents cause weight loss and which are weight-neutral?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: GLP-1 + SGLT2i cause weight loss — the obesity-friendly pair. Metformin + DPP-4i are weight-neutral.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Exam pearl: when is metformin first-line and when is it stopped?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Metformin 1st-line always. Stop if eGFR <30 — lactic acidosis. Titrate slowly for GI tolerance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Exam pearl: what are the two modern guideline additions for CVD/HF and obesity?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Established CVD/HF → add SGLT2i — cardiorenal protection. Obese → add GLP-1 mimetic. The two modern guideline additions.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Exam pearl: why avoid pioglitazone in HF, and what else does it cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Pioglitazone → avoid in HF (fluid retention). Also fractures, bladder cancer.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Exam pearl: what is the SGLT2i trap and its other key harms?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: SGLT2i → euglycaemic DKA (the trap — normal glucose, still DKA), Fournier's gangrene, genital thrush.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Exam pearl: how do GLP-1 mimetics and DPP-4i differ on the incretin axis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: GLP-1 mimetics replace GLP-1; DPP-4i preserve it. Same pathway, two ways in.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: Exam pearl: what is the insulin regimen of choice and key cautions?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Insulin: basal-bolus = T1 choice. Rotate sites (lipodystrophy). Glargine = flat basal profile. Glibenclamide = avoid elderly/renal (prolonged hypos).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the SELECT trial and its significance for T2DM management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: SELECT (Semaglutide Effects on Cardiovascular Outcomes in People with Overweight or Obesity) trial: semaglutide 2.4mg sc weekly reduced MACE by 20% in non-diabetic obese people with CVD. Extends GLP-1 agonist CV benefit beyond T2DM → licensed for CV risk reduction in obesity without diabetes.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the triple combination regimen at step 4 in T2DM when two agents fail?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Triple therapy options: metformin + SGLT2i + GLP-1 agonist (preferred if CVD/obesity); or metformin + SGLT2i + DPP-4i; or metformin + sulfonylurea + SGLT2i. After triple therapy, consider insulin initiation. Always reassess HbA1c and individualise.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.front: What is the role of bariatric surgery in T2DM, and which procedure has the most evidence?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.back: Bariatric surgery produces T2DM remission in 50–80% of patients. Best evidence for Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. NICE criteria: BMI ≥35 + T2DM (or BMI ≥30 in some Asian patients). Mechanism: GLP-1 surge + weight loss + gut microbiome changes. Remission rate depends on duration of T2DM.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is DKA, and what is its biochemical triad?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: DKA = life-threatening emergency. Biochemical triad: hyperglycaemia + ketonaemia + acidosis. This is the 'no insulin → ketones' decompensation from the T1DM note.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why does T2DM cause HHS rather than DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: T2DM retains enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis → HHS instead. (DKA is the textbook raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the precipitants of DKA ('the I's')?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Infection — commonest precipitant (sepsis drives counter-regulatory hormones); insulin omission / interruption — missed doses, pump failure; intercurrent illness — MI, surgery, trauma; initial presentation — first presentation of undiagnosed T1DM.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the commonest precipitant of DKA, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Infection — sepsis drives counter-regulatory hormones.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Arm 1 (glucose) of DKA pathogenesis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: No insulin → ↑gluconeogenesis / ↑glycogenolysis → hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → profound dehydration + electrolyte loss.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Arm 2 (ketones) of DKA pathogenesis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: No insulin → ↑lipolysis → free fatty acids → hepatic ketogenesis → acidic ketones → metabolic acidosis → vomiting → worsens dehydration.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What accelerates both arms of DKA, and why is it a vicious cycle?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Both arms are accelerated by stress hormones (catecholamines, glucagon, cortisol). Vomiting from ketoacidosis worsens dehydration — a vicious cycle that kills if untreated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the dehydration features of DKA (often 5–8L)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, dry tongue; hypotension, tachycardia, shock; polyuria / polydipsia (osmotic diuresis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the GI / respiratory features of DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Vomiting, abdominal pain (can mimic surgical abdomen); Kussmaul respiration — deep, rapid; blowing off CO₂ to compensate acidosis; acetone breath (pear-drop smell).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the neurological features of DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Lethargy, confusion; impaired consciousness / coma in severe cases; headache (early sign of cerebral oedema — a red flag).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the JBDS hyperglycaemia criterion for DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glucose >11 mmol/L (or known diabetic at any glucose if ketonaemia + acidosis present).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the JBDS ketonaemia criterion for DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Blood ketones >3 mmol/L (finger-prick) or 2+ on urine dipstick.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the JBDS acidosis criterion for DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: pH <7.3 and/or HCO₃⁻ <15 mmol/L — raised anion gap (ketones are the unmeasured anions).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the potassium paradox in DKA — the single most important investigation point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Total body K⁺ is LOW (osmotic diuresis depletes it) but serum K⁺ is HIGH/normal on admission — because absent insulin lets K⁺ shift OUT of cells. Insulin treatment then drives K⁺ back in → serum K⁺ crashes → fatal arrhythmia if not pre-empted. This is why you check K⁺ before every step.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What other investigations are done in DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: U&E — urea/creatinine raised (dehydration); K⁺ as above. FBC, CRP, blood cultures — septic screen (infection is the commonest precipitant). ECG — hyperkalaemia on admission; later hypokalaemia with treatment. Septic screen: MSU, CXR, wound swabs.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the management mantra for DKA, and the two iatrogenic killers?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Fluids first, then insulin, watch potassium. Two iatrogenic killers: (1) hypokalaemia from insulin driving K⁺ into cells; (2) cerebral oedema from over-rapid correction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Step 1 of DKA management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: IV fluids (0.9% saline) — FIRST. Aggressive rehydration — often 5–8L deficit. Start even if acidotic. Restores perfusion. Fluids before insulin — do NOT start insulin first.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Step 2 of DKA management (fixed-rate IV insulin infusion)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hr). Switches off ketogenesis. Continue long-acting background insulin; stop short-acting. Add 10% dextrose once glucose <14 mmol/L — keep insulin running to clear ketones (do NOT stop insulin to protect glucose).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Step 3 of DKA management (potassium replacement per serum level)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: K⁺ >5.5 → none. K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L in fluids. K⁺ <3.5 → senior review; do NOT start insulin until K⁺ replaced (insulin will crash it further → fatal arrhythmia).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is iatrogenic killer 1 in DKA, and how is it pre-empted?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Hypokalaemia: insulin drives K⁺ into cells → serum K⁺ crashes → fatal arrhythmia. Pre-empt: check K⁺ before starting insulin; replace if <3.5; reassess every 1–2h.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is iatrogenic killer 2 in DKA, who is at higher risk, and what is the analogous principle?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Cerebral oedema: from over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality. Headache + irritability + ↓GCS. Higher risk in young/children. Correct glucose slowly. Same principle as osmotic demyelination in SIADH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the resolution targets for DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Ketones <0.6 mmol/L, pH >7.3, HCO₃⁻ >15 = resolved.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How is the transition off IV insulin managed in DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Transition to subcutaneous insulin — overlap with IV infusion by 30–60 min before stopping.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the role of bicarbonate in DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Bicarbonate NOT routine — only pH <7.0 under senior guidance; risks paradoxical intracellular acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the DKA triad?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glucose >11 + ketones >3 + pH <7.3 / HCO₃⁻ <15. Raised anion gap. DKA = T1 emergency.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what are the precipitants of DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: The I's: Infection (commonest), Insulin omission, Intercurrent illness, Initial T1 presentation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what does Kussmaul breathing indicate, and what if CO₂ isn't falling?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Kussmaul breathing = respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. If CO₂ is NOT falling → respiratory fatigue / mixed disturbance. Cross-ref Acid-Base.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: summarise the potassium paradox.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Serum K⁺ high on admission (cells shift), total body K⁺ low. Insulin crashes serum K⁺ → fatal arrhythmia. Replace K⁺ before/during insulin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what are the potassium thresholds for starting insulin and replacement?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Don't start insulin if K⁺ <3.5 — replace first. K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L in fluids. K⁺ >5.5 → none.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: when is dextrose added, and why keep insulin running?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Add dextrose when glucose <14 — but keep insulin running to clear ketones. Do NOT stop insulin to protect glucose.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: who is most at risk of cerebral oedema, and what are the red flags?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Cerebral oedema from over-rapid correction — young patients most at risk. Headache + ↓GCS = red flag. Correct slowly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the insulin rule about background vs short-acting during DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Bicarbonate NOT routine. Continue long-acting insulin; stop short-acting during infusion.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is HHS, and what are its two dangers?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: HHS = marked hyperglycaemia + hyperosmolality + mild/no ketosis. The metabolic emergency of uncontrolled T2DM — often elderly, often previously undiagnosed. Residual insulin blocks ketogenesis. The two dangers: extreme osmolality → altered consciousness and hyperviscosity → thrombosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the pathophysiology chain of HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Relative insulin lack + ↑counter-regulatory hormones → profound hyperglycaemia → ↑osmolality → massive osmotic diuresis → severe volume depletion. But residual insulin blocks ketogenesis → no acidosis, no ketones.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why are there no ketones or acidosis in HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Residual insulin blocks ketogenesis → no acidosis, no ketones.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: On the discriminator table, how do DKA and HHS differ on diabetes type and onset?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Diabetes type: DKA T1; HHS T2 (often elderly, undiagnosed). Onset: DKA hours; HHS days (→ more extreme dehydration).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: On the discriminator table, how do DKA and HHS differ on insulin and ketones?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Insulin: DKA absent; HHS present (residual). Ketones: DKA >3 (high); HHS <3 / trace / none.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: On the discriminator table, how do DKA and HHS differ on acidosis and glucose?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Acidosis: DKA pH <7.3, HCO₃⁻ <15; HHS normal pH. Glucose: DKA >11; HHS >30 (much higher).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: On the discriminator table, how do DKA and HHS differ on osmolality and key extra risk?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Osmolality: DKA ~normal / mild ↑; HHS >320 mOsm/kg. Key extra risk: DKA cerebral oedema (young); HHS thrombosis (hyperviscosity).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the three SBA discriminators between DKA and HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Ketones/acidosis present = DKA; absent = HHS. Glucose and osmolality much higher in HHS. DKA = young T1 over hours; HHS = old T2 over days.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the clinical features of HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Profound dehydration (often 100–220 mL/kg deficit — more severe than DKA): polyuria, polydipsia, dry mucous membranes, hypotension. Altered consciousness — directly proportional to osmolality; focal neurology/seizures (can mimic stroke). Lethargy, nausea/vomiting. NO Kussmaul, NO ketotic breath — the bedside contrast with DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the bedside contrast between HHS and DKA on examination?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: NO Kussmaul, NO ketotic breath in HHS — the bedside contrast with DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the diagnostic criteria for HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glucose >30 mmol/L; osmolality >320 mOsm/kg; ketones <3 / negative–trace; no significant acidosis (pH normal).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the osmolality formula used in HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Osmolality = 2(Na⁺) + glucose + urea.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What workup is done in HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: U&E, FBC, CRP, cultures, ECG, troponin (silent MI), CT head if ↓GCS/focal signs.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the precipitants of HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Infection (commonest), MI, high-dose steroids, glucose-rich IV fluids, new T2DM presentation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the key difference from DKA in HHS management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Fluids are the priority; insulin is secondary and cautious. Residual insulin + fluid correction does much of the work. These patients crash their glucose easily — over-rapid insulin causes dangerous osmotic shift.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Step 1 of HHS management (IV fluids)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: IV fluids (0.9% saline) — the mainstay. 0.5–1 L/hr — slower than DKA. Replace gradually over 24–48h. The deficit is huge but rapid shifts → cerebral oedema. Fluids alone often bring glucose down significantly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Step 2 of HHS management (insulin)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Insulin (cautious, only if significant ketones). Low rate (~0.05 units/kg/hr). Patients are insulin-sensitive — do NOT give full DKA-dose insulin. Only start if ketones present; otherwise fluids may be sufficient.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Step 3 of HHS management (VTE prophylaxis)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: VTE prophylaxis (mandatory). Prophylactic LMWH for all HHS patients. Hyperviscosity + dehydration → very high thrombosis risk (MI, stroke, DVT/PE). This is unique to HHS and not required in DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is Step 4 of HHS management (potassium)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Potassium (same rule as DKA). Insulin shifts K⁺ into cells. Check before each step. K⁺ >5.5 → none. K⁺ 3.5–5.5 → 40 mmol/L in fluids. K⁺ <3.5 → senior review.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why must osmolality be corrected slowly in HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Rapid drop → cerebral oedema. Same 'treat slowly' principle as DKA (glucose) and SIADH (sodium).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the thrombosis complication — the HHS signature?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Hyperviscosity + severe dehydration → MI, stroke, DVT, PE, arterial thrombosis. Higher mortality than DKA because of older, comorbid population. LMWH is mandatory — not optional.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the cerebral oedema (iatrogenic) complication of HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: From over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality. Headache, ↓GCS, irritability. Prevent by correcting slowly over 24–48h. Same mechanism as DKA — cross-ref.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: summarise HHS as a T2 emergency.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: HHS = T2 emergency: insulin present → no ketones/acidosis, but glucose >30 + osmolality >320 over days.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the fork between HHS and DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Ketones/acidosis = DKA (T1, hours). No ketones/normal pH = HHS (T2, days). HHS has higher glucose + osmolality.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: how does fluid/insulin emphasis differ in HHS vs DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Fluids are the priority in HHS — cautious/low-dose insulin only if ketonaemic. Reverse emphasis from DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: why is VTE prophylaxis mandatory in HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) is mandatory — hyperviscosity → MI/stroke/DVT/PE. The HHS signature risk not shared by DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what does altered consciousness track in HHS, and how is it calculated?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Altered consciousness tracks osmolality. Osmolality = 2Na⁺ + glucose + urea. Correct slowly to avoid cerebral oedema.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the potassium rule in HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Same potassium rule as DKA — insulin shifts K⁺ in; check before each step; replace if <3.5.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the bedside contrast between HHS and DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: No Kussmaul, no pear-drop breath — bedside contrast with DKA. pH and HCO₃⁻ normal.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: why is HHS higher mortality, and what are its precipitants?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: High mortality — older, comorbid population. Precipitants: infection (commonest), silent MI, steroids.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What defines hypoglycaemia ('four is the floor'), and what is the symptom fork?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Hypoglycaemia = blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L. 'Four is the floor.' The fork: autonomic symptoms (early warning, <~3.3) → neuroglycopenic (brain starving, <~2.8) → seizure/coma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why are HbA1c targets relaxed to 53 once on ≥2 agents?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Hypoglycaemia is the rate-limiting risk of diabetes treatment — the reason HbA1c targets are relaxed to 53 (vs 48) once on ≥2 agents.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the counter-regulatory defence cascade as glucose falls?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: ↓Insulin → ↑glucagon (first line) → ↑adrenaline (drives autonomic warning symptoms) → hours later: ↑cortisol + ↑GH. This sequence explains why symptoms come in two phases — adrenaline drives the warning; once defences are overwhelmed the brain is starved.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the commonest (diabetic treatment) causes of hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Insulin — too large a dose, wrong timing; sulfonylureas — the oral agent that causes hypos; prolonged half-life → hypos can last hours/days. Precipitants: missed meals, exercise, alcohol, renal impairment (↓insulin clearance).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Which oral antidiabetic agent causes hypos, and why are they prolonged?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Sulfonylureas — they have a prolonged half-life, so hypos can last hours/days.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the non-diabetic causes of hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Insulinoma — β-cell tumour; ↑proinsulin:insulin ratio; cross-ref MEN1 (pancreatic tumours). Alcohol — impairs gluconeogenesis; exaggerates insulin effect. Liver failure — no gluconeogenesis or glycogen stores. Addison's disease — cortisol deficiency → hypoglycaemia is a feature of adrenal crisis. Sepsis, malnutrition, GH deficiency.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the insulinoma picture in hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: β-cell tumour; ↑proinsulin:insulin ratio; cross-ref MEN1 (pancreatic tumours).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why does alcohol cause hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: It impairs gluconeogenesis and exaggerates the insulin effect.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the autonomic (warning) phase of hypoglycaemia — threshold, mechanism, symptoms?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Threshold <~3.3 mmol/L; mechanism: adrenaline / glucagon release; symptoms: sweating, shaking, hunger, anxiety, palpitations, nausea.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the neuroglycopenic phase of hypoglycaemia — threshold, mechanism, symptoms?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Threshold <~2.8 mmol/L; mechanism: insufficient cerebral glucose; symptoms: confusion, visual change, weakness, dizziness, slurred speech, odd behaviour.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the features of severe hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Threshold lower; symptoms: seizures, coma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is impaired hypoglycaemia awareness, and how do β-blockers interact?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Recurrent hypos blunt the autonomic warning response — patients skip the warning phase and collapse without warning. β-blockers also mask the autonomic symptoms (sweating is preserved; other adrenergic signs are blocked). Classic SBA link.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Which autonomic symptom is preserved with β-blockers despite masking?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Sweating is preserved; other adrenergic signs are blocked.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the single decision that determines hypoglycaemia management?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Can the patient swallow safely?

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How is a conscious patient who can swallow treated for hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Oral fast-acting carbohydrate: 15–20g fast-acting carb (glucose tablets, GlucoGel/Dextrogel, fruit juice). Recheck glucose in 15 min — repeat if still <4. Then give long-acting carbohydrate (toast, biscuits) to prevent rebound drop.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why give a long-acting carbohydrate after fast-acting treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: To prevent a rebound drop in glucose.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How is an unconscious patient who can't swallow treated in the community?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: IM glucagon: mobilises hepatic glycogen to release glucose. Works only if glycogen stores are adequate. Fails in: alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition, prolonged fast — no glycogen to release. In these patients: IV glucose is essential.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How is an unconscious patient who can't swallow treated in hospital (IV access)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: IV glucose: 20% glucose IV via large vein (less tissue damage than 50%). Reliable regardless of glycogen stores — always works.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the glucagon caveat in hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen — ineffective if no glycogen stores (alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition, prolonged fasting). Always give IV glucose in these patients instead.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why must sulfonylurea hypos be admitted?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Sulfonylureas have a long half-life → hypos can recur for hours to days after apparent recovery. Always admit for observation and prolonged glucose monitoring. Do not discharge after a single correction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: After recovery from hypoglycaemia, what should be done to identify and treat the cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Review insulin or sulfonylurea dose; assess meal pattern, exercise, alcohol intake, renal function; consider HbA1c target relaxation if recurrent hypos; address impaired awareness: structured education, continuous glucose monitoring.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what does 'four is the floor' mean and what is the symptom sequence?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: <4.0 mmol/L. Symptom sequence: autonomic warning (sweating/shaking/hunger) → neuroglycopenic (confusion/coma).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the commonest cause of hypoglycaemia, and what is special about sulfonylurea hypos?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Commonest cause = insulin / sulfonylurea. Sulfonylurea hypos are prolonged (long half-life) → always admit and observe.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the classic SBA trap regarding impaired awareness and β-blockers?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Impaired awareness from recurrent hypos blunts the warning phase. β-blockers mask autonomic symptoms — classic SBA trap.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the treatment ladder for hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Oral carb (conscious) → IM glucagon (unconscious, community) → IV glucose (hospital / glucagon fails).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: when does glucagon fail, and what is given instead?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glucagon fails in alcohol / liver failure / malnutrition — no glycogen stores. Give IV glucose instead.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: why always give a long-acting carb after fast-acting treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: To prevent rebound hypoglycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what are the key non-diabetic causes of hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Insulinoma (cross-ref MEN1), Addison's (cortisol deficiency), alcohol, liver failure.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: why are HbA1c targets relaxed to 53 on ≥2 agents?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Hypoglycaemia risk is why — it is the rate-limiting constraint on tight control.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the core mechanism underlying diabetes complications?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Chronic hyperglycaemia → endothelial damage (leaky, non-regenerating vessels) + immune dysfunction (↑ infection risk).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the microvascular (glucose-driven) complications, and the lever to prevent them?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: The three -opathies — retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy. Lever: glycaemic control (HbA1c target).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the macrovascular (CV-risk-driven) complications, and the lever to prevent them?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Atherosclerosis → IHD/MI, stroke, PAD. Lever: BP control, statin, smoking cessation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the 'third bucket' of diabetes complications?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Infection & other — skin, rheumatological, hepatic complications — recognition-level for exams.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the prevention fork for diabetes complications?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glycaemic control prevents microvascular; BP/statin/smoking cessation prevents macrovascular — both matter, different levers.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the mechanism of diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Retinal ischaemia → VEGF release → fragile new vessels → bleed / retinal detachment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the findings in background (R1) diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Dot-and-blot haemorrhages (microaneurysms), hard exudates, cotton-wool spots (retinal infarcts).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the findings in pre-proliferative (R2) diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA), venous beading/looping.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the findings in proliferative (R3) diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Neovascularisation (NVD/NVE — VEGF-driven), vitreous haemorrhage, fibrosis, retinal detachment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What defines diabetic maculopathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Any retinopathy within 1 disc-diameter of macula; exudative/diffuse/ischaemic → central vision loss.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and how does it work?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) — destroys ischaemic peripheral retina → ↓VEGF → regression of new vessels.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the treatment for diabetic maculopathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab) for diabetic macular oedema.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the screening cornerstone for diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Annual dilated fundoscopy / digital retinal photography — cornerstone of prevention.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the timeline and characteristic pathology of diabetic nephropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Develops >15 years after onset; pathology = Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules (glomerulosclerosis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the diagnostic triad of diabetic nephropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Hypertension; albuminuria (microalbuminuria = earliest sign); declining eGFR.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the ACR staging of diabetic nephropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: A1 <3 mg/mmol — normal; A2 3–30 — microalbuminuria; A3 >30 — macroalbuminuria.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the first-line management of diabetic nephropathy, and why is it used even if normotensive?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: ACE inhibitor / ARB — renoprotective; reduces intraglomerular pressure; use even if normotensive. Monitor K⁺ and eGFR on initiation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: When must metformin be stopped in diabetic nephropathy, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Stop metformin if eGFR <30 — risk of lactic acidosis (cross-ref T2DM treatments).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the clinical picture of symmetric sensory polyneuropathy (the commonest diabetic neuropathy)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glove-and-stocking, feet first; ↓ vibration/pain/temp; 'walking on cotton wool' → unrecognised trauma → ulcers.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the clinical picture of diabetic mononeuropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Single nerve — CN III palsy (pupil-sparing); median nerve → carpal tunnel.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is diabetic amyotrophy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Lumbosacral plexus — proximal leg pain and wasting (asymmetric).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the clinical picture of diabetic autonomic neuropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Postural hypotension, gastroparesis, gustatory sweating, erectile dysfunction, bladder/bowel dysfunction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the stepwise management of painful diabetic neuropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Amitriptyline / duloxetine / gabapentin / pregabalin (1st-line — switch if one fails).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the convergence point that produces the diabetic foot?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Neuropathy (loss of protective sensation) + PAD (ischaemia) acting together.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the features of a neuropathic ulcer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Painless; pressure points (heel, metatarsal heads); warm foot, pulses present; punched-out edges.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the features of an ischaemic ulcer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Painful; tips and margins of toes; cold foot, pulses absent; pale/necrotic base.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the mechanism and presentation of Charcot arthropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Microtrauma in an insensate, hypervascular foot → osteoclast activation → joint remodelling/destruction (classically midfoot). Presents: hot, swollen, red foot — must distinguish from cellulitis/osteomyelitis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the complication cascade of the diabetic foot?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Calluses → ulcers → cellulitis / osteomyelitis → necrosis → amputation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: By how much does diabetes increase cardiovascular risk?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Diabetes = major atherosclerosis accelerator — 2–4× increased CV risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the significance of IHD/MI in diabetes, including the silent MI point?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Most common cause of death in T2DM. Silent MI — autonomic neuropathy blunts chest pain warning.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the stroke/TIA risk in diabetes, and what comorbidity is common?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Cerebrovascular disease — 2–3× increased risk. Atrial fibrillation comorbidity common.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the PAD picture in diabetes, and what does it synergise with?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Peripheral arterial disease — claudication, critical limb ischaemia. Synergises with neuropathy → diabetic foot.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the macrovascular prevention bundle?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Smoking cessation · statin (atorvastatin 20–40mg) · BP control (<130/80) · weight loss/exercise · antiplatelet if indicated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the recognisable skin manifestations of diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Necrobiosis lipoidica — T1DM; shin plaques → waxy brown/yellow centre, erythematous border. Acanthosis nigricans — insulin resistance; velvety hyperpigmentation (axillae/neck). Diabetic dermopathy — shin spots (small brown atrophic lesions). Granuloma annulare — ring-shaped papules. Candidiasis — vulvovaginal, oral, skin folds.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the hepatic complications of diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: NAFLD → NASH → cirrhosis: strong association with T2DM/insulin resistance. Exclude haemochromatosis if deranged LFTs — iron overload also causes 'bronze diabetes' (cross-ref).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why is infection susceptibility increased in diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Impaired neutrophil function; skin barrier breakdown; stasis of urine (autonomic bladder) → UTI; emphysematous infections (gas-forming organisms in soft tissue / gallbladder).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the rheumatological / musculoskeletal associations of diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Charcot arthropathy (see foot section); frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis); cheiroarthropathy (prayer sign — T1DM); Dupuytren's / flexor tendinopathy; DISH (diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the prevention fork for diabetes complications?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glycaemic control → microvascular; BP/statin/smoking → macrovascular — both matter, different levers.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: summarise retinopathy staging and treatment.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Background (dots/blots/exudates/cotton-wool) → pre-proliferative (venous beading) → proliferative (neovascularisation) → treat with PRP; anti-VEGF for maculopathy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: summarise diabetic nephropathy key points.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Earliest sign = microalbuminuria (ACR); ACEi/ARB first-line even if normotensive; Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules; stop metformin eGFR <30.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: why is CN III palsy in diabetes pupil-sparing, and what is the painful neuropathy ladder?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: CN III palsy in diabetes = pupil-sparing (ischaemia spares outer parasympathetic fibres); painful neuropathy → amitriptyline/duloxetine/gabapentin/pregabalin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what is the classic SBA discriminator between neuropathic and ischaemic ulcers?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Neuropathic ulcer: painless, warm, pulses present; ischaemic ulcer: painful, cold, pulseless — classic SBA discriminator.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: why is silent MI important in diabetics?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Silent MI in diabetics — autonomic neuropathy blunts chest pain; always think atypical presentation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what do necrobiosis lipoidica and acanthosis nigricans indicate?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Necrobiosis lipoidica = T1DM, shins, waxy brown plaques; acanthosis nigricans = insulin resistance marker.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Exam pearl: what must deranged LFTs in diabetes prompt you to exclude?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Deranged LFTs in diabetes → exclude haemochromatosis (bronze diabetes) as well as NAFLD.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why are patients with DKA specifically at risk of mucormycosis compared to other diabetics?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: In DKA, metabolic acidosis impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and killing. Crucially, acidosis reduces transferrin's iron-binding capacity, releasing free serum iron — an essential growth factor for Mucor/Rhizopus species. Combined with hyperglycaemia and immunosuppression, this creates the classic permissive environment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: A poorly controlled diabetic man presents with itching and white plaques on his glans penis. What is the likely diagnosis and what should you do next?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Candidal balanitis — caused by Candida albicans flourishing in glucose-rich secretions. This is a recognised presenting feature of undiagnosed Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. Action: check fasting glucose and HbA1c. Treat with topical clotrimazole and optimise glycaemic control.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Describe the histological appearance of Mucormycosis vs Aspergillosis on tissue biopsy.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back:
Mucormycosis: wide, non-septate (aseptate), ribbon-like hyphae branching at ~90° (right angles), with angioinvasion and necrosis.
Aspergillosis: narrow, septate hyphae branching at ~45° (acute angles), also angioinvasive.
Memory: Mucor = wide + 90° + no septa. Aspergillus = narrow + 45° + septa.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: A DKA patient develops fever, bloody nasal discharge, and a black lesion on the hard palate. What is the diagnosis, and what are the immediate management steps?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back:
Diagnosis: Rhinocerebral Mucormycosis — a life-threatening emergency.
Management:
1. Urgent CT sinuses/orbit/brain (assess extent)
2. IV liposomal amphotericin B immediately (do NOT use voriconazole — no activity against Mucor)
3. Emergency surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue
4. Treat underlying DKA aggressively
Mortality >50% if treatment delayed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why does tinea pedis carry particular danger in a patient with diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Tinea pedis causes interdigital maceration and skin breakdown, creating a portal of entry for bacteria (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus). In diabetics, peripheral neuropathy means the patient may not feel early infection, and peripheral arterial disease impairs healing. This can rapidly escalate to cellulitis, osteomyelitis, or necrotising fasciitis. Feet should be examined at every diabetic review.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Which antifungal has NO activity against Mucormycosis and must NOT be used as sole therapy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Voriconazole — the first-line agent for invasive Aspergillosis — has no clinically meaningful activity against Mucorales. Using voriconazole alone for mucormycosis is potentially fatal. First-line treatment is liposomal amphotericin B (+ surgical debridement). Posaconazole and isavuconazole have activity and are used for step-down or salvage therapy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why is diabetes mellitus a major risk factor for fungal infections?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Diabetes mellitus is one of the strongest risk factors for invasive and recurrent fungal infections. Both poor glycaemic control and the downstream immune defects converge to create a highly permissive environment for fungal proliferation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How does impaired neutrophil function predispose diabetics to fungal infection?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Hyperglycaemia reduces neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and intracellular killing (oxidative burst).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How does reduced complement activity predispose diabetics to fungal infection?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glycosylation of complement proteins diminishes opsonisation and fungal clearance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How does impaired T-cell function predispose diabetics to fungal infection?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Defective cell-mediated immunity reduces antifungal defences, especially important in mucosal candidiasis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How does high glucose act as a fungal substrate in diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Glucose-rich secretions (saliva, urine, vaginal fluid) directly fuel Candida and other fungal growth.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How do peripheral vascular disease and the acidic environment in DKA predispose to fungal infection?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Peripheral vascular disease: poor tissue perfusion reduces delivery of immune cells and antifungal drugs to infected sites. Acidic environment in DKA: ketoacidosis impairs transferrin-mediated iron chelation → free iron available for Mucor growth.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the causative organism of candidiasis in diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Candida albicans (most common); also C. glabrata, C. tropicalis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush): presentation, clinical pearl, and treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Presentation: white, creamy plaques on an erythematous base; scrape off to reveal bleeding mucosa. Clinical pearl: common in poorly controlled T2DM/T1DM and with inhaled steroids/immunosuppression. Treatment: nystatin suspension or oral fluconazole. (Note: SGLT2 inhibitors predispose to GENITAL candidiasis, not oral thrush.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Vulvovaginal candidiasis: presentation, clinical pearl, and treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Presentation: recurrent thick white discharge, pruritus, erythema. Clinical pearl: recurrent episodes (>4/year) → screen for T2DM. Treatment: topical clotrimazole or oral fluconazole.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Candidal balanitis: presentation, clinical pearl, and treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Presentation: erythema, white plaques, itch on glans penis. Clinical pearl: presenting feature of undiagnosed T2DM in men — always check HbA1c. Treatment: topical clotrimazole; treat underlying hyperglycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Oesophageal candidiasis: presentation, clinical pearl, and treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Presentation: odynophagia, dysphagia; white plaques on endoscopy. Clinical pearl: occurs in immunosuppressed diabetics (e.g. on steroids, post-transplant). Treatment: oral/IV fluconazole; itraconazole if resistant.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Candidaemia: presentation, clinical pearl, and treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Presentation: persistent fever unresponsive to antibiotics. Clinical pearl: hospitalised diabetics with IV lines, post-surgery, TPN — high mortality. Treatment: IV echinocandin (caspofungin) or amphotericin B; remove IV lines.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: How do SGLT2 inhibitors increase the risk of candidiasis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin cause glycosuria, directly increasing the glucose substrate available in the genital tract. Genital mycotic infections are a recognised class side-effect — counsel patients at initiation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why is mucormycosis (zygomycosis) so high-yield, and what is the classic exam scenario?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Mortality >50% if diagnosis or treatment is delayed. This is a medical and surgical emergency. Classic exam scenario: DKA patient with black nasal eschar and orbital signs.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the causative organisms of mucormycosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Rhizopus arrhizus (formerly R. oryzae) is the commonest species, plus other Mucorales (Mucor, Rhizopus, Lichtheimia spp.) — the 'bread mould fungi'.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the classic risk triad for mucormycosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: DKA + diabetes + immunosuppression (steroids, haematological malignancy, transplant).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why is DKA uniquely permissive for mucormycosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Acidosis impairs neutrophil killing AND reduces transferrin iron-binding capacity → free serum iron becomes available as an essential fungal growth factor for Mucor species.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the clinical forms of mucormycosis and their frequency/features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Rhinocerebral — most common (~50%); nasal sinuses → hard palate → orbit → cavernous sinus → brain. Pulmonary — haematological malignancy > diabetes; cavitating pneumonia, haemoptysis. Cutaneous — trauma, burns, IV sites; rapidly spreading necrotic wound. Gastrointestinal — rare; neonates, malnutrition; bowel necrosis, perforation. Disseminated — profound immunosuppression; multi-organ failure, near 100% mortality.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the four stages of rhinocerebral mucormycosis progression?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: 1. Nasal/sinus stage: nasal congestion, bloody discharge, facial pain, fever. 2. Palatal stage: black eschar on hard palate or nasal septum (pathognomonic — do not debride without surgical prep). 3. Orbital stage: proptosis, periorbital oedema, ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI palsy), loss of vision. 4. Cerebral stage: cavernous sinus thrombosis, altered consciousness, hemiplegia, death.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why is angioinvasion the hallmark of mucormycosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Mucor invades blood vessel walls → vascular thrombosis → tissue ischaemia → black necrotic tissue. This explains the rapid, devastating spread and the black eschar.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What investigations are used in mucormycosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: CT sinuses + orbit + brain (with contrast): sinus opacification, bony erosion, orbital infiltration. MRI brain: cavernous sinus involvement, cerebral extension. Biopsy (gold standard): histology shows wide, non-septate (aseptate), ribbon-like hyphae branching at ~90° angles with vascular invasion and necrosis. Fungal culture: slow — do not wait for culture before treating.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Mucormycosis vs aspergillosis: how do the hyphae and branching angle differ?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Mucormycosis: wide, non-septate (ribbon-like) hyphae; branching ~90° (right angle). Aspergillosis: narrow, septate hyphae; branching ~45° (acute angle).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Mucormycosis vs aspergillosis: how do the classic setting, serum galactomannan, and first-line treatment differ?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Classic setting: mucormycosis — DKA, diabetics; aspergillosis — neutropenia, haematological malignancy. Serum galactomannan: mucormycosis negative; aspergillosis positive. First-line treatment: mucormycosis — liposomal amphotericin B; aspergillosis — voriconazole.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the dual-pronged emergency treatment approach for mucormycosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: 1. Surgical: urgent, aggressive surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue (repeated if necessary); orbital exenteration may be required to prevent cerebral spread. 2. Medical: IV liposomal amphotericin B (preferred — less nephrotoxic), 5–10 mg/kg/day; posaconazole or isavuconazole as step-down or salvage therapy. 3. Control the predisposing condition: treat DKA, reverse immunosuppression where possible, optimise glycaemic control.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Why is voriconazole a critical distinction in mucormycosis treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Voriconazole (used for Aspergillus) has no activity against Mucor — a critical distinction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the causative organisms of dermatophytosis (tinea infections)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum spp.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Tinea pedis: site, clinical significance in diabetes, and treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Site: interdigital spaces of feet. Clinical significance: portal of entry for bacterial cellulitis and diabetic foot infections — examine feet at every visit. Treatment: topical terbinafine or clotrimazole × 2–4 weeks.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Tinea unguium (onychomycosis): site, clinical significance in diabetes, and treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Site: nails (toenails > fingernails). Clinical significance: thickened, crumbling, discoloured nails — trauma risk in neuropathy; portal of entry for serious infection. Treatment: oral terbinafine × 6 weeks (fingernail) or 12 weeks (toenail); amorolfine lacquer for mild cases.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Tinea cruris and tinea corporis: site, significance, and treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Tinea cruris: site groin; more frequent and severe in obese, poorly controlled diabetics; topical terbinafine or clotrimazole. Tinea corporis: site trunk/limbs; ring-shaped lesion with central clearing, may be extensive; topical antifungals, oral if widespread.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the diabetic foot care pearl regarding tinea pedis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Tinea pedis in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease is a high-risk combination. The patient may not feel the interdigital maceration, which provides a route for Staphylococcus/Streptococcus entry and rapidly ascending cellulitis or necrotising fasciitis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What is the causative organism of cryptococcosis, and how diabetic-specific is it?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Cryptococcus neoformans (encapsulated yeast). Less diabetic-specific; predominantly a disease of profound cell-mediated immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS CD4 <100, solid organ transplant). However, poorly controlled diabetics with additional immunosuppression (e.g. steroid use) may be at risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: What are the key presentations, diagnosis, and treatment of cryptococcosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Key presentations: cryptococcal meningitis (subacute; headache, fever, stiff neck), pulmonary cryptococcosis. Diagnosis: India ink stain (encapsulated yeast), serum/CSF cryptococcal antigen (CrAg), fungal culture. Treatment: liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine (induction) → fluconazole (consolidation/maintenance).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Summary — Candida spp. in diabetes: common form, high-yield fact, and first-line treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Common form: oropharyngeal, vulvovaginal, balanitis. High-yield fact: recurrent VVC or balanitis → screen for T2DM; SGLT2i increases risk. First-line: fluconazole / nystatin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Summary — Rhizopus/Mucor in diabetes: common form, high-yield fact, and first-line treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Common form: rhinocerebral mucormycosis. High-yield fact: DKA + black eschar = emergency; non-septate hyphae at 90°; liposomal amphotericin B + surgery. First-line: liposomal amphotericin B + surgical debridement.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Summary — Trichophyton in diabetes: common form, high-yield fact, and first-line treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Common form: tinea pedis, onychomycosis. High-yield fact: entry point for bacterial cellulitis in diabetic foot. First-line: terbinafine (topical/oral).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.front: Summary — Cryptococcus neoformans in diabetes: common form, high-yield fact, and first-line treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.back: Common form: meningitis (severe immunosuppression). High-yield fact: India ink + CrAg; encapsulated yeast; less diabetic-specific. First-line: amphotericin B + flucytosine → fluconazole.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Neck Lumps — Approach
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Thyroid vs non-thyroid lumps: thyroid lumps move with swallowing (tethered to trachea). Non-thyroid neck lumps: lymph nodes (most common), cysts (thyroglossal, branchial, cystic hygroma), salivary gland pathology. Assess: site, size, consistency, mobility, transillumination.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Goitre — Investigation Approach
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: 1. TFTs (euthyroid vs hyper/hypothyroid) | 2. Thyroid USS (nodule characterisation) | 3. FNA if USS suspicious | 4. Radionuclide scan if functional nodule | 5. CT/MRI if retrosternal

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Solitary thyroid nodule — red flags
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Male sex, age <20 or >70, rapid growth, hard/fixed, hoarseness (RLN invasion), lymphadenopathy, prior neck irradiation → urgent FNA/USS

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: What is a goitre, and what is the assessment triad?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Goitre = any enlargement of the thyroid gland, regardless of thyroid function. The majority of goitres in clinical practice are euthyroid — normal TFTs. Always assess: function (TFTs), morphology (USS), and cytology (FNA) when indicated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Simple / colloid goitre — key features, TFTs, and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Soft, diffuse; commonest worldwide; due to iodine deficiency. TFTs normal (euthyroid). Endemic in iodine-poor regions; moves on swallowing; usually no treatment needed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Multinodular goitre (MNG) — key features, TFTs, and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Irregular, lobulated; multiple nodules; most common cause in iodine-sufficient countries. TFTs usually normal; may become toxic (toxic MNG). Can cause compressive symptoms; risk of malignant transformation low but present.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Physiological goitre — key features, TFTs, and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Diffuse, soft; puberty or pregnancy. TFTs normal. Increased thyroid demand; resolves spontaneously; no treatment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Hashimoto's thyroiditis — key features, TFTs, and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Firm, rubbery, may be irregular; autoimmune. TFTs euthyroid early → hypothyroid later; anti-TPO antibodies positive. Most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient world; increased lymphoma risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Graves' disease — key features, TFTs, and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Diffuse, smooth, bruit; TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb). TFTs hyperthyroid (↓TSH, ↑FT4). Thyroid bruit is pathognomonic; associated with pretibial myxoedema, exophthalmos.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis — key features, TFTs, and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Painful, tender goitre; post-viral; elevated ESR/CRP. TFTs: transient thyrotoxicosis → hypothyroid → euthyroid. Treat with NSAIDs/aspirin; steroids for severe cases; usually self-limiting.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Riedel's thyroiditis — key features, TFTs, and notes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Woody hard, fibrous; can invade local structures; rare. TFTs hypothyroid (if extensive fibrosis). Can mimic malignancy clinically; associated with IgG4-related disease; treat with steroids/tamoxifen.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Thyroid malignancy — key features, TFTs, and the types by prognosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Hard, irregular, rapidly growing; lymphadenopathy; hoarseness (RLN invasion). TFTs usually normal. Papillary (most common, good prognosis); follicular; medullary (MEN2); anaplastic (worst prognosis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Approach to a neck lump: what does movement with swallowing vs tongue protrusion tell you?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Does it move with swallowing? If YES → thyroid origin (thyroid moves with larynx during swallowing). Does it move with tongue protrusion? If YES → thyroglossal cyst (attached to hyoid bone / thyroglossal tract).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Approach to a neck lump: what is the differential for midline vs lateral lumps?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Midline: thyroid, thyroglossal cyst, dermoid, submental lymph node. Lateral: lymph node, branchial cyst, parotid, carotid body tumour.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Approach to a neck lump: what does consistency suggest?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Soft (colloid/simple goitre), firm (Hashimoto's, MNG), hard (malignancy, Riedel's), fluctuant (cyst, abscess).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Approach to a neck lump: what do a pulsatile lump and transillumination suggest?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Pulsatile? → carotid artery aneurysm, carotid body tumour (mobile side-to-side, not vertically). Transilluminates? → cystic lesion (hygroma, branchial cyst).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Neck lump table: thyroid goitre/nodule — location, key features, movement?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Location: anterior midline/bilateral. Key features: moves with thyroid; TFTs + USS. Moves with swallowing: yes. Moves with tongue protrusion: no.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Neck lump table: thyroglossal cyst — location, key features, movement?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Location: midline, at/below hyoid. Key features: young patient; smooth, cystic. Moves with swallowing: yes. Moves with tongue protrusion: yes (pathognomonic).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Neck lump table: cervical lymph node — location, key features, movement?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Location: along sternocleidomastoid. Key features: reactive, lymphoma, metastatic; assess for primary. Moves with swallowing: no. Moves with tongue protrusion: no.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Neck lump table: branchial cyst — location, key features, movement?
