conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Location: lateral, anterior to SCM (upper third). Key features: young adult; smooth, fluctuant, transilluminates. Moves with swallowing: no. Moves with tongue protrusion: no.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Neck lump table: parotid swelling — location, key features, movement?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Location: preauricular / angle of jaw. Key features: fills the space between mandible and mastoid. Moves with swallowing: no. Moves with tongue protrusion: no.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Neck lump table: carotid body tumour — location, key features, movement?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Location: bifurcation of carotid (upper neck). Key features: pulsatile; mobile side-to-side only; splays carotids on angiography. Moves with swallowing: no. Moves with tongue protrusion: no.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Investigations for goitre/thyroid nodule: role of TFTs?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: TFTs (TSH, FT4, FT3) assess function (hypo/hyper/euthyroid). First-line; suppressed TSH → consider toxic nodule; always do before FNA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Investigations for goitre/thyroid nodule: role of thyroid antibodies?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Anti-TPO (Hashimoto's); TRAb (Graves'); anti-Tg. Useful for autoimmune aetiology; anti-TPO present in 95% of Hashimoto's.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Investigations for goitre/thyroid nodule: role of USS neck and malignant features?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: USS neck assesses morphology, nodule characteristics, lymph nodes. U-TIRADS classification guides FNA; malignant features: hypoechoic, microcalcification, irregular margins, taller-than-wide, increased vascularity.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Investigations for goitre/thyroid nodule: Bethesda/Thy classification on FNA — which grades go to surgery?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) gives cytological diagnosis. Bethesda / Thy classification: Thy1 (inadequate), Thy2 (benign), Thy3a/3f (follicular lesion), Thy4 (suspicious), Thy5 (malignant). Thy3–5 → surgery.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Investigations for goitre/thyroid nodule: what does an isotope scan show for hot, cold, and warm nodules?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Isotope scan (Tc-99m or I-123) assesses function of individual nodules. Hot nodule = autonomous/functioning → benign (rarely malignant). Cold nodule = non-functioning → ~5–15% malignancy risk → needs FNA. Warm = indeterminate.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Investigations for goitre/thyroid nodule: role of CT/MRI neck and chest?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Assess extent of disease, retrosternal/substernal extension. Assess tracheal deviation/compression, SVC obstruction; CT with contrast may interfere with radioiodine treatment (iodine load).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Investigations for goitre/thyroid nodule: role of calcitonin?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Screen for medullary thyroid carcinoma. Elevated in MTC; also check CEA; genetic testing (RET mutation) for MEN2.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Investigations for goitre/thyroid nodule: role of laryngoscopy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Vocal cord assessment. Pre-operatively or if hoarseness present — assess RLN function.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: What are the indications for surgery (thyroidectomy) — compressive and cytology criteria?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Compressive symptoms: dysphagia, dyspnoea, stridor, SVC obstruction, tracheal deviation >1 cm. Suspicious or malignant cytology: Thy3f (follicular lesion — diagnostic lobectomy), Thy4, Thy5.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: What are the remaining indications for thyroidectomy (beyond compression and malignant cytology)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Retrosternal / substernal goitre with symptoms or airway compromise; hyperthyroidism not controlled medically (toxic MNG, Graves' refractory to antithyroids); cosmetic / psychosocial: significant goitre causing distress; rapid growth or features of malignancy (hardness, lymphadenopathy, RLN palsy).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Post-thyroidectomy complication: how does hypocalcaemia arise and how is it managed?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Parathyroid gland damage/removal → hypoparathyroidism → tetany (Chvostek's, Trousseau's signs). Monitor Ca²⁺ post-op; replace calcium ± calcitriol.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Post-thyroidectomy complication: what does RLN palsy cause, and what may bilateral injury require?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → hoarseness (unilateral) or stridor/respiratory distress (bilateral). Bilateral RLN injury may require tracheostomy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Post-thyroidectomy complication: what precipitates thyroid storm and how is it prevented?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Precipitated by surgery in an inadequately prepared hyperthyroid patient — prevent by rendering euthyroid pre-operatively.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.front: Post-thyroidectomy complication: why does hypothyroidism occur and what is the consequence?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Neck Lumps.back: Expected after total thyroidectomy → lifelong levothyroxine replacement.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: How does thyroid cancer usually present?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: As a thyroid nodule or neck lump — usually painless, in a euthyroid patient.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Are most thyroid nodules benign or malignant?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Most are benign — only ~5% are malignant, and most patients are euthyroid.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Name the four main types of thyroid cancer (plus one other).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Papillary, follicular, medullary and anaplastic — plus thyroid lymphoma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Which two thyroid cancers are 'differentiated', and what do they share?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Papillary and follicular — both arise from follicular cells, take up iodine, are TSH-dependent, and have an excellent prognosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the commonest type of thyroid cancer, and its prognosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Papillary carcinoma (~80%) — excellent prognosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Describe papillary thyroid cancer (patient, spread, histology).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Young patients (20–40s), often female, with a radiation link; spreads via lymphatics; histology shows Orphan-Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies. Best prognosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Describe follicular thyroid cancer (spread and a key diagnostic caveat).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Older patients; spreads haematogenously (lung, bone); it cannot be diagnosed on FNA — histology is needed to show capsular/vascular invasion (distinguishing it from a follicular adenoma).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Describe medullary thyroid cancer (cell of origin, marker, association).
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Arises from parafollicular C cells → secretes calcitonin (and CEA); ~25% familial, associated with MEN 2A/2B (RET proto-oncogene); it does NOT take up radioiodine.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Describe anaplastic thyroid cancer.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Elderly patients; undifferentiated, rapidly growing and locally invasive (hoarseness, stridor), often unresectable; very poor prognosis and usually managed palliatively.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Which thyroid malignancy arises on a background of Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Thyroid lymphoma (typically a rapidly enlarging thyroid).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the tumour marker for follow-up of differentiated thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Thyroglobulin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the tumour marker for medullary thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Calcitonin (and CEA).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Why do radioiodine and TSH suppression work in differentiated thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Because papillary and follicular cancers arise from follicular cells — they take up iodine and are TSH-dependent (TSH drives their growth).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the main environmental risk factor for thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Ionising radiation, especially childhood exposure (e.g. Chernobyl) — linked to papillary carcinoma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the genetic association of medullary thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: MEN 2A/2B (RET proto-oncogene).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Which conditions are associated with thyroid cancer besides MEN2?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: FAP/Gardner's syndrome and Cowden syndrome (and Hashimoto's for lymphoma).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: List red-flag features suggesting malignancy in a thyroid nodule.
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Rapid growth, a hard or fixed nodule, hoarse voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve), cervical lymphadenopathy, age <20 or >60, male sex, and a radiation or family history.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Why can thyroid cancer cause a hoarse voice?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What are the first-line investigations for a thyroid nodule?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: TFTs (usually normal), ultrasound of the neck (U/TIRADS risk grading), and FNA cytology (Thy 1–5) — the key diagnostic test.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Which ultrasound features of a thyroid nodule suggest malignancy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Hypoechoic, microcalcification, irregular margins, taller-than-wide shape, and increased vascularity.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: Why can't follicular carcinoma be diagnosed on FNA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: FNA cannot demonstrate capsular or vascular invasion; excision biopsy/histology is needed (this distinguishes it from a benign follicular adenoma).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What must be done before surgery for medullary thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Screen for phaeochromocytoma (as part of MEN 2) and perform RET genetic testing.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the surgical management of differentiated thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Lobectomy for small, low-risk tumours, or total thyroidectomy for larger/higher-risk disease, ± lymph node dissection.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What adjuncts follow surgery for higher-risk differentiated thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation of remnant/metastatic tissue, and TSH-suppressive levothyroxine; thyroglobulin is monitored for recurrence.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the management of medullary thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Total thyroidectomy + central node dissection; it does NOT respond to radioiodine or TSH suppression; monitor calcitonin/CEA; offer genetics and prophylactic thyroidectomy to RET carriers.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the management of anaplastic thyroid cancer?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Usually palliative — secure the airway (tracheostomy) and consider surgery/radiotherapy/chemotherapy; prognosis is poor.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.front: What is the prognosis of thyroid cancer by type?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Thyroid Cance.back: Papillary and follicular are excellent (>90% 10-year survival); medullary is intermediate; anaplastic is dismal (survival often only months).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: TSH 0.01, FT4 32, FT3 10. TRAb positive. Diagnosis?
options: Graves' disease — TRAb stimulates TSH receptor → autonomous hormone production
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Graves': positive TRAb (pathognomonic) + suppressed TSH + raised FT4/FT3. Eye disease + pretibial myxoedema if present. Treat: carbimazole titration or radioiodine or thyroidectomy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Hyperthyroid patient develops sore throat on carbimazole. Action?
options: Urgent FBC — agranulocytosis (rare but life-threatening). Stop carbimazole if WCC <3 or neutrophils <1.5.
Reduce carbimazole dose — mild allergic reaction
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Agranulocytosis: rare (<0.5%) but potentially fatal. Warn ALL patients to get urgent FBC for any sore throat/fever/mouth ulcers on carbimazole. Stop immediately if confirmed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Thyroid storm management?
options: PTU 200mg 4-hourly + propranolol + Lugol's iodine (2h after PTU) + dexamethasone + IVF + ITU
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Thyroid storm: life-threatening hyperthyroidism. PTU (blocks synthesis + peripheral T4→T3 conversion) + beta-blocker + iodine (Lugol's — given AFTER PTU to prevent organification) + dexamethasone + supportive ITU care.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Graves' ophthalmopathy: which treatment is contraindicated?
options: Radioiodine (worsens active moderate-severe Graves' eye disease)
Thyroidectomy (safe in active Graves' eye disease)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Radioiodine: contraindicated in active moderate-severe Graves' eye disease (worsens it in ~15%). If radioiodine used with mild TED → give concurrent prednisolone to prevent worsening.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Subclinical hyperthyroidism: when to treat?
options: If TSH <0.1 with AF risk, osteoporosis, age >65, or cardiac symptoms
Treat only if TSH is completely undetectable (<0.01)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Subclinical hyperthyroidism (TSH <0.4, normal FT4/FT3): treat if TSH persistently <0.1 AND high risk of AF (age >65, cardiac disease) or osteoporosis. Else monitor 3–6 monthly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Hyperthyroid patient 14 weeks pregnant. Carbimazole should be?
options: Switched to PTU for first trimester (aplasia cutis risk with carbimazole), then back to carbimazole from 2nd trimester
Continue carbimazole — PTU is contraindicated in pregnancy
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Carbimazole: teratogenic in 1st trimester (aplasia cutis, choanal/oesophageal atresia). PTU is safer in 1st trimester but has hepatotoxicity risk long-term → switch back to carbimazole in 2nd/3rd trimester.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: De Quervain's thyroiditis: clinical features?
options: Painful tender goitre + fever + viral prodrome + transient hyperthyroidism then hypothyroidism
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: De Quervain's (subacute granulomatous thyroiditis): painful, tender thyroid + systemic upset + transient hyperthyroidism (stored hormone release) → transient hypothyroidism → usually recovery. High ESR, low TRAb.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Radioiodine (I-131) mechanism?
options: Destroys thyroid follicular cells via beta radiation — most become permanently hypothyroid (≈50% by 1 year, ≈80% by 10 years)
Acts as a TSH receptor antagonist
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: I-131: beta emitter → destroys thyroid tissue. ~50% become hypothyroid within 1 year, ~80% at 10 years → lifelong levothyroxine. Excreted in urine/saliva → radiation precautions 3 weeks.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Block-replace vs titration regime for carbimazole?
options: Block-replace: fixed high carbimazole + levothyroxine added (avoids frequent dose changes, more stable but more SEs). Titration: adjust carbimazole to maintain euthyroid (lower total dose).
Block-replace is preferred in pregnancy due to lower fetal exposure
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Block-replace: high-dose carbimazole (completely blocks thyroid) + levothyroxine replacement. Less monitoring but more agranulocytosis risk. Titration: lower carbimazole adjusted to achieve euthyroid — preferred in UK.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Toxic multinodular goitre: best definitive treatment?
options: Radioiodine (I-131) OR thyroidectomy — carbimazole controls but rarely achieves remission in TMNG
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: TMNG: autonomous nodules → don't remit on carbimazole. Definitive: radioiodine (1st choice if no compressive symptoms) or hemithyroidectomy/total thyroidectomy (if large goitre/compression).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Hashimoto's thyroiditis: initial phase?
options: Transient hyperthyroidism (hashitoxicosis) as thyroid destroyed → then progressive hypothyroidism
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Hashimoto's: autoimmune destruction. Initial release of stored hormone → transient hyperthyroidism (hashitoxicosis). Then hypothyroidism as follicles destroyed. Anti-TPO antibodies positive (very high).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Propranolol in hyperthyroidism — what does it also block?
options: Blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 (active hormone) — unique property of propranolol among beta-blockers
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Propranolol: non-selective beta-blocker. Also inhibits peripheral 5'-deiodinase → reduces T4 → T3 conversion. Useful for rapid symptom control in hyperthyroidism + thyroid storm.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Thyroid scan with hot nodule: diagnosis?
options: Toxic adenoma — autonomous hyperfunction of a single nodule; rest of thyroid suppressed
De Quervain's thyroiditis — transient warm nodule
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Hot nodule: single area of increased isotope uptake = autonomous functioning adenoma. Rest of thyroid suppressed (low TSH). Treat: radioiodine or surgical excision.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Sick euthyroid syndrome: pattern?
options: Low T3, normal/low T4, normal TSH — seen in acute illness
High TSH + low T3 + elevated free T4
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Sick euthyroid (non-thyroidal illness syndrome): acute illness → ↓5'-deiodinase → ↓T3 (active). T4 normal or low. TSH normal. Treat the underlying illness — do NOT give thyroxine.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Postpartum thyroiditis: sequence?
options: Hyperthyroidism (1–4 months post-partum) → hypothyroidism (4–8 months) → usually euthyroid by 12 months
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Postpartum thyroiditis: silent autoimmune thyroiditis. Classic sequence: transient hyper → hypo → recovery. ~25% remain permanently hypothyroid. Anti-TPO positive. TRAb negative (distinguishes from Graves').

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma: biochemistry?
options: High TSH + high T4 (TSH not suppressed by high T4 — inappropriate secretion)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: TSHoma: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma → ↑TSH inappropriately + ↑T4/T3. Usually other hormone excess (GH, prolactin). MRI pituitary confirms. Treat: transsphenoidal surgery + somatostatin analogues.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with weight loss, palpitations, tremor, and eye protrusion. TSH is undetectable, T4 is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Graves' disease
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Young woman + autoimmune features (exophthalmos) + diffuse goitre + undetectable TSH + raised T4 = Graves' disease. Confirmed by positive TRAb (TSH receptor antibodies). Most common cause of hyperthyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is the most serious side effect of carbimazole requiring immediate discontinuation?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Agranulocytosis (life-threatening neutropenia)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Agranulocytosis occurs in ~0.5% — presents as fever, sore throat, infection. Must stop carbimazole immediately and check FBC. Prescribe PTU instead. All carbimazole patients must be warned: fever/sore throat = stop drug + seek urgent review.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A pregnant woman at 8 weeks gestation is diagnosed with Graves' hyperthyroidism. What antithyroid drug is preferred in the first trimester?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Propylthiouracil (PTU)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Carbimazole is teratogenic in the first trimester (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia). PTU is used in T1; switch to carbimazole in T2/T3 (PTU hepatotoxic with prolonged use). RAI is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A 55-year-old man with known AF develops palpitations and tremor. TFTs show TSH 0.01 mU/L, T4 24 pmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?
options: Hyperthyroidism — treat with antithyroid drugs (carbimazole) + beta-blocker for rate control
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Hyperthyroidism — treat with antithyroid drugs (carbimazole) + beta-blocker for rate control
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Low TSH + raised T4 = hyperthyroidism. AF is a common complication of thyrotoxicosis — rate control with beta-blocker (propranolol) + antithyroid drugs. AF may revert after euthyroidism is restored.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is radioactive iodine (131I) used for in hyperthyroidism and what is its main long-term consequence?
options: Definitive treatment that destroys thyroid tissue — main consequence: hypothyroidism requiring lifelong levothyroxine
Requires hospital admission for radiation isolation always
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Definitive treatment that destroys thyroid tissue — main consequence: hypothyroidism requiring lifelong levothyroxine
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: RAI is taken orally, concentrates in thyroid, destroys tissue by β radiation. Effective and definitive. ~50% develop hypothyroidism within first year; virtually all eventually become hypothyroid. Lifelong TFT monitoring needed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A 70-year-old presents with new AF, weight loss, and minimal neck swelling. Ultrasound shows multiple nodules. TFTs: TSH 0.02, T4 raised. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Toxic multinodular goitre
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Elderly patient + multiple nodules + hyperthyroidism = toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's disease). No exophthalmos (not Graves'). Treated with RAI or thyroidectomy. AF is a common presentation of thyrotoxicosis in elderly.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is thyroid storm and what is the immediate treatment?
options: Life-threatening thyrotoxicosis: PTU + Lugol's iodine + propranolol + hydrocortisone + supportive care
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Life-threatening thyrotoxicosis: PTU + Lugol's iodine + propranolol + hydrocortisone + supportive care
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45): PTU (blocks synthesis + T4→T3 conversion), Lugol's iodine (after PTU — blocks thyroid hormone release), propranolol (symptoms/rate), hydrocortisone (reduces T4→T3 conversion + relative adrenal insufficiency). ICU level care.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What three findings are specific to Graves' disease (not other causes of hyperthyroidism)?
options: Hot nodule on scan + autonomy + no antibodies
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Exophthalmos + pretibial myxoedema + thyroid acropachy
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: The Graves' triad: exophthalmos (proptosis from orbital inflammation), pretibial myxoedema (non-pitting brawny skin on shins), and thyroid acropachy (periosteal new bone formation like clubbing). These do NOT occur in TMNG or toxic adenoma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A patient with hyperthyroidism complains of double vision and eye pain. What investigation is needed?
options: Ophthalmology referral + CT/MRI orbits (assess Graves' ophthalmopathy)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Ophthalmology referral + CT/MRI orbits (assess Graves' ophthalmopathy)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Graves' ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease): diplopia, proptosis, corneal exposure. Urgent ophthalmology referral. CT/MRI orbits shows enlarged extraocular muscles. Severe cases: IV methylprednisolone. RAI can worsen TED.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is the effect of hyperthyroidism on the cardiovascular system?
options: Tachycardia, increased cardiac output, AF, hypertension (systolic), heart failure in severe cases
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Tachycardia, increased cardiac output, AF, hypertension (systolic), heart failure in severe cases
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Thyroid hormones increase cardiac contractility, heart rate, and cardiac output. Systolic hypertension (high stroke volume) with wide pulse pressure. AF in ~10–15%. High output cardiac failure in severe/prolonged cases.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A patient on carbimazole develops a fever and sore throat. What is the immediate management?
options: Stop carbimazole immediately + check FBC urgently + seek emergency review
Reassure — this is a common benign side effect
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Stop carbimazole immediately + check FBC urgently + seek emergency review
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Agranulocytosis warning: all patients on carbimazole must be told — fever/sore throat = STOP drug immediately + attend A&E for FBC. Neutrophil count <0.5 × 10⁹/L = agranulocytosis = risk of life-threatening infection. Never delay.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is subclinical hyperthyroidism and when should it be treated?
options: TSH <0.1 with normal T4/T3 — treat if: AF, osteoporosis risk, >65 years, symptomatic
Only treat if T4 is also elevated
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: TSH <0.1 with normal T4/T3 — treat if: AF, osteoporosis risk, >65 years, symptomatic
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Subclinical hyperthyroidism: asymptomatic low TSH with normal T4/T3. Higher risk of AF (3-fold) and osteoporosis. Treat if persistent TSH <0.1 mIU/L, especially in elderly, post-menopausal women, those with AF or bone disease.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: How does Lugol's iodine work in thyroid storm?
options: High iodine load transiently inhibits thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: High iodine load transiently inhibits thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Lugol's iodine: high iodine load inhibits iodine organification and thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff). Must be given 1 hour AFTER PTU (otherwise iodine provides substrate for more hormone synthesis). Used in thyroid storm and pre-operatively.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is the mechanism of beta-blockers in managing acute hyperthyroid symptoms?
options: Block peripheral effects of thyroid hormone (sympathomimetic effects) — not reduce T4/T3
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Block peripheral effects of thyroid hormone (sympathomimetic effects) — not reduce T4/T3
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Beta-blockers block catecholamine-mediated effects (tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, sweating) — rapid symptom relief while waiting for ATDs to take effect. Propranolol also inhibits T4→T3 conversion. Do not reduce thyroid hormone levels.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Why can thyroid surgery cause hypocalcaemia post-operatively?
options: Accidental removal or devascularisation of parathyroid glands → hypoparathyroidism
Calcium binds to the new scar
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Accidental removal or devascularisation of parathyroid glands → hypoparathyroidism
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: The four parathyroid glands are closely related to the thyroid — at risk during thyroidectomy. Temporary or permanent hypoparathyroidism → hypocalcaemia. Post-op: monitor calcium, check for tingling/Trousseau's sign. Treat with calcium + calcitriol.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis Type 2 and how is it treated?
options: Destructive thyroiditis from amiodarone — treated with prednisolone (not antithyroid drugs)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Destructive thyroiditis from amiodarone — treated with prednisolone (not antithyroid drugs)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: AIT Type 2: amiodarone causes direct toxic thyroiditis → follicle destruction releases T4/T3. Not driven by hormone synthesis — antithyroid drugs ineffective. Prednisolone reduces inflammation. Type 1: iodine-excess in goitre — carbimazole.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is the thyroid scan appearance in Graves' disease vs toxic adenoma?
options: Graves': diffuse increased uptake throughout gland; toxic adenoma: 'hot' single nodule with suppressed surrounding tissue
Graves': cold nodule; toxic adenoma: diffuse
Graves': normal uptake; toxic adenoma: diffuse
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Graves': diffuse increased uptake throughout gland; toxic adenoma: 'hot' single nodule with suppressed surrounding tissue
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Isotope thyroid scan: Graves' = diffuse uniform uptake (whole gland stimulated). Toxic adenoma = single hot nodule (autonomous) with suppressed surrounding tissue. TMNG = multiple hot nodules.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Which complication of hyperthyroidism is most dangerous in elderly patients?
options: Atrial fibrillation with risk of stroke and heart failure
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Atrial fibrillation with risk of stroke and heart failure
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: AF in thyrotoxicosis: older patients are more prone → risk of stroke (thromboembolism) and heart failure (loss of atrial contraction + high rate). Anticoagulate as per CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Rate control with beta-blocker. Revert to SR once euthyroid.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A patient is successfully treated for Graves' disease and is now euthyroid. What is the remission rate after 12–18 months of antithyroid drugs?
options: ~50% remission (relapse in ~50% within 2 years — need definitive therapy)
Remission is not possible without RAI/surgery
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: ~50% remission (relapse in ~50% within 2 years — need definitive therapy)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Antithyroid drugs achieve remission in ~50% at 12–18 months. The other 50% relapse — especially with large goitre, high TRAb, young patients. Relapse = consider definitive therapy (RAI or thyroidectomy).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What investigation should be performed on all thyroid nodules to exclude malignancy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Thyroid nodule >1 cm (or <1 cm with suspicious USS features): USS-guided FNAC for cytology using Bethesda/Thy classification. Thyroid function tests determine hyper/hypothyroidism but don't exclude malignancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the biochemical result that distinguishes primary hyperthyroidism from TSH-secreting pituitary tumour?
options: Primary: low TSH; TSH-secreting tumour: inappropriately normal/high TSH + raised T4
Primary: normal TSH; secondary: high TSH
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Primary: low TSH; TSH-secreting tumour: inappropriately normal/high TSH + raised T4
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: TSH-secreting pituitary tumour (rare) = raised T4 + normal or raised TSH (dissociation). Primary hyperthyroidism: TSH is always suppressed (negative feedback). Inappropriately non-suppressed TSH + raised T4 = pituitary tumour or thyroid hormone resistance.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What is block-and-replace antithyroid therapy?
options: High-dose carbimazole (blocks all synthesis) + levothyroxine added to prevent hypothyroidism
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: High-dose carbimazole (blocks all synthesis) + levothyroxine added to prevent hypothyroidism
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Block-and-replace: high-dose carbimazole completely blocks thyroid synthesis + add levothyroxine to maintain euthyroidism. Advantage: stable TFTs without frequent dose adjustments. Disadvantage: higher drug burden, not used in pregnancy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Which non-thyroidal condition most commonly causes a suppressed TSH (not hyperthyroidism)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid syndrome)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Sick euthyroid: any severe acute illness suppresses TSH transiently (pituitary stress response). T3 is usually low. T4 can be low or normal. TFTs normalise as illness resolves — avoid treating unless TSH very low and symptoms suggest true thyrotoxicosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the first-line investigation for a new diagnosis of hyperthyroidism?
options: TSH + free T4 (and free T3 if TSH suppressed but T4 normal — T3 toxicosis)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: TSH + free T4 (and free T3 if TSH suppressed but T4 normal — T3 toxicosis)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: TFTs: TSH is the most sensitive marker. Suppressed TSH = hyperthyroidism until proven otherwise. Add fT3 if TSH low but T4 normal (T3 toxicosis — some toxic adenomas or early Graves' raise T3 before T4). Always pair TSH with T4.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Why are lid retraction and lid lag NOT Graves'-specific?
options: They result from sympathetic overstimulation of levator palpebrae — present in any thyrotoxicosis
They are caused by TSHR antibodies
They are due to GAG accumulation
They only occur in thyroid storm
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: They result from sympathetic overstimulation of levator palpebrae — present in any thyrotoxicosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Lid retraction and lid lag are due to sympathetic overstimulation of levator palpebrae and occur in any thyrotoxicosis, not just Graves'.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: What does low/absent uptake on radioiodine scan indicate?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Thyroiditis, exogenous levothyroxine, struma ovarii
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Low/absent uptake indicates thyroiditis, exogenous levothyroxine, or struma ovarii — the leaking (not making) group where antithyroid drugs are useless.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Why must potassium iodide be given at least 1 hour AFTER carbimazole in thyroid storm?
options: Synthesis must be blocked first or iodine will fuel more hormone
Iodide must be absorbed before carbimazole works
It is given before to speed release
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Synthesis must be blocked first or iodine will fuel more hormone
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: KI is given ≥1h after carbimazole because synthesis must be blocked first — otherwise the iodine load will fuel more hormone production. Order matters: KI before carbimazole can worsen storm.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: In thyroid storm, which agent blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion and covers relative adrenal insufficiency?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Hydrocortisone
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Hydrocortisone 100mg IV 6-hourly inhibits peripheral T4→T3 conversion and also covers relative adrenal insufficiency in thyroid storm.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Which thyroid cancer is most common and shows Psammoma bodies on histology?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Papillary (70%)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Papillary cancer is the most common (70%), seen in young females, with an excellent prognosis, lymph node spread, and Psammoma bodies on histology.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: An elderly patient has a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass with stridor and a very poor prognosis. Which cancer is this?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Anaplastic (1%)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Anaplastic cancer (1%) occurs in the elderly, enlarges rapidly, has a very poor prognosis, and causes pressure symptoms → stridor.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Which thyroid cancer arises from C-cells, raises calcitonin, and is part of MEN-2?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Medullary (5%) — RET oncogene; screen family
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Medullary cancer (5%) arises from C-cells with raised calcitonin, is part of MEN-2A/2B, involves the RET oncogene, and warrants family screening.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: Why does follicular thyroid cancer require histology rather than FNA alone?
options: FNA cannot distinguish benign from malignant follicular lesions
FNA is contraindicated in the thyroid
Follicular cancer never forms a nodule
Follicular cancer only spreads to nodes
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: FNA cannot distinguish benign from malignant follicular lesions
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Follicular cancer (20%) presents as a solitary nodule with haematogenous spread (lung/bone), and benign cannot be distinguished from malignant on FNA alone — it needs histology.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A patient with thyrotoxicosis has a smooth diffuse goitre with a bruit, exophthalmos, and positive TSHR antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Graves' disease
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: A smooth diffuse goitre with a bruit, exophthalmos, and positive TSHR antibodies is Graves' disease (the Graves'-specific signs are all TSHR antibody-driven).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.question: A woman 3 months postpartum develops transient thyrotoxicosis with low radioiodine uptake. What is the likely cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.answer: Postpartum thyroiditis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Hyperthyroidi.explanation: Postpartum thyroiditis occurs 1–6 months post-delivery with the same 3-phase pattern as De Quervain's (thyrotoxicosis → hypothyroid → recovery) and is a low-uptake (leaking) cause of thyrotoxicosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: What is the general structure of an endocrine axis, and how is it regulated?
options: Pituitary → hypothalamus → target gland, regulated by positive feedback
Hypothalamus → pituitary → target gland → hormone, regulated by negative feedback (the final hormone switches off the levels above it)
Target gland → hypothalamus → pituitary, with no feedback
Hypothalamus → target gland directly, bypassing the pituitary
Pituitary → target gland → hypothalamus, regulated by the autonomic nervous system
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Hypothalamus → pituitary → target gland → hormone, regulated by negative feedback (the final hormone switches off the levels above it)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Most hormones are controlled by an axis: hypothalamus → pituitary → target gland → hormone, regulated by negative feedback (the final hormone switches off the levels above it). Almost every endocrine disease/test is understood by asking where the problem is and which way feedback is going.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which statement about the posterior pituitary is correct?
options: It is glandular tissue controlled by portal blood vessels
It is neural (an extension of the hypothalamus) and stores/releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus
It is controlled by hypothalamic releasing hormones via the portal supply
It synthesises ADH and oxytocin itself
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: It is neural (an extension of the hypothalamus) and stores/releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is neural — an extension of the hypothalamus, connected by direct neurons. It is a storage/release site for ADH and oxytocin, which are made in the hypothalamus, not the pituitary.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which hypothalamic-pituitary-target chain is CORRECT?
options: CRH → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol (the HPA axis)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: CRH → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol (the HPA axis)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: CRH → ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol is the HPA axis. TRH → TSH → thyroid → T3/T4; GnRH → LH+FSH → gonads → sex steroids; GHRH → GH → IGF-1/growth.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient develops a pituitary stalk lesion. Which hormone rises, and why, illustrating the 'stalk effect'?
options: Prolactin, because it is under tonic dopamine inhibition — interrupting the stalk removes dopamine's suppression
ADH, because it is made in the pituitary
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Prolactin, because it is under tonic dopamine inhibition — interrupting the stalk removes dopamine's suppression
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Prolactin is unique — under tonic inhibition by dopamine. Anything interrupting the pituitary stalk (tumour, compression) removes dopamine inhibition → ↑prolactin ('stalk effect'). Dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) also raise prolactin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient has ↓T4 with a HIGH TSH. What does this pattern indicate?
options: Primary hypothyroidism (gland fails; pituitary shouts louder)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Primary hypothyroidism (gland fails; pituitary shouts louder)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Low target hormone + HIGH pituitary hormone = primary gland failure (the gland can't respond, so the pituitary shouts louder). ↓T4 + ↑TSH = primary hypothyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient has ↑cortisol with a HIGH ACTH. How is this interpreted?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Pituitary-driven (secondary) overactivity — Cushing's disease
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: High target hormone + HIGH pituitary hormone = pituitary-driven (secondary) overactivity. ↑cortisol + ↑ACTH = Cushing's disease (pituitary).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why do endocrine tests measure hormones in pairs (e.g. TSH + T4, ACTH + cortisol)?
options: Because single hormones cannot be measured accurately
Because the combination localises the lesion to gland vs pituitary
Because pairs are cheaper to assay
Because feedback only affects one hormone
Because the target hormone alone gives the diagnosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Because the combination localises the lesion to gland vs pituitary
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Endocrine tests measure hormones in pairs because the combination (e.g. TSH + T4) localises the lesion to gland vs pituitary — the paired pattern distinguishes primary from secondary disease.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient is suspected of having Cushing's syndrome (cortisol overproduction). Which dynamic test is used and what result confirms autonomy?
options: Short Synacthen test; a rise in cortisol confirms it
Dexamethasone suppression test; failure to suppress cortisol = autonomous overproduction
Oral glucose tolerance test; a fall in GH confirms it
TRH stimulation test; a rise in TSH confirms it
Water deprivation test; concentrated urine confirms it
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Dexamethasone suppression test; failure to suppress cortisol = autonomous overproduction
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Suppression tests are used for suspected overproduction: give something that should switch the axis off; failure to suppress = autonomous overproduction. The dexamethasone suppression test is used for Cushing's.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient with suspected Addison's undergoes a short Synacthen test. What does the test involve and what result suggests the diagnosis?
options: Give dexamethasone; failure to suppress cortisol
Give ACTH (Synacthen); a failure of cortisol to rise indicates the adrenal cannot produce cortisol
Give glucose; a rise in GH
Give TRH; a rise in TSH
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Give ACTH (Synacthen); a failure of cortisol to rise indicates the adrenal cannot produce cortisol
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Stimulation tests are used for suspected underproduction: give the stimulating hormone; failure to respond = gland can't produce. The short Synacthen test gives ACTH and measures the cortisol response, testing the adrenal for Addison's.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: ADH is made where, acts where, and what results from too much?
options: Made in the posterior pituitary; acts on the gut; too much = diabetes insipidus
Made in the hypothalamus (stored/released posteriorly); acts on the renal collecting duct; too much = SIADH
Made in the anterior pituitary; acts on the adrenal; too much = Cushing's
Made in the thyroid; acts on tissues; too much = hyperthyroidism
Made in the kidney; acts on the pituitary; too much = SIADH
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Made in the hypothalamus (stored/released posteriorly); acts on the renal collecting duct; too much = SIADH
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: ADH (vasopressin) is made in the hypothalamus, stored/released posteriorly, and acts on the renal collecting duct (water reabsorption). Too little = diabetes insipidus; too much = SIADH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why must chronic exogenous steroids not be stopped abruptly?
options: Exogenous steroids suppress CRH/ACTH → adrenal atrophy, so abrupt withdrawal leaves the patient unable to produce cortisol
They stimulate the adrenal to overgrow
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Exogenous steroids suppress CRH/ACTH → adrenal atrophy, so abrupt withdrawal leaves the patient unable to produce cortisol
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Exogenous steroids suppress CRH/ACTH → adrenal atrophy → the patient cannot mount a stress response, which is why steroids cannot be stopped abruptly (sick-day rules apply).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which map of the thyroid axis levels to hormones is CORRECT?
options: Hypothalamus → TSH; pituitary → TRH; thyroid → T3/T4
Hypothalamus → TRH; anterior pituitary → TSH; thyroid → T4 + T3
Hypothalamus → T4; pituitary → T3; thyroid → TSH
Hypothalamus → GnRH; pituitary → TSH; thyroid → T3/T4
Pituitary → TRH; hypothalamus → TSH; thyroid → T4
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Hypothalamus → TRH; anterior pituitary → TSH; thyroid → T4 + T3
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Hypothalamus makes TRH (stimulates pituitary); anterior pituitary makes TSH (stimulates thyroid); thyroid makes T4 + T3 (act on tissues). T3/T4 suppress both TRH and TSH by negative feedback.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: In thyroid hormone synthesis, which enzyme oxidises iodide and organifies it onto thyroglobulin, and which drugs block it?
options: The Na⁺/I⁻ symporter; blocked by β-blockers
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO); blocked by carbimazole/propylthiouracil
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidises iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin (organification). Carbimazole/propylthiouracil block TPO (↓synthesis); PTU also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why is levothyroxine (T4) rather than T3 used as thyroid replacement?
options: T4 is a prohormone with a long half-life (~7 days), converted peripherally to active T3, allowing stable once-daily dosing
T4 is more potent than T3
T3 has a longer half-life than T4
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: T4 is a prohormone with a long half-life (~7 days), converted peripherally to active T3, allowing stable once-daily dosing
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: The thyroid mostly secretes T4 (~90%), a less active prohormone converted to the active T3 peripherally by deiodinase. T4's long half-life (~7 days) makes levothyroxine a stable, once-daily treatment titrated to TSH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient has a HIGH TSH with a LOW free T4. Which diagnosis fits, and what is a typical cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Primary hypothyroidism; Hashimoto's
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: HIGH TSH + LOW free T4 = primary hypothyroidism (thyroid fails → ↓T4 → feedback drives TSH up), e.g. Hashimoto's.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A young woman has a LOW TSH with a HIGH free T4. What does this indicate?
options: Primary hyperthyroidism (thyroid overactive → ↑T4 → suppresses TSH), e.g. Graves'
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Primary hyperthyroidism (thyroid overactive → ↑T4 → suppresses TSH), e.g. Graves'
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: LOW TSH + HIGH free T4 = primary hyperthyroidism (thyroid overactive → ↑T4 → suppresses TSH), e.g. Graves'.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why is TSH the most sensitive screening test for thyroid status?
options: Because T4 is protein-bound and unmeasurable
Because the feedback loop is so sensitive that TSH changes early and dramatically before T4 moves much
Because TSH is made by the thyroid
Because TSH is unaffected by feedback
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Because the feedback loop is so sensitive that TSH changes early and dramatically before T4 moves much
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: The feedback loop is so sensitive that TSH changes early and dramatically before T4 moves much, making TSH the most sensitive marker of thyroid status.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: State the pattern logic that distinguishes primary from secondary thyroid disease.
options: In primary disease TSH and T4 move together; in secondary they move oppositely
In primary disease TSH moves opposite to T4; in secondary disease they move together
TSH is always high in both
T4 is always normal in primary disease
The direction of change is irrelevant
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: In primary disease TSH moves opposite to T4; in secondary disease they move together
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: In primary disease, TSH moves opposite to T4 (high TSH + low T4, or low TSH + high T4). In secondary disease, they move together.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which set of features would you expect in HYPERthyroidism, derived from the physiology?
options: Weight gain, bradycardia, cold intolerance, lethargy, constipation
Weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, anxiety, diarrhoea
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, anxiety, diarrhoea
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Thyroid hormone sets the metabolic thermostat, so hyperthyroidism = everything sped up: weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, anxiety, diarrhoea. Hypothyroidism is the reverse (everything slowed).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why are β-blockers such as propranolol useful in hyperthyroidism?
options: They block TPO and reduce synthesis
The thyroid increases β-adrenergic sensitivity, so propranolol controls tremor and tachycardia
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: The thyroid increases β-adrenergic sensitivity, so propranolol controls tremor and tachycardia
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Thyroid hormone increases β-adrenergic sensitivity, so propranolol controls symptoms such as tremor and tachycardia in hyperthyroidism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which correctly pairs an adrenal cortical zone with its product and controller?
options: Zona fasciculata → cortisol → ACTH; zona glomerulosa → aldosterone → RAAS (not mainly ACTH)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Zona fasciculata → cortisol → ACTH; zona glomerulosa → aldosterone → RAAS (not mainly ACTH)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Using 'GFR → salt, sugar, sex': zona glomerulosa → aldosterone (RAAS-controlled, not mainly ACTH); zona fasciculata → cortisol (ACTH-controlled); zona reticularis → androgens (ACTH-controlled).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why is aldosterone preserved in SECONDARY adrenal insufficiency but lost in Addison's (primary)?
options: Aldosterone is ACTH-driven, so both lose it
Aldosterone is primarily RAAS-driven, so it is preserved when only ACTH is low (secondary), but lost in primary failure where both zones fail
Aldosterone is made in the medulla
Cortisol replaces aldosterone in secondary insufficiency
Aldosterone is not affected by any adrenal disease
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Aldosterone is primarily RAAS-driven, so it is preserved when only ACTH is low (secondary), but lost in primary failure where both zones fail
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Cortisol + androgens are ACTH-driven, but aldosterone is primarily RAAS-driven (angiotensin II + potassium). So in secondary insufficiency (↓ACTH) aldosterone is preserved (RAAS still works); in primary (Addison's) both zones fail and both are lost.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: The adrenal cortex and medulla differ in origin. Which is correct?
options: Cortex from neural crest; medulla from mesoderm
Cortex from mesoderm (steroids from cholesterol); medulla from neural crest (catecholamines), a modified sympathetic ganglion
Cortex makes catecholamines; medulla makes steroids
Medulla is controlled by ACTH; cortex by the sympathetic nervous system
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Cortex from mesoderm (steroids from cholesterol); medulla from neural crest (catecholamines), a modified sympathetic ganglion
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: The cortex arises from mesoderm and makes steroid hormones (from cholesterol), controlled mostly by ACTH (+ RAAS for aldosterone). The medulla arises from neural crest (a modified sympathetic ganglion), makes catecholamines, and is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why is cortisol measured at 9am, and why do sick-day rules exist?
options: Cortisol peaks at night; a stressed body needs less cortisol
Cortisol peaks in the early morning (diurnal rhythm); stress raises CRH/ACTH → ↑cortisol, so a stressed body needs more cortisol
Cortisol is constant throughout the day
Cortisol is only made during sleep
Timing has no effect on cortisol
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Cortisol peaks in the early morning (diurnal rhythm); stress raises CRH/ACTH → ↑cortisol, so a stressed body needs more cortisol
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Cortisol has a diurnal rhythm, peaking in the early morning (hence 9am measurement). Stress raises CRH/ACTH → ↑cortisol, so a stressed body needs more cortisol — the basis of sick-day rules.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which cluster of features fits cortisol EXCESS (Cushing's), derivable from cortisol's actions?
options: ↑glucose (diabetes), ↑BP, central obesity, immunosuppression, osteoporosis, thin skin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: ↑glucose (diabetes), ↑BP, central obesity, immunosuppression, osteoporosis, thin skin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Cortisol raises glucose, maintains BP, is anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive and drives protein/bone breakdown, so excess (Cushing's) gives ↑glucose (diabetes), ↑BP, central obesity, immunosuppression, osteoporosis and thin skin. Deficiency (Addison's) is the reverse.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient with Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) would be expected to have which biochemical picture?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Hypertension + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Aldosterone drives Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺/H⁺ excretion. Excess (Conn's) therefore gives hypertension + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis. Deficiency (part of Addison's) gives hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypotension.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient has episodes of hypertension, palpitations, sweating and headache. Which adrenal lesion is suggested and why?
options: Phaeochromocytoma — a catecholamine-secreting medullary tumour, giving episodic symptoms from excess catecholamines
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Phaeochromocytoma — a catecholamine-secreting medullary tumour, giving episodic symptoms from excess catecholamines
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: A phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting medullary tumour → episodic hypertension, palpitations, sweating and headache, derivable from excess catecholamines.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient with primary adrenal failure (Addison's) presents with fatigue, low BP and skin pigmentation. Which biochemistry and mechanism fit?
options: ↓cortisol + ↓aldosterone (both zones fail), hyperkalaemia + hyponatraemia, and ↑ACTH driving pigmentation
↓ACTH with preserved aldosterone and no pigmentation
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: ↓cortisol + ↓aldosterone (both zones fail), hyperkalaemia + hyponatraemia, and ↑ACTH driving pigmentation
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Addison's = ↓cortisol + ↓aldosterone (both zones fail) → fatigue, ↓BP, ↓glucose, hyperkalaemia + hyponatraemia; the compensatory ↑ACTH causes pigmentation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: How does secondary adrenal insufficiency differ biochemically from Addison's?
options: It has ↓ACTH → ↓cortisol but aldosterone preserved (RAAS intact) → no hyperkalaemia, no pigmentation
It has both cortisol and aldosterone lost
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: It has ↓ACTH → ↓cortisol but aldosterone preserved (RAAS intact) → no hyperkalaemia, no pigmentation
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Secondary adrenal insufficiency (↓ACTH from pituitary disease or steroid suppression) gives ↓cortisol but preserved aldosterone (RAAS intact) → no hyperkalaemia and no pigmentation, unlike Addison's.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why can primary hypothyroidism cause mild hyperprolactinaemia?
options: Because low T4 stimulates prolactin directly
Because TRH (raised in primary hypothyroidism) also stimulates prolactin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Because TRH (raised in primary hypothyroidism) also stimulates prolactin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: TRH also stimulates prolactin, so primary hypothyroidism (with high TRH) can cause mild hyperprolactinaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which statement captures the key asymmetry of glucose homeostasis?
options: Many hormones lower glucose but only glucagon raises it
Many hormones raise glucose (glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline, GH) but only insulin lowers it
Insulin and glucagon both lower glucose
Somatostatin is the sole glucose-lowering hormone
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Many hormones raise glucose (glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline, GH) but only insulin lowers it
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Many hormones raise glucose (glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline, GH — counter-regulatory), but only insulin lowers it. This is why insulin deficiency (diabetes) is so impactful and hypoglycaemia is dangerous — redundant defences against high glucose, a single defence against low.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which islet cell secretes which hormone, with the correct glucose effect?
options: β cells → insulin → lower glucose; α cells → glucagon → raise glucose; δ cells → somatostatin → inhibit both
α cells → somatostatin; β cells → glucagon
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: β cells → insulin → lower glucose; α cells → glucagon → raise glucose; δ cells → somatostatin → inhibit both
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: β (beta) cells make insulin (lowers glucose — the only hormone that does); α (alpha) cells make glucagon (raises glucose); δ (delta) cells make somatostatin (inhibits both).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why can the brain still take up glucose without insulin, making it vulnerable to hypoglycaemia rather than lack of insulin?
options: The brain uses GLUT4 transporters like muscle
The brain and liver use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT1/2/3), unlike muscle/fat which need insulin-driven GLUT4
The brain stores its own insulin
The brain does not use glucose
Insulin actively blocks brain glucose uptake
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: The brain and liver use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT1/2/3), unlike muscle/fat which need insulin-driven GLUT4
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Insulin moves GLUT4 to the surface in muscle + fat for glucose uptake, but the brain and liver use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT1/2/3). So the brain takes up glucose without insulin and is vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, not lack of insulin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: What is insulin's overall metabolic role and its effect on the liver?
options: The fed/anabolic/storage hormone ('store it'); ↑glycogen synthesis and ↓gluconeogenesis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: The fed/anabolic/storage hormone ('store it'); ↑glycogen synthesis and ↓gluconeogenesis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Insulin is the 'fed state'/anabolic/storage hormone ('fuel is plentiful, store it'). In the liver it increases glycogen synthesis and decreases gluconeogenesis (stops making glucose).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Describe the progression of fuel use during prolonged fasting.
options: Glycogen stores (hours) → gluconeogenesis (amino acids/glycerol) → ketogenesis (ketones fuel the brain, sparing protein)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Glycogen stores (hours) → gluconeogenesis (amino acids/glycerol) → ketogenesis (ketones fuel the brain, sparing protein)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Fasting progresses: glycogen stores (hours) → gluconeogenesis (from amino acids/glycerol) → ketogenesis (fat-derived ketones fuel the brain in prolonged starvation, sparing protein).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which counter-regulatory hormone raises glucose via ↑gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, explaining steroid hyperglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Cortisol
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Cortisol is counter-regulatory: ↑gluconeogenesis + insulin resistance — which is why steroids cause hyperglycaemia. (Adrenaline drives glycogenolysis/lipolysis; GH is an insulin antagonist; glucagon is the primary acute responder.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes develops DKA. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Absolute insulin deficiency → unrestrained lipolysis → ketogenesis → ketoacidosis (the fasted state gone unchecked)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Absolute insulin deficiency → unrestrained lipolysis → ketogenesis → ketoacidosis (the fasted state gone unchecked)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: DKA results from absolute insulin deficiency → unrestrained lipolysis → ketogenesis → ketoacidosis — the fasted state gone unchecked. Type 1 diabetes itself is autoimmune β-cell destruction → no insulin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient with hyperkalaemia is given insulin with dextrose. Why does insulin help, and why is dextrose co-administered?
options: Insulin raises serum K⁺; dextrose prevents this
Insulin drives K⁺ into cells (lowering serum K⁺); dextrose prevents hypoglycaemia
Insulin excretes K⁺ renally; dextrose provides energy
Insulin has no effect on potassium
Dextrose drives K⁺ into cells and insulin prevents hyperglycaemia
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Insulin drives K⁺ into cells (lowering serum K⁺); dextrose prevents hypoglycaemia
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Insulin drives K⁺ into cells, lowering serum potassium — the basis of insulin-dextrose treatment for hyperkalaemia. Dextrose is co-given to prevent the resulting hypoglycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: How does metformin lower glucose?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: ↓hepatic gluconeogenesis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Metformin lowers glucose by reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis. (Sulfonylureas ↑insulin release; GLP-1 agonists ↑insulin/incretin; SGLT2i cause renal glucose loss; insulin is replacement.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: What is the normal blood calcium range, and which hormone is the master minute-to-minute controller?
options: ~2.2–2.6 mmol/L; PTH (with vitamin D as its essential partner)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: ~2.2–2.6 mmol/L; PTH (with vitamin D as its essential partner)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Blood calcium is kept at ~2.2–2.6 mmol/L. It is regulated across bone, kidney and gut, with PTH as the master minute-to-minute controller and vitamin D as its essential partner (especially for gut absorption).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient hyperventilates and develops peri-oral tingling and carpopedal spasm. What is the calcium mechanism?
options: Alkalosis → ↑calcium binding to albumin → ↓ionised Ca²⁺ → tetany
Total calcium falls due to albumin loss
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Alkalosis → ↑calcium binding to albumin → ↓ionised Ca²⁺ → tetany
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Alkalosis (from hyperventilation) increases calcium binding to albumin → ↓ionised (free) Ca²⁺ → tetany, causing peri-oral tingling and carpopedal spasm. Only the ionised fraction is active.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: How does PTH raise calcium across the three organs?
options: ↑osteoclast activity (bone resorption); ↑renal calcium reabsorption + ↑phosphate excretion + ↑vitamin D activation; ↑gut calcium absorption (indirectly via vitamin D)
It acts only on the gut directly
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: ↑osteoclast activity (bone resorption); ↑renal calcium reabsorption + ↑phosphate excretion + ↑vitamin D activation; ↑gut calcium absorption (indirectly via vitamin D)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: PTH raises calcium by ↑osteoclast activity (bone resorption releasing Ca²⁺ + phosphate), ↑renal calcium reabsorption + ↑phosphate excretion + ↑vitamin D activation (1-α-hydroxylase), and ↑gut calcium absorption indirectly via activated vitamin D.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: What is the 'phosphate point' regarding PTH, and the diagnostic pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism?
options: PTH raises both calcium and phosphate; 1° hyperPTH = ↑Ca²⁺ + ↑phosphate
PTH raises calcium but LOWERS phosphate (↑renal excretion), so primary hyperparathyroidism = ↑Ca²⁺ + ↓phosphate
PTH has no effect on phosphate
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: PTH raises calcium but LOWERS phosphate (↑renal excretion), so primary hyperparathyroidism = ↑Ca²⁺ + ↓phosphate
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: PTH raises calcium but lowers phosphate (via increased renal phosphate excretion), so primary hyperparathyroidism gives ↑Ca²⁺ + ↓phosphate — a key diagnostic pattern.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which describes the vitamin D activation pathway correctly?
options: Skin/diet → vitamin D3 → liver (25-hydroxylase) → 25-OH (storage form) → kidney (1-α-hydroxylase, PTH-stimulated) → 1,25-(OH)₂ (calcitriol, active)
The liver makes the active form and the kidney the storage form
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Skin/diet → vitamin D3 → liver (25-hydroxylase) → 25-OH (storage form) → kidney (1-α-hydroxylase, PTH-stimulated) → 1,25-(OH)₂ (calcitriol, active)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Vitamin D is activated sequentially: skin (UV) + diet → vitamin D3 → liver (25-hydroxylase) → 25-OH vitamin D (storage form, what we measure) → kidney (1-α-hydroxylase, stimulated by PTH) → 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D (calcitriol, the active form).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: How does chronic kidney disease cause bone disease (renal osteodystrophy)?
options: The kidney over-activates vitamin D, raising calcium
The failing kidney can't do the 1-α-hydroxylation → ↓active vitamin D → ↓calcium → ↑PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) + phosphate retention
The liver fails to make 25-OH vitamin D
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: The failing kidney can't do the 1-α-hydroxylation → ↓active vitamin D → ↓calcium → ↑PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) + phosphate retention
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: In CKD the failing kidney cannot perform 1-α-hydroxylation → ↓active vitamin D → ↓calcium → ↑PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), with phosphate retention → renal osteodystrophy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient has ↑calcium, ↑PTH (inappropriately high) and ↓phosphate. What is the diagnosis and cause?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Primary hyperparathyroidism — autonomous PTH (adenoma)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: ↑calcium with inappropriately ↑PTH and ↓phosphate is primary hyperparathyroidism, caused by an autonomous PTH-secreting adenoma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient with cancer has hypercalcaemia. Bloods show ↑calcium with SUPPRESSED (low) PTH. What does this indicate, and what is the discriminator between the two commonest causes?
options: Primary hyperparathyroidism; phosphate is the discriminator
Malignancy (non-PTH hypercalcaemia, e.g. PTHrP/mets); PTH is the discriminator between primary hyperparathyroidism (↑PTH) and malignancy (↓PTH)
Secondary hyperparathyroidism; calcium is the discriminator
Hypoparathyroidism; vitamin D is the discriminator
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism; phosphate is the discriminator
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Malignancy (non-PTH hypercalcaemia, e.g. PTHrP/mets); PTH is the discriminator between primary hyperparathyroidism (↑PTH) and malignancy (↓PTH)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: ↑calcium with suppressed PTH indicates malignancy (non-PTH hypercalcaemia, e.g. PTHrP/mets). The two commonest hypercalcaemia causes are primary hyperparathyroidism (↑Ca²⁺ + ↑PTH) and malignancy (↑Ca²⁺ + ↓PTH) — PTH is the discriminator.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A patient develops tetany, positive Trousseau/Chvostek signs and a long QT after thyroid surgery. What is the mechanism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Hypocalcaemia from accidental parathyroid damage → ↓PTH
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia results from accidental parathyroid damage → ↓PTH. Hypocalcaemia causes tetany, Trousseau/Chvostek signs and a long QT.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Why must GnRH be released in pulses, and what is the clinical application of this?
options: Continuous GnRH stimulates the axis maximally; used to boost fertility
Continuous GnRH paradoxically suppresses the axis (receptor downregulation); GnRH analogues are used to suppress sex hormones (prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty)
GnRH pulsatility has no clinical relevance
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Continuous GnRH paradoxically suppresses the axis (receptor downregulation); GnRH analogues are used to suppress sex hormones (prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: GnRH must be pulsatile — continuous GnRH paradoxically suppresses the axis by downregulating receptors. This is the basis of GnRH analogues used to suppress sex hormones in prostate cancer, endometriosis and precocious puberty.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: Which correctly assigns the roles of LH and FSH in the male?
options: LH → Sertoli cells → spermatogenesis; FSH → Leydig cells → testosterone
LH → Leydig cells → testosterone; FSH → Sertoli cells → spermatogenesis
LH and FSH both stimulate Leydig cells
FSH triggers ovulation in the male
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: LH → Leydig cells → testosterone; FSH → Sertoli cells → spermatogenesis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: In the male, LH stimulates Leydig cells → testosterone; FSH stimulates Sertoli cells → spermatogenesis. Memory hook: LH → Leydig; FSH → Follicle/Sertoli. Inhibin selectively suppresses FSH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: By what enzyme is testosterone converted to DHT, and which drug blocks this in BPH and hair loss?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: 5-α-reductase; finasteride
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: Testosterone → dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5-α-reductase (active in prostate/skin). Finasteride is a 5-α-reductase inhibitor used in BPH and hair loss. (Aromatase converts testosterone → oestrogen.)

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: During the menstrual cycle, which hormonal event triggers ovulation, and what is unusual about its feedback?
options: The progesterone peak via negative feedback
The mid-cycle oestrogen peak switches feedback to positive → LH surge → ovulation (the one place feedback is positive)
The FSH surge via negative feedback
The LH surge is driven by progesterone
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: The mid-cycle oestrogen peak switches feedback to positive → LH surge → ovulation (the one place feedback is positive)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: For most of the cycle oestrogen gives negative feedback, but at the mid-cycle oestrogen peak feedback switches to positive → triggers the LH surge → ovulation. This is the one place in endocrinology where feedback is positive.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: What happens to the corpus luteum when pregnancy occurs, and what is the clinical link?
options: hCG from the embryo rescues the corpus luteum → progesterone maintained (the basis of pregnancy tests)
Oestrogen rescues the corpus luteum → the basis of pregnancy tests
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: hCG from the embryo rescues the corpus luteum → progesterone maintained (the basis of pregnancy tests)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: After ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum → secretes progesterone. With no pregnancy it regresses → menstruation. In pregnancy, hCG (from the embryo) rescues the corpus luteum → progesterone maintained — the basis of pregnancy tests.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A 52-year-old woman has vasomotor symptoms and amenorrhoea. Which hormonal pattern confirms menopause, and why does it occur?
options: Ovarian follicles depleted → ↓oestrogen → loss of negative feedback → ↑↑FSH/LH (high FSH = menopause)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Ovarian follicles depleted → ↓oestrogen → loss of negative feedback → ↑↑FSH/LH (high FSH = menopause)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: At menopause, ovarian follicles are depleted → ↓oestrogen → loss of negative feedback → ↑↑FSH/LH. High FSH is the diagnostic pattern. Consequences include vasomotor symptoms, osteoporosis and urogenital atrophy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: How does the combined oral contraceptive prevent ovulation?
options: Oestrogen + progesterone provide negative feedback → ↓FSH/LH → no follicle development or ovulation
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Oestrogen + progesterone provide negative feedback → ↓FSH/LH → no follicle development or ovulation
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.explanation: The combined oral contraceptive provides oestrogen + progesterone → negative feedback → ↓FSH/LH → no follicle development or ovulation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.question: A young man is investigated for hypogonadism. He has low testosterone with HIGH LH/FSH. Where is the lesion?
options: Primary (testes) — the gonad fails, so LH/FSH rise
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Foundations o.answer: Primary (testes) — the gonad fails, so LH/FSH rise
