conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: Stop metformin (eGFR <45 for caution, contraindicated at <30); switch sulfonylurea to short-acting gliclazide not glibenclamide; consider SGLT2i (dapagliflozin has renal indication)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Metformin: dose reduce at eGFR 30–45, stop <30 (lactic acidosis risk). Avoid long-acting sulfonylureas in renal failure (hypoglycaemia risk). Glibenclamide is specifically dangerous in renal impairment — use gliclazide. Dapagliflozin is now licensed down to eGFR 25 for renal protection.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A T2DM patient has type 2 diabetes diagnosed by opportunistic HbA1c of 51 mmol/mol. No symptoms. What is required to confirm the diagnosis?
options: A second confirmatory test on a different day (HbA1c, fasting glucose, or OGTT) is required
Single HbA1c ≥48 is diagnostic without repeat in asymptomatic patients
Fasting glucose must be done — HbA1c alone cannot diagnose diabetes
No further testing — diagnosis is confirmed
Symptoms are required to diagnose on a single test
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: A second confirmatory test on a different day (HbA1c, fasting glucose, or OGTT) is required
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: In asymptomatic patients, diabetes diagnosis requires two abnormal results (same or different tests, on different days). A single HbA1c ≥48 in an asymptomatic patient is insufficient without confirmation. In symptomatic patients, a single test is diagnostic.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A 48-year-old South Asian man has a waist circumference of 92 cm, fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.1 mmol/L, HDL 1.0 mmol/L, and BP 128/82 mmHg. According to IDF 2006 criteria, does he have metabolic syndrome?
options: A. No — his waist circumference does not meet the South Asian threshold
B. No — he needs at least 3 additional features beyond central obesity
C. Yes — he meets the South Asian waist threshold and has all 4 additional features
D. Yes — he meets the Europid waist threshold and 2 additional features
E. No — fasting glucose must be ≥7.0 mmol/L to count as a criterion
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: C
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: IDF South Asian waist threshold for males is ≥90 cm (he has 92 cm — met). He also has ↑TG (≥1.7), ↓HDL (<1.03), ↑BP (≥130/85 — borderline, 128 is just below, but ↑fasting glucose ≥5.6 is met). He meets 3 of 4 additional criteria (TG, HDL, glucose), satisfying the ≥2 required. Answer C is the best available option.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: Which of the following best explains the hypertriglyceridaemia seen in metabolic syndrome?
options: B. Hyperinsulinaemia stimulating hepatic VLDL synthesis
C. Increased lipoprotein lipase activity in adipose tissue
D. Reduced chylomicron clearance due to low LPL
E. Excess dietary saturated fat intake
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: B
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Compensatory hyperinsulinaemia (secondary to insulin resistance) upregulates hepatic VLDL synthesis, raising triglycerides and — because VLDL and HDL share triglyceride via CETP exchange — lowering HDL-cholesterol.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A 35-year-old woman with PCOS and metabolic syndrome asks about medication. Which drug would address both her insulin resistance and help with menstrual irregularity?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: C
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity. In PCOS, reducing hyperinsulinaemia lowers LH-driven androgen production by the ovarian theca cells, restoring menstrual regularity. It does not directly block androgens (unlike spironolactone).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: Which antihypertensive class is preferred in metabolic syndrome and why?
options: A. Thiazide diuretics — reduce fluid overload
C. ACE inhibitors or ARBs — improve insulin sensitivity and are renoprotective
E. Calcium channel blockers — metabolically neutral
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: C
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred in metabolic syndrome: they improve insulin sensitivity (unlike thiazides or beta-blockers which worsen it), reduce albuminuria, and lower progression to T2DM. Beta-blockers and thiazides can worsen glycaemia and dyslipidaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: Metabolic syndrome is most directly linked to which hepatic condition?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: C
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: NAFLD is the hepatic manifestation of insulin resistance. Hyperinsulinaemia drives hepatic de novo lipogenesis and VLDL synthesis; ↑FFA delivery from visceral fat causes hepatic steatosis. ~70% of patients with metabolic syndrome have NAFLD.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A patient with metabolic syndrome achieves 8% weight loss through diet and exercise. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A. Improvement in blood pressure only
C. Reversal of metabolic syndrome in most patients
D. No significant change as pharmacotherapy is required
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: C
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: A 5–10% weight reduction improves all components of metabolic syndrome simultaneously (BP, TG, HDL, fasting glucose) and can reverse the diagnosis entirely. Lifestyle modification is the cornerstone of treatment and is more effective than treating individual components pharmacologically.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A 58-year-old man presents with skin bronzing, new-onset diabetes, and abnormal liver function tests. Ferritin is 2800 μg/L. What is the underlying diagnosis and its genetic basis?
options: A. Wilson's disease — ATP7B gene mutation
B. Haemochromatosis — HFE gene C282Y mutation
C. Primary biliary cholangitis — AMA antibody positive
D. Porphyria cutanea tarda — UROD gene mutation
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: B
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: The triad of skin bronzing + diabetes + liver disease ('bronze diabetes') is classic hereditary haemochromatosis. The most common mutation is C282Y in the HFE gene (chromosome 6). Iron deposition destroys pancreatic β-cells. Treatment is venesection; early treatment may reverse diabetes.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A 24-year-old non-obese woman presents with diabetes. Her mother and maternal grandfather also have diabetes. C-peptide is 0.9 nmol/L (normal), GAD antibodies are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Type 1 diabetes mellitus with late onset
C. Maturity onset diabetes of the young (MODY)
E. Latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: C
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: MODY is characterised by: onset <25 years, non-obese, autosomal dominant family history (3 generations), detectable C-peptide, negative autoantibodies. LADA would have positive GAD antibodies. T1DM would have undetectable C-peptide. T2DM is unlikely in a non-obese 24-year-old with this family pattern. Confirm with MODY genetic panel.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: Which mechanism best explains hyperglycaemia in a patient with a phaeochromocytoma?
options: A. Direct destruction of β-cells by catecholamines
B. Catecholamines stimulate α₂-adrenoceptors on β-cells inhibiting insulin secretion, and promote glycogenolysis
C. Excess cortisol co-secretion stimulates gluconeogenesis
D. Noradrenaline activates β₂-adrenoceptors causing lipolysis only
E. Tumour mass effect on the pancreas reduces insulin output
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: B
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Catecholamines (adrenaline/noradrenaline) act on α₂-adrenoceptors on pancreatic β-cells to inhibit insulin secretion. They also stimulate glycogenolysis (liver and muscle via β₂) and gluconeogenesis (liver via β₂/α₁), raising blood glucose. This is reversible after adrenalectomy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A renal transplant patient develops hyperglycaemia 6 weeks post-transplant. Which immunosuppressant is most likely responsible and what is its mechanism?
options: A. Azathioprine — bone marrow suppression impairs insulin production
B. Mycophenolate mofetil — purine synthesis inhibition affects β-cells
C. Tacrolimus — calcineurin inhibition causes direct β-cell toxicity and inhibits insulin gene transcription
D. Prednisolone — only causes diabetes after years of use
E. Basiliximab — IL-2 receptor blockade causes insulin resistance
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: C
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM) is most strongly associated with tacrolimus (> ciclosporin). Calcineurin inhibitors block calcineurin in β-cells, inhibiting NFAT-driven insulin gene transcription and impairing insulin secretion. Tacrolimus carries ~2–3× greater PTDM risk than ciclosporin. Prednisolone also contributes but acts via insulin resistance rather than β-cell toxicity.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: In acromegaly, what is the primary mechanism by which excess growth hormone causes diabetes?
options: A. GH directly destroys pancreatic β-cells
C. GH antagonises post-receptor insulin signalling and promotes lipolysis raising circulating FFAs
D. GH stimulates glucagon release from α-cells
E. GH upregulates hepatic glucose transporter expression
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: C
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: GH is a counter-regulatory hormone that antagonises insulin at the post-receptor level (reduces IRS-1 phosphorylation). GH also promotes lipolysis, raising plasma free fatty acids which further impair insulin signalling (Randle cycle). ~25% of acromegaly patients develop overt diabetes. Treatment of acromegaly (surgery, somatostatin analogues) improves glycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A 52-year-old woman develops new-onset diabetes while taking prednisolone 40 mg/day for an autoimmune condition. Fasting glucose is 6.2 mmol/L, but post-lunch glucose is 14.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
options: A. Dietary advice alone and recheck in 3 months
C. Basal insulin (e.g. insulin glargine once daily at night)
D. Prandial insulin (e.g. short-acting insulin with meals) titrated to post-meal glucose
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.answer: D
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Steroid-induced diabetes characteristically causes predominantly post-prandial hyperglycaemia (steroids peak 4–8 hours after morning dose → afternoon/evening glucose rise) with relatively preserved fasting glucose. Prandial (short-acting) insulin given with meals, especially lunch and dinner, targets this pattern most effectively. Basal insulin alone addresses overnight fasting glucose but not the post-prandial spike. Sulphonylureas can be used but prandial insulin is preferred for significant hyperglycaemia on high-dose steroids.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: What is the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes, and its characteristic glucose pattern?
options: Glucocorticoids — post-lunch/evening (post-prandial) hyperglycaemia with near-normal morning fasting glucose
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Glucocorticoids are the most common cause of drug-induced diabetes; steroid-induced hyperglycaemia peaks post-lunch/evening (post-prandial), with morning fasting glucose often near-normal initially.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: How do thiazide diuretics impair insulin secretion?
options: Hypokalaemia inhibits insulin secretion (K⁺ is required for β-cell depolarisation)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Thiazides cause hypokalaemia, which inhibits insulin secretion because potassium is required for β-cell depolarisation; low-dose thiazides have minimal effect, and risk increases with hypokalaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: A transplant patient on tacrolimus develops diabetes. What is the mechanism, and how does tacrolimus compare with ciclosporin for diabetes risk?
options: Calcineurin inhibition → direct β-cell toxicity; tacrolimus > ciclosporin for diabetes risk
Cortisol excess; tacrolimus has no effect
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Tacrolimus and ciclosporin are calcineurin inhibitors causing direct β-cell toxicity (inhibiting insulin gene transcription), producing post-transplant diabetes mellitus; tacrolimus carries a higher diabetes risk than ciclosporin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: Which atypical antipsychotics most warrant metabolic monitoring for drug-induced diabetes?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Olanzapine and clozapine cause weight gain and impair insulin signalling (clozapine may have direct β-cell toxicity); monitor fasting glucose and lipids at baseline and 3-monthly per NICE.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: What is the most common subtype of MODY, and how does it respond to treatment?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: HNF-1α (MODY3) is the most common MODY subtype (~70%) and responds to sulphonylureas; MODY2 (glucokinase) gives mild stable hyperglycaemia usually needing no treatment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: What does DIDMOAD (Wolfram syndrome) stand for?
options: Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, Deafness
Diabetes Insipidus, Dwarfism, Optic Atrophy, Dementia
Diabetes Mellitus, Insulinoma, Deafness, Optic Atrophy, Dystonia
Deafness, Insipidus, Dyslipidaemia, Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, Dementia
Diabetes Insipidus, Dermopathy, Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, Deafness
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) comprises Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy and Deafness, due to a WFS1 mutation with mitochondrial dysfunction; it is autosomal recessive.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.question: How is MODY reliably distinguished from T1DM?
options: MODY has detectable C-peptide and negative GAD/islet-cell antibodies; T1DM has undetectable C-peptide and positive antibodies
MODY has positive GAD antibodies; T1DM has negative antibodies
MODY has undetectable C-peptide; T1DM has detectable C-peptide
MODY presents over age 40; T1DM under 25
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Type 2 Diabet.explanation: MODY shows detectable C-peptide, negative GAD/islet-cell antibodies, strong autosomal-dominant family history, onset <25 and non-obese; T1DM shows undetectable C-peptide and positive GAD/IA2/ZnT8 antibodies. Confirm MODY with targeted genetic testing.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What are the three axes that drive agent selection in diabetes treatment?
options: Hypoglycaemia risk, weight effect, special benefit/harm
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Hypoglycaemia risk, weight effect, special benefit/harm
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: The framework picks agents by patient feature using three axes: hypoglycaemia risk, weight effect and special benefit/harm — not rote mechanism.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: How do GLP-1 mimetics and DPP-4 inhibitors each act on the incretin axis?
options: GLP-1 mimetics replace GLP-1; DPP-4 inhibitors preserve it by blocking its breakdown
GLP-1 mimetics break down GLP-1; DPP-4 inhibitors replace it
GLP-1 mimetics raise glucagon; DPP-4i lower insulin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: GLP-1 mimetics replace GLP-1; DPP-4 inhibitors preserve it by blocking its breakdown
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: DPP-4 breaks down GLP-1, so GLP-1 mimetics replace it while DPP-4 inhibitors preserve it — the same pathway, two ways in.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which two drug classes are the ONLY ones that cause hypoglycaemia, and why?
options: Sulfonylureas and insulin — they force insulin release regardless of glucose level
Metformin and SGLT2i — they block glucose reabsorption
GLP-1 and DPP-4i — they raise insulin
Pioglitazone and metformin — they increase sensitivity
SGLT2i and pioglitazone — they cause glucosuria
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Sulfonylureas and insulin — they force insulin release regardless of glucose level
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Only sulfonylureas and insulin cause hypos because they force insulin release regardless of glucose level; all other agents are hypo-safe.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which pairing of agents causes weight loss (the obesity-friendly pair)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: GLP-1 mimetics and SGLT2 inhibitors
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: GLP-1 mimetics and SGLT2 inhibitors cause weight loss — the obesity-friendly pair; metformin and DPP-4i are weight-neutral.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the mechanism of metformin, and at what eGFR must it be stopped?
options: Stimulates β-cell insulin release; stop if eGFR <60
Blocks renal glucose reabsorption; stop if eGFR <45
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: ↓Hepatic gluconeogenesis + ↑insulin sensitivity; stop if eGFR <30
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Metformin reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases insulin sensitivity; it is first-line in all T2DM and stopped if eGFR <30 due to lactic acidosis risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which sulfonylurea is specifically described as the worst in elderly/renal patients?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Glibenclamide
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Sulfonylureas cause hypos and weight gain and should be avoided in elderly/renal patients, with glibenclamide being the worst.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the mechanism of pioglitazone, and what are its key harms?
options: PPAR-γ → ↑peripheral insulin sensitivity; avoid in HF (fluid retention); fractures, bladder cancer
Blocks renal glucose reabsorption; causes DKA
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: PPAR-γ → ↑peripheral insulin sensitivity; avoid in HF (fluid retention); fractures, bladder cancer
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Pioglitazone acts via PPAR-γ to increase peripheral insulin sensitivity; it must be avoided in heart failure (fluid retention) and is linked to fractures and bladder cancer.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which key adverse effect is associated with both GLP-1 mimetics and DPP-4 inhibitors?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Pancreatitis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Both GLP-1 mimetics and DPP-4 inhibitors carry a pancreatitis risk; GI upset (nausea, vomiting) is common with GLP-1 mimetics while DPP-4i are generally well-tolerated.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors, and which serious infective complication can occur?
options: Block renal glucose reabsorption → glucosuria; Fournier's gangrene
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Block renal glucose reabsorption → glucosuria; Fournier's gangrene
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption causing glucosuria; harms include DKA, genital thrush and Fournier's gangrene, with cardiorenal/HF benefit.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes and established heart failure needs an additional agent. Which is preferred, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: SGLT2 inhibitor — proven cardiorenal/HF benefit
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: For established CVD/heart failure, an SGLT2 inhibitor (± GLP-1) is preferred for its proven cardiorenal/HF benefit — the modern guideline fork.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: An obese patient (BMI ≥35) with T2DM needs treatment intensification. Which agent is best, and why?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: GLP-1 mimetic — weight loss
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: For an obese patient (BMI ≥35), a GLP-1 mimetic is best because of its weight-loss effect.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: An elderly patient who lives alone and drives needs glucose-lowering therapy. Which agents should be AVOIDED, and what is preferred?
options: Avoid sulfonylureas/insulin; use weight-neutral, hypo-safe agents (DPP-4i, metformin)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Avoid sulfonylureas/insulin; use weight-neutral, hypo-safe agents (DPP-4i, metformin)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: When hypos are dangerous (elderly, driver, lives alone), avoid sulfonylureas and insulin and use weight-neutral, hypo-safe agents such as DPP-4i and metformin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which agent is best avoided in heart failure due to fluid retention?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Pioglitazone
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Pioglitazone is avoided in heart failure because its fluid retention worsens HF.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which treatment is preferred in pregnancy, and what is avoided?
options: Insulin (± metformin); avoid sulfonylureas and most orals
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Insulin (± metformin); avoid sulfonylureas and most orals
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: In pregnancy, insulin (± metformin) is used while sulfonylureas and most orals are avoided.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: A patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor presents acidotic but with near-normal glucose. What is the diagnosis, described as 'the trap'?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Euglycaemic DKA
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycaemic DKA, which occurs at near-normal glucose — the trap; other harms include genital thrush/UTI, Fournier's gangrene and amputation risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Besides prolonged hypoglycaemia and weight gain, which electrolyte disturbance is linked to sulfonylureas?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: SIADH / hyponatraemia
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Sulfonylureas cause prolonged hypoglycaemia and weight gain, with glibenclamide worst in elderly/renal patients, and are also linked to SIADH/hyponatraemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Under which circumstances should metformin be stopped to avoid lactic acidosis?
options: eGFR <30, renal/hepatic impairment, HF, contrast/sepsis/acute illness
Only when HbA1c is at target
Only if the patient is obese
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: eGFR <30, renal/hepatic impairment, HF, contrast/sepsis/acute illness
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Metformin should be stopped if eGFR <30, in renal/hepatic impairment, HF, and with contrast/sepsis/acute illness due to lactic acidosis risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: How should insulin injections be managed to avoid lipodystrophy, and what increases hypo risk?
options: Rotate injection sites; alcohol increases hypo risk
Inject the same site each time; caffeine increases hypo risk
Use only the abdomen; exercise prevents hypos
Never rotate sites; food increases hypo risk
Inject intramuscularly; dehydration increases hypo risk
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Rotate injection sites; alcohol increases hypo risk
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Insulin injection sites should be rotated to avoid lipohypertrophy/atrophy, and hypo risk increases with alcohol.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which insulin is described as having a flat 24h profile and is preferred when hypos are a problem?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Long-acting (Lantus/glargine, Levemir)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Long-acting insulins (Lantus/glargine, Levemir) provide a flat 24h basal profile and are preferred if hypos are a problem.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the insulin regimen of choice in T1DM?
options: Basal-bolus: long-acting once daily plus rapid-acting before each meal
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Basal-bolus: long-acting once daily plus rapid-acting before each meal
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: The T1DM regimen of choice is basal-bolus: long-acting once daily (basal) plus rapid-acting before each meal (bolus).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: How is insulin typically initiated as an add-on in T2DM?
options: NPH once/twice daily initially; switch to glargine if hypos a problem or carer-dependent; basal-bolus if needed
Basal-bolus from the outset in all patients
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: NPH once/twice daily initially; switch to glargine if hypos a problem or carer-dependent; basal-bolus if needed
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: In T2DM, insulin is usually started as NPH once/twice daily, switched to long-acting glargine if hypos are a problem or the patient is carer-dependent, with basal-bolus used if needed.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which two agents are weight-neutral (neither causing weight gain nor loss)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral, whereas GLP-1 mimetics and SGLT2 inhibitors cause weight loss and sulfonylureas, pioglitazone and insulin cause weight gain.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which drug is used first-line in T2DM with established cardiovascular disease, regardless of HbA1c?
options: SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist (cardioprotective benefit proven in CVOTs) — added to metformin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist (cardioprotective benefit proven in CVOTs) — added to metformin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: In T2DM with established CVD, NICE/ADA guidelines mandate SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist as second-line alongside metformin, regardless of HbA1c — because of proven cardiovascular outcome benefit (not just glucose lowering).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the glucose-lowering mechanism of DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins)?
options: Inhibit DPP-4 enzyme → preserve endogenous GLP-1 and GIP → glucose-dependent insulin release
Stimulate GLP-1 receptors directly — longer acting than endogenous GLP-1
Block SGLT2 in proximal tubule → glucosuria
Close KATP channels on β-cells → insulin secretion
Activate PPARγ → improve insulin sensitivity in adipose tissue
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Inhibit DPP-4 enzyme → preserve endogenous GLP-1 and GIP → glucose-dependent insulin release
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: DPP-4 normally rapidly degrades endogenous GLP-1 and GIP. DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin) block this enzyme → GLP-1/GIP levels rise → glucose-dependent insulin release + suppressed glucagon. Weight neutral; no hypoglycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the key advantage of glucose-dependent insulin release from GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors over sulfonylureas?
options: No hypoglycaemia — insulin only released when glucose is elevated (glucose-dependent mechanism)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: No hypoglycaemia — insulin only released when glucose is elevated (glucose-dependent mechanism)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors stimulate insulin only when glucose is raised (glucose-dependent). When glucose is normal/low, the stimulus diminishes → no hypoglycaemia. Sulfonylureas close KATP channels constitutively → can cause hypoglycaemia regardless of glucose level.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the correct management of an SGLT2 inhibitor before a surgical procedure?
options: Stop 3–5 days before surgery — risk of euglycaemic DKA during fasting/perioperative period
Continue throughout perioperative period — no interaction with surgery
Switch to metformin on the day of surgery
Double the dose to maintain glucose control while fasting
Stop only if the patient will receive IV fluids
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Stop 3–5 days before surgery — risk of euglycaemic DKA during fasting/perioperative period
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors should be stopped 3–5 days before surgery (or any prolonged fast). Perioperative fasting + SGLT2i → euglycaemic DKA can occur. Glucose may be near-normal (misleading) while ketones are high. Restart when eating normally post-operatively.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which insulin preparation is described as intermediate-acting with a peak at 4–8 hours?
options: NPH insulin (isophane) — intermediate; peaks 4–8h; some nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk
Pre-mixed 70/30 — biphasic but no single peak
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: NPH insulin (isophane) — intermediate; peaks 4–8h; some nocturnal hypoglycaemia risk
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: NPH (isophane) insulin is intermediate-acting: onset ~1–2h, peak ~4–8h, duration ~12h. The peak can cause nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Replaced by glargine/degludec in many patients for flatter profiles, but NPH is still widely used as twice-daily basal.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the mechanism of sulfonylureas, and which receptor do they act on?
options: Close ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels (KATP) on β-cell membrane → membrane depolarisation → Ca²⁺ influx → insulin exocytosis
Sensitise peripheral tissues to insulin via PPARγ
Inhibit hepatic glucose output via AMPK
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Close ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels (KATP) on β-cell membrane → membrane depolarisation → Ca²⁺ influx → insulin exocytosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Sulfonylureas bind to the SUR1 subunit of KATP channels on β-cells → channel closes → membrane depolarises → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open → insulin exocytosis. This occurs independently of glucose level → hypoglycaemia risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the first-line insulin choice for bedtime once-daily insulin addition in T2DM?
options: Long-acting basal insulin (glargine or degludec) — flat profile, less nocturnal hypoglycaemia
NPH twice daily from the start
Rapid-acting bolus insulin at each meal
Inhaled insulin — most convenient for T2DM initiation
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Long-acting basal insulin (glargine or degludec) — flat profile, less nocturnal hypoglycaemia
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: For T2DM insulin initiation, a once-daily basal insulin (glargine, degludec, or detemir) is added to oral agents. Start at 10 units bedtime, titrate by 2 units every 3 days targeting fasting glucose 4–7 mmol/L. Flat profile reduces nocturnal hypoglycaemia vs NPH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which T2DM drug class is preferred in a patient with T2DM and CKD (eGFR 35) to slow renal progression?
options: SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or canagliflozin — CREDENCE/DAPA-CKD trials show renal protection) + ACE inhibitor
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or canagliflozin — CREDENCE/DAPA-CKD trials show renal protection) + ACE inhibitor
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: CREDENCE (canagliflozin) and DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin) trials showed SGLT2 inhibitors reduce ESRD, doubling of creatinine, and CV death in T2DM with CKD. Dapagliflozin is now licensed for CKD protection down to eGFR 25. Combine with ACEi/ARB for maximum renoprotection.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: A patient with T2DM and no CVD is started on metformin. After 3 months HbA1c is 68 mmol/mol (target <53). What is the next step?
options: Add a second agent — SGLT2 inhibitor (if CVD risk present) or DPP-4 inhibitor/sulfonylurea (if not); reassess in 3 months
Wait 12 months — HbA1c monitoring is annual
Start both an SGLT2 inhibitor and GLP-1 agonist simultaneously
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Add a second agent — SGLT2 inhibitor (if CVD risk present) or DPP-4 inhibitor/sulfonylurea (if not); reassess in 3 months
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: If HbA1c above target on monotherapy, add a second agent (combination therapy). The choice of second agent is driven by: CVD/HF (→SGLT2i), obesity (→GLP-1), hypoglycaemia risk (→DPP-4i or SGLT2i, not SU), CKD (→SGLT2i + ACEi).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What are the main side effects of GLP-1 agonists that limit their use?
options: Nausea and vomiting (especially on initiation), pancreatitis risk — start low dose and titrate
Hypoglycaemia — the main dose-limiting side effect
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Nausea and vomiting (especially on initiation), pancreatitis risk — start low dose and titrate
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: GLP-1 agonists delay gastric emptying → nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, especially on initiation. Titrate dose slowly. Rare but important: pancreatitis (avoid in personal/family history of pancreatitis or MEN2). Contraindicated in personal/family history of medullary thyroid cancer (rodent data).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which insulin type is used as a rapid-acting bolus (meal-time insulin) in T1DM basal-bolus regimen?
options: Rapid analogues: aspart (NovoRapid), lispro (Humalog), glulisine (Apidra) — onset 15 min, peak 1–2h, duration 3–5h
Glargine — too long-acting for meal-time use
Inhaled insulin — for T1DM meal coverage only
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Rapid analogues: aspart (NovoRapid), lispro (Humalog), glulisine (Apidra) — onset 15 min, peak 1–2h, duration 3–5h
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Rapid-acting analogues have onset within 15 min (can be given just before or even after meals) and peak around 1–2h matching the postprandial glucose rise. Duration 3–5h. Used as bolus components of basal-bolus regimens in T1DM and intensive T2DM.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: When is metformin specifically contraindicated due to lactic acidosis risk beyond eGFR <30?
options: Contrast media administration (iodinated dye) — hold metformin on day of procedure + 48h after; severe illness/sepsis; acute liver failure; excessive alcohol
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Contrast media administration (iodinated dye) — hold metformin on day of procedure + 48h after; severe illness/sepsis; acute liver failure; excessive alcohol
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Metformin should be held at/after iodinated contrast administration (AKI risk → metformin accumulation → lactic acidosis). Also hold in severe illness (AKI risk), hepatic failure (lactate cannot be metabolised), excessive alcohol (enhanced lactic acidosis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is the advantage of insulin degludec (Tresiba) over insulin glargine in T1DM?
options: Ultra-long action (>42h) and extremely flat profile — even less nocturnal hypoglycaemia; flexible dosing timing
Can be mixed with rapid-acting insulin in same syringe
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Ultra-long action (>42h) and extremely flat profile — even less nocturnal hypoglycaemia; flexible dosing timing
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Degludec has a half-life >25h and duration >42h with an ultra-flat profile. It allows flexible injection timing (can vary by ±8h day-to-day). Lower nocturnal hypoglycaemia compared to glargine in trials (SWITCH 1, DEVOTE). Useful in T1DM with hypoglycaemia unawareness.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is Fournier's gangrene and which T2DM drug class is associated with its rare occurrence?
options: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/genitalia — rare but serious adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors (glucosuria → local infection risk)
Breast gangrene — from warfarin interaction with insulin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/genitalia — rare but serious adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors (glucosuria → local infection risk)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Fournier's gangrene (necrotising fasciitis of perineum/genitalia) is a rare but life-threatening adverse effect reported with SGLT2 inhibitors. The glucosuria environment promotes bacterial growth. Patients should seek urgent attention for any perineal pain/swelling/redness.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: Which drug used in T2DM causes water and sodium retention as a mechanism of fluid retention side effect?
options: Pioglitazone — activates PPARγ in collecting duct → Na⁺ and water retention → oedema and heart failure risk
DPP-4 inhibitor — mainly saxagliptin causes fluid retention
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Pioglitazone — activates PPARγ in collecting duct → Na⁺ and water retention → oedema and heart failure risk
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Pioglitazone is a PPARγ agonist. PPARγ activation in the renal collecting duct increases ENaC sodium channel expression → sodium and water reabsorption → oedema → worsening heart failure. This is why pioglitazone is contraindicated in heart failure.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: A T2DM patient is started on a sulfonylurea. Which counselling point is most important?
options: Hypoglycaemia risk — do not skip meals; do not drive if glucose is low; long-acting sulfonylureas (glibenclamide) are particularly dangerous in the elderly
Take only with food — no other restrictions
Can be combined safely with insulin without hypoglycaemia risk
Monitor urine glucose daily to assess response
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Hypoglycaemia risk — do not skip meals; do not drive if glucose is low; long-acting sulfonylureas (glibenclamide) are particularly dangerous in the elderly
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Sulfonylurea counselling: must eat regular meals, carry fast-acting glucose, inform DVLA (hypo risk when driving). Glibenclamide is long-acting and particularly dangerous in elderly/renal impairment → prolonged hypoglycaemia. Prefer gliclazide (shorter-acting).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: What is exenatide and how does it differ from liraglutide in its pharmacology?
options: Exenatide is GLP-1 mimetic (exendin-4 from Gila monster) — twice-daily or once-weekly (Bydureon); liraglutide is human GLP-1 analogue (once-daily); both are GLP-1 receptor agonists
Exenatide is a DPP-4 inhibitor; liraglutide is a GLP-1 agonist
Exenatide is the long-acting form; liraglutide is short-acting
Exenatide is only for T1DM; liraglutide is only for T2DM
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Exenatide is GLP-1 mimetic (exendin-4 from Gila monster) — twice-daily or once-weekly (Bydureon); liraglutide is human GLP-1 analogue (once-daily); both are GLP-1 receptor agonists
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Exenatide is based on exendin-4 (a peptide from Gila monster saliva that binds GLP-1 receptors). Twice-daily (Byetta) or once-weekly extended-release (Bydureon). Liraglutide is a human GLP-1 analogue (97% homology) once daily. Semaglutide is once-weekly or oral.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.question: In which T2DM context is insulin initiation most immediately indicated?
options: Symptomatic hyperglycaemia (markedly elevated glucose), diabetic emergency (DKA/HHS), or failure of multiple oral agents
All T2DM patients should start insulin immediately at diagnosis
Only if HbA1c >86 mmol/mol for 2 years
Only when eGFR <30 and all oral agents are stopped
When patient requests it, regardless of HbA1c
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.answer: Symptomatic hyperglycaemia (markedly elevated glucose), diabetic emergency (DKA/HHS), or failure of multiple oral agents
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetes Trea.explanation: Insulin is initiated in T2DM urgently for: acute symptomatic hyperglycaemia (very high glucose, osmotic symptoms), acute metabolic emergency, or after failure of multiple oral agents. For elective intensification, start with once-daily basal added to oral agents.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the biochemical triad of DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Hyperglycaemia + ketonaemia + acidosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: DKA is defined by the triad of hyperglycaemia + ketonaemia + acidosis — the 'no insulin → ketones' decompensation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why does T2DM tend to cause HHS rather than DKA?
options: It retains enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis
It produces no insulin at all
It causes more lipolysis than T1
It always presents with normal glucose
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: It retains enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: T2DM retains enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis, so it tends to cause HHS instead of DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the commonest precipitant of DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Infection
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Infection is the commonest precipitant of DKA, as sepsis drives counter-regulatory hormones.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: In Arm 1 (glucose) of DKA pathogenesis, what does the absence of insulin lead to?
options: ↑Gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis → hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → dehydration + electrolyte loss
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: ↑Gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis → hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → dehydration + electrolyte loss
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Arm 1: no insulin → ↑gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis → hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → profound dehydration and electrolyte loss.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: In Arm 2 (ketones) of DKA, what is the sequence from absent insulin to acidosis?
options: ↑Lipolysis → free fatty acids → hepatic ketogenesis → acidic ketones → metabolic acidosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: ↑Lipolysis → free fatty acids → hepatic ketogenesis → acidic ketones → metabolic acidosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Arm 2: no insulin → ↑lipolysis → free fatty acids → hepatic ketogenesis → acidic ketones → metabolic acidosis, with vomiting worsening dehydration.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A DKA patient is breathing deeply and rapidly with pear-drop smelling breath. What does the breathing represent?
options: Kussmaul respiration compensating for metabolic acidosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Kussmaul respiration compensating for metabolic acidosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Kussmaul respiration is deep, rapid breathing that blows off CO₂ to compensate for the metabolic acidosis; acetone (pear-drop) breath is also characteristic.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: In a DKA patient, a headache is described as a red flag for which complication?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Cerebral oedema
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Headache is an early sign of cerebral oedema in DKA — a red flag.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What are the JBDS hyperglycaemia and acidosis criteria for DKA?
options: Glucose >11 mmol/L (or any glucose if ketonaemia + acidosis); pH <7.3 and/or HCO₃⁻ <15
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Glucose >11 mmol/L (or any glucose if ketonaemia + acidosis); pH <7.3 and/or HCO₃⁻ <15
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: JBDS criteria: glucose >11 mmol/L (or any glucose if ketonaemia + acidosis present), with pH <7.3 and/or HCO₃⁻ <15 mmol/L — a raised anion gap from ketones.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What blood ketone level meets the JBDS ketonaemia criterion for DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: >3 mmol/L (or 2+ on urine dipstick)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: The ketonaemia criterion is blood ketones >3 mmol/L on finger-prick or 2+ on urine dipstick.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the potassium paradox in DKA?
options: Total body K⁺ is low but serum K⁺ is high/normal on admission; insulin then crashes serum K⁺
Total body K⁺ is high but serum K⁺ is low; insulin raises serum K⁺
Both total body and serum K⁺ are high throughout
Both total body and serum K⁺ are low throughout
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Total body K⁺ is low but serum K⁺ is high/normal on admission; insulin then crashes serum K⁺
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Total body K⁺ is low (osmotic diuresis) but serum K⁺ is high/normal on admission because absent insulin shifts K⁺ out of cells; insulin then drives it back in, crashing serum K⁺ → fatal arrhythmia if not pre-empted.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the management mantra for DKA?
options: Fluids first, then insulin, watch potassium
Insulin first, then fluids, then bicarbonate
Potassium first, then fluids, then insulin
Bicarbonate first, then insulin, then fluids
Dextrose first, then insulin, then potassium
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Fluids first, then insulin, watch potassium
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: The mantra is fluids first, then insulin, watch potassium; the two iatrogenic killers are hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the first step in managing DKA, even if the patient is acidotic?
options: IV fluids (0.9% saline) for aggressive rehydration
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: IV fluids (0.9% saline) for aggressive rehydration
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Step 1 is IV fluids (0.9% saline) — aggressive rehydration started even if acidotic; do not start insulin first.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: At what fixed rate is the IV insulin infusion run in DKA, and what is its purpose?
options: Variable rate titrated to glucose only
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: 0.1 units/kg/hr — switches off ketogenesis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: A fixed-rate IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr switches off ketogenesis; long-acting background insulin is continued and short-acting stopped.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L during DKA treatment, what is done?
options: Add 10% dextrose but keep insulin running to clear ketones
Stop the insulin to protect glucose
Halve the dextrose and stop insulin
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Add 10% dextrose but keep insulin running to clear ketones
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: When glucose <14 mmol/L, add 10% dextrose but keep insulin running to clear ketones; do not stop insulin to protect glucose.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A DKA patient has a serum K⁺ of 3.2 mmol/L. What is the correct action regarding insulin?
options: Senior review; do NOT start insulin until K⁺ is replaced
Start insulin immediately at standard rate
Start insulin and add no potassium
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Senior review; do NOT start insulin until K⁺ is replaced
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: With K⁺ <3.5, get senior review and do not start insulin until K⁺ is replaced, because insulin will crash it further and cause fatal arrhythmia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A DKA patient has a serum K⁺ of 4.5 mmol/L. How is potassium managed?
options: Add 40 mmol/L potassium to the fluids
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Add 40 mmol/L potassium to the fluids
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: For K⁺ 3.5–5.5, add 40 mmol/L potassium to the fluids; K⁺ >5.5 needs none and K⁺ <3.5 needs replacement before insulin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which patients are at higher risk of cerebral oedema in DKA, and what is the preventive principle?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Young patients/children; correct glucose slowly
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Cerebral oedema from over-rapid correction is higher risk in young patients/children; correct glucose slowly — the same principle as osmotic demyelination in SIADH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What are the resolution targets for DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Ketones <0.6 mmol/L, pH >7.3, HCO₃⁻ >15
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: DKA is resolved when ketones <0.6 mmol/L, pH >7.3 and HCO₃⁻ >15.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: How should transition from IV to subcutaneous insulin be managed in DKA?
options: Overlap subcutaneous insulin with the IV infusion by 30–60 min before stopping
Stop IV insulin and start subcutaneous the next day
Give double subcutaneous dose and stop IV
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Overlap subcutaneous insulin with the IV infusion by 30–60 min before stopping
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Transition to subcutaneous insulin by overlapping with the IV infusion for 30–60 min before stopping.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the role of bicarbonate in DKA?
options: Not routine — only if pH <7.0 under senior guidance; risks paradoxical intracellular acidosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Not routine — only if pH <7.0 under senior guidance; risks paradoxical intracellular acidosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Bicarbonate is not routine; it is only used if pH <7.0 under senior guidance because it risks paradoxical intracellular acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: During the insulin infusion in DKA, what should happen to the patient's usual insulins?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Continue long-acting; stop short-acting
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Long-acting background insulin is continued and short-acting is stopped during the infusion.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A patient with abdominal pain and vomiting in DKA could be misdiagnosed as having what, and what causes these symptoms?
options: A surgical abdomen; the ketoacidosis itself causes the GI symptoms
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: A surgical abdomen; the ketoacidosis itself causes the GI symptoms
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Vomiting and abdominal pain in DKA can mimic a surgical abdomen, but the ketoacidosis itself is the cause.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the defining biochemical picture of HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Marked hyperglycaemia + hyperosmolality + mild/no ketosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: HHS is marked hyperglycaemia + hyperosmolality + mild/no ketosis — the metabolic emergency of uncontrolled T2DM.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What are the two dangers of HHS?
options: Extreme osmolality → altered consciousness; hyperviscosity → thrombosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Extreme osmolality → altered consciousness; hyperviscosity → thrombosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: The two dangers of HHS are extreme osmolality leading to altered consciousness and hyperviscosity leading to thrombosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why does HHS produce no significant ketones or acidosis?
options: There is no insulin at all
Glucose is too low for ketogenesis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Residual insulin blocks ketogenesis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: In HHS, residual insulin blocks ketogenesis, so there is no acidosis and no ketones.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: How do DKA and HHS differ in onset and typical patient?
options: DKA = young T1 over hours; HHS = old T2 over days
DKA = old T2 over days; HHS = young T1 over hours
Both occur over hours in T1
Both occur over days in T2
DKA = elderly over weeks; HHS = young over minutes
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: DKA = young T1 over hours; HHS = old T2 over days
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: DKA is typically a young T1 patient over hours, whereas HHS is an older T2 patient over days, producing more extreme dehydration.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Compared with DKA, how do glucose and osmolality differ in HHS?
options: Both glucose and osmolality are much higher in HHS
Glucose is higher but osmolality is lower in HHS
Glucose is lower but osmolality is higher in HHS
Both are identical in DKA and HHS
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Both glucose and osmolality are much higher in HHS
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: In HHS, glucose (>30) and osmolality (>320 mOsm/kg) are much higher than in DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which bedside finding is ABSENT in HHS, contrasting it with DKA?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Kussmaul respiration and ketotic breath
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: HHS has no Kussmaul respiration and no ketotic breath — the bedside contrast with DKA, since there is no acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: An elderly patient presents with focal neurology and seizures that mimic a stroke, with very high glucose. What links the neurological picture in HHS?
options: Altered consciousness is directly proportional to osmolality
It is due to metabolic alkalosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Altered consciousness is directly proportional to osmolality
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: In HHS, altered consciousness is directly proportional to osmolality and can include focal neurology/seizures that mimic stroke.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What are the diagnostic criteria for HHS?
options: Glucose >30, osmolality >320, ketones <3/negative–trace, no significant acidosis
Glucose >20, osmolality normal, ketones trace, pH <7.2
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Glucose >30, osmolality >320, ketones <3/negative–trace, no significant acidosis
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: HHS criteria: glucose >30 mmol/L, osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, ketones <3 (negative–trace) and no significant acidosis (normal pH).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which formula is used to estimate osmolality in HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: 2(Na⁺) + glucose + urea
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Osmolality is estimated as 2(Na⁺) + glucose + urea.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why is troponin specifically included in the HHS workup?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: To detect a silent MI
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Troponin is included to detect a silent MI; the workup also includes U&E, FBC, CRP, cultures, ECG and CT head if ↓GCS/focal signs.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the commonest precipitant of HHS?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Infection
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Infection is the commonest precipitant of HHS, alongside MI, high-dose steroids, glucose-rich IV fluids and new T2DM presentation.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: How does the management emphasis of HHS differ from DKA?
options: Fluids are the priority; insulin is secondary and cautious
Insulin is the priority; fluids are secondary
Potassium is given before fluids in all cases
Insulin is given at full DKA dose first
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Fluids are the priority; insulin is secondary and cautious
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: In HHS, fluids are the priority and insulin is secondary and cautious, because residual insulin plus fluid correction does much of the work and patients crash their glucose easily.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: At what rate are IV fluids typically given in HHS, and over what period is the deficit replaced?
options: As fast as possible to correct osmolality quickly
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: 0.5–1 L/hr, replacing gradually over 24–48h
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Fluids are given at 0.5–1 L/hr (slower than DKA), replacing the deficit gradually over 24–48h, because rapid shifts cause cerebral oedema.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: When is insulin started in HHS, and at what rate?
options: Only if significant ketones; low rate ~0.05 units/kg/hr
Before fluids at full DKA dose
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Only if significant ketones; low rate ~0.05 units/kg/hr
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Insulin in HHS is cautious — a low rate (~0.05 units/kg/hr) started only if significant ketones are present; patients are insulin-sensitive and should not receive full DKA-dose insulin.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which management step is mandatory in HHS but not required in DKA, and why?
options: VTE prophylaxis with LMWH — hyperviscosity and dehydration give very high thrombosis risk
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: VTE prophylaxis with LMWH — hyperviscosity and dehydration give very high thrombosis risk
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Prophylactic LMWH is mandatory in HHS because hyperviscosity and dehydration create a very high thrombosis risk (MI, stroke, DVT/PE) — unique to HHS and not required in DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: How is potassium managed in HHS?
options: Same rule as DKA: K⁺ >5.5 none, 3.5–5.5 give 40 mmol/L, <3.5 senior review
Always given as a bolus regardless of level
Given before fluids in all cases
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Same rule as DKA: K⁺ >5.5 none, 3.5–5.5 give 40 mmol/L, <3.5 senior review
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Potassium follows the same rule as DKA: insulin shifts K⁺ into cells, so check before each step — K⁺ >5.5 none, 3.5–5.5 give 40 mmol/L in fluids, <3.5 senior review.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why must osmolality be corrected slowly in HHS?
options: A rapid drop causes cerebral oedema
Slow correction is needed to raise glucose
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: A rapid drop causes cerebral oedema
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Osmolality must be corrected slowly because a rapid drop causes cerebral oedema — the same 'treat slowly' principle as DKA (glucose) and SIADH (sodium).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the thrombosis complication described as 'the HHS signature'?
options: Hyperviscosity + dehydration → MI, stroke, DVT, PE, arterial thrombosis; LMWH mandatory
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Hyperviscosity + dehydration → MI, stroke, DVT, PE, arterial thrombosis; LMWH mandatory
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: The HHS signature is thrombosis: hyperviscosity plus severe dehydration causes MI, stroke, DVT, PE and arterial thrombosis, with higher mortality than DKA and mandatory LMWH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What causes iatrogenic cerebral oedema in HHS, and how is it prevented?
options: Over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality; prevent by correcting slowly over 24–48h
Excess LMWH; prevent by stopping anticoagulation
Too little fluid; prevent by rapid boluses
High-dose insulin only; prevent by stopping insulin entirely
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality; prevent by correcting slowly over 24–48h
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Iatrogenic cerebral oedema arises from over-rapid correction of glucose/osmolality (headache, ↓GCS, irritability) and is prevented by correcting slowly over 24–48h — the same mechanism as in DKA.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why does HHS carry a higher mortality than DKA?
options: It affects an older, comorbid population
It occurs only in young patients
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: It affects an older, comorbid population
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: HHS has higher mortality than DKA because of its older, comorbid population, with thrombosis as the signature risk.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A patient has glucose >30, osmolality >320, no ketones and a normal pH over several days. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: HHS
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Glucose >30 with osmolality >320, no ketones and a normal pH evolving over days is HHS (T2), distinguished from DKA by the absence of ketones/acidosis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: How does the dehydration of HHS compare to DKA?
options: More severe — often a 100–220 mL/kg deficit
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: More severe — often a 100–220 mL/kg deficit
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: HHS causes profound dehydration, often a 100–220 mL/kg deficit, more severe than DKA, with polyuria, polydipsia, dry mucous membranes and hypotension.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What blood glucose level defines hypoglycaemia ('four is the floor')?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: <4.0 mmol/L
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Hypoglycaemia is defined as blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L — 'four is the floor'.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the symptom fork as glucose falls in hypoglycaemia?
options: Autonomic only, with no neuroglycopenic phase
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Autonomic (early warning, <~3.3) → neuroglycopenic (<~2.8) → seizure/coma
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: The fork is autonomic symptoms (early warning, <~3.3) → neuroglycopenic (brain starving, <~2.8) → seizure/coma.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why are HbA1c targets relaxed from 48 to 53 once a patient is on ≥2 agents?
options: Hypoglycaemia is the rate-limiting risk of diabetes treatment
HbA1c becomes unreliable on multiple agents
It reduces the risk of DKA
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Hypoglycaemia is the rate-limiting risk of diabetes treatment
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Hypoglycaemia is the rate-limiting risk of diabetes treatment, which is why HbA1c targets are relaxed to 53 (vs 48) once on ≥2 agents.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: In the counter-regulatory defence cascade, which hormone is the first-line response after insulin falls?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Glucagon
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: As glucose falls, ↓insulin → ↑glucagon (first line) → ↑adrenaline (drives autonomic warning) → hours later ↑cortisol + ↑GH.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which hormone drives the autonomic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Adrenaline
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Adrenaline drives the autonomic warning symptoms; once defences are overwhelmed the brain is starved (neuroglycopenic phase).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the commonest cause of hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Insulin or sulfonylurea (diabetic treatment)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Diabetic treatment with insulin or sulfonylurea is the commonest cause of hypoglycaemia.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which oral antidiabetic agent causes hypoglycaemia, and why are these hypos prolonged?
options: Sulfonylureas — prolonged half-life means hypos can last hours/days
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Sulfonylureas — prolonged half-life means hypos can last hours/days
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Sulfonylureas are the oral agent that causes hypos, and their prolonged half-life means hypos can last hours/days.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: An insulinoma classically shows which biochemical finding?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Raised proinsulin:insulin ratio
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: An insulinoma is a β-cell tumour with a raised proinsulin:insulin ratio, cross-referenced with MEN1 (pancreatic tumours).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why does alcohol cause hypoglycaemia?
options: It impairs gluconeogenesis and exaggerates the insulin effect
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: It impairs gluconeogenesis and exaggerates the insulin effect
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Alcohol causes hypoglycaemia by impairing gluconeogenesis and exaggerating the insulin effect.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Hypoglycaemia is a feature of adrenal crisis in which condition, due to cortisol deficiency?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Addison's disease
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Addison's disease causes cortisol deficiency, and hypoglycaemia is a feature of adrenal crisis.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A patient with glucose 3.1 mmol/L has sweating, shaking, hunger and palpitations. Which phase is this, and what drives it?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Autonomic (warning) phase — adrenaline/glucagon release
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: At <~3.3 mmol/L, the autonomic (warning) phase produces sweating, shaking, hunger, anxiety, palpitations and nausea via adrenaline/glucagon release.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A patient with glucose 2.6 mmol/L has confusion, slurred speech and odd behaviour. Which phase is this, and what is the mechanism?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Neuroglycopenic phase — insufficient cerebral glucose
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: At <~2.8 mmol/L, the neuroglycopenic phase causes confusion, visual change, weakness, dizziness, slurred speech and odd behaviour from insufficient cerebral glucose.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why might a patient with recurrent hypos collapse without warning, and how do β-blockers contribute (the classic SBA trap)?
options: Impaired awareness blunts the autonomic warning; β-blockers mask autonomic symptoms
Recurrent hypos raise the glucose threshold for symptoms
Impaired awareness only affects neuroglycopenic symptoms
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Impaired awareness blunts the autonomic warning; β-blockers mask autonomic symptoms
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Recurrent hypos blunt the autonomic warning response (impaired awareness), and β-blockers mask the autonomic symptoms (though sweating is preserved) — a classic SBA trap.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Despite β-blockers masking autonomic symptoms, which symptom is preserved?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Sweating
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: With β-blockers, sweating is preserved while other adrenergic signs are blocked.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the single decision that determines hypoglycaemia management?
options: Is the patient on a β-blocker?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Can the patient swallow safely?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Management is determined by a single decision: can the patient swallow safely?

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A conscious patient who can swallow is treated for hypoglycaemia. What is the correct approach?
options: 15–20g fast-acting carb, recheck in 15 min, then long-acting carb
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: 15–20g fast-acting carb, recheck in 15 min, then long-acting carb
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Conscious patients who can swallow get 15–20g fast-acting carb (glucose tablets, GlucoGel/Dextrogel, fruit juice), recheck in 15 min (repeat if still <4), then a long-acting carb to prevent rebound.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Why is a long-acting carbohydrate given after the fast-acting treatment?
options: To prevent a rebound drop in glucose
To replace glycogen stores in the liver
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: To prevent a rebound drop in glucose
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: A long-acting carbohydrate (toast, biscuits) is given to prevent a rebound drop in glucose.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: An unconscious patient with hypoglycaemia in the community is given IM glucagon. How does it work, and when does it fail?
options: Mobilises hepatic glycogen; fails in alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition, prolonged fast
Directly raises glucose regardless of stores
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Mobilises hepatic glycogen; fails in alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition, prolonged fast
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: IM glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen but works only if glycogen stores are adequate; it fails in alcohol excess, liver failure, malnutrition and prolonged fasting, where IV glucose is essential.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: An unconscious alcoholic patient with hypoglycaemia is found to have no IV access initially. Once in hospital with IV access, what is the definitive treatment?
options: 20% glucose IV via a large vein — reliable regardless of glycogen stores
50% glucose via a small peripheral vein
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: 20% glucose IV via a large vein — reliable regardless of glycogen stores
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: In hospital with IV access, 20% glucose IV via a large vein (less tissue damage than 50%) is reliable regardless of glycogen stores; glucagon would be ineffective in an alcoholic with no glycogen.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A patient has a sulfonylurea-induced hypo that corrects with treatment. What is the appropriate disposition?
options: Admit for observation and prolonged glucose monitoring — do not discharge after a single correction
No monitoring needed once glucose is normal
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Admit for observation and prolonged glucose monitoring — do not discharge after a single correction
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Sulfonylureas have a long half-life, so hypos can recur for hours to days after apparent recovery; always admit for observation and prolonged monitoring, and do not discharge after a single correction.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: After recovery from a hypo, which step is recommended to identify and treat the cause?
options: Review insulin or sulfonylurea dose and assess meal pattern, exercise, alcohol, renal function
Start a β-blocker to control symptoms
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Review insulin or sulfonylurea dose and assess meal pattern, exercise, alcohol, renal function
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: After recovery, review the insulin or sulfonylurea dose, assess meal pattern/exercise/alcohol/renal function, consider HbA1c target relaxation if recurrent, and address impaired awareness with education and continuous glucose monitoring.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which set lists key NON-diabetic causes of hypoglycaemia?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Insulinoma (MEN1), Addison's, alcohol, liver failure
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Key non-diabetic causes are insulinoma (cross-ref MEN1), Addison's (cortisol deficiency), alcohol and liver failure, along with sepsis, malnutrition and GH deficiency.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the core mechanism underlying diabetes complications?
options: Chronic hyperglycaemia → endothelial damage + immune dysfunction
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Chronic hyperglycaemia → endothelial damage + immune dysfunction
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: The core mechanism is chronic hyperglycaemia causing endothelial damage (leaky, non-regenerating vessels) plus immune dysfunction (increased infection risk).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which lever prevents microvascular complications, and which prevents macrovascular (the prevention fork)?
options: Glycaemic control → microvascular; BP/statin/smoking cessation → macrovascular
BP control → microvascular; glycaemic control → macrovascular
Smoking cessation → microvascular; weight loss → macrovascular
Both are prevented by glycaemic control alone
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Glycaemic control → microvascular; BP/statin/smoking cessation → macrovascular
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: The prevention fork: glycaemic control prevents microvascular complications, while BP/statin/smoking cessation prevents macrovascular — both matter, different levers.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which three '-opathies' are the microvascular (glucose-driven) complications?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: The microvascular complications are the three -opathies: retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy, driven by glucose and prevented by glycaemic control.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the mechanism of diabetic retinopathy?
options: Retinal ischaemia → VEGF release → fragile new vessels → bleed/detachment
Direct glucose toxicity to the lens
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Retinal ischaemia → VEGF release → fragile new vessels → bleed/detachment
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Retinal ischaemia drives VEGF release, producing fragile new vessels that bleed or cause retinal detachment.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Fundoscopy shows dot-and-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates and cotton-wool spots. Which stage of retinopathy is this?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Background (R1)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Background (R1) retinopathy shows dot-and-blot haemorrhages (microaneurysms), hard exudates and cotton-wool spots (retinal infarcts).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: Which findings define pre-proliferative (R2) retinopathy?
options: Any change within 1 disc-diameter of macula
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA), venous beading/looping
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Pre-proliferative (R2) retinopathy shows IRMA and venous beading/looping.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A patient with proliferative diabetic retinopathy is treated with panretinal photocoagulation. How does PRP work?
options: Destroys ischaemic peripheral retina → ↓VEGF → regression of new vessels
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Destroys ischaemic peripheral retina → ↓VEGF → regression of new vessels
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: PRP destroys ischaemic peripheral retina, lowering VEGF and causing regression of the new vessels.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the treatment for diabetic macular oedema (maculopathy)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Diabetic macular oedema is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab); maculopathy is any retinopathy within 1 disc-diameter of the macula.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the cornerstone of prevention for diabetic retinopathy?
options: Annual dilated fundoscopy / digital retinal photography
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Annual dilated fundoscopy / digital retinal photography
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Annual dilated fundoscopy / digital retinal photography is the cornerstone of prevention for diabetic retinopathy.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the characteristic renal pathology of diabetic nephropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules (glomerulosclerosis)
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy develops >15 years after onset and is characterised by Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules (glomerulosclerosis).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: What is the earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: Microalbuminuria
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: Microalbuminuria is the earliest sign in the diagnostic triad of hypertension, albuminuria and declining eGFR.

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: On ACR staging, which value corresponds to microalbuminuria (A2)?
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: 3–30 mg/mmol
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.explanation: ACR staging: A1 <3 (normal), A2 3–30 (microalbuminuria), A3 >30 (macroalbuminuria).

conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.question: A normotensive diabetic patient has microalbuminuria. What is the first-line management, and why is it used despite normal BP?
options: ACE inhibitor/ARB — renoprotective, reduces intraglomerular pressure
conditions__ENDOCRINOLOGY__Diabetic Comp.answer: ACE inhibitor/ARB — renoprotective, reduces intraglomerular pressure
